retrieved_contexts: ['Aliphatic polyesters are extensively applied in agriculture, medicine, automotive manufacturing, packaging, etc. attributable to their inherent biocompatibility and biodegradability [1-5]. Catalyst-mediated ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of cyclic esters (e.g. lactides, lactones) enables efficient synthesis of aliphatic polyesters, offering polymers with predetermined molecular weights, narrow polydispersity, and well-defined microstructures [6-14]. Among these polymers, polylactic acid (PLA), synthesized from sustainable resources like corn or sugar beets, has attracted significant research interest due to its versatile biomedical applications and potential as a sustainable replacement for conventional petroleum-based thermoplastics [15]. In contrast, poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) exhibits a markedly slower degradation behavior, making it especially advantageous for extended-duration therapeutic delivery compared to other biodegradable polymer [16]. Metal-based catalysts, enzymes, and organic compounds are all viable options for catalyzing ROP. The exceptional catalytic performance of metal-based systems enables their dominant application in cyclic ester ROP, particularly through their unparalleled ability to regulate polyester structural parameters such as molecular weight distribution, dispersity (Đ), chain microstructure, and stereochemical regularity [8-11]. Recently, organocatalysts have attracted growing interest in ROPs owing to their multiple advantages, including commercial availability, high tolerance to moisture and oxygen, and negligible metal contamination [17-25]. A breakthrough was achieved in 2001 when Hedrick and Waymouth’s team pioneered the use of organocatalysts for lactide ROP [26]. Since then, numerous organocatalysts such as bases [27-29], acids [30-33], (thio)ureas [34], squaramides [35], exhibit exceptional catalytic activity in ROP processes. The thiourea/base bifunctional catalyst exhibits remarkable selectivity and activity by mediating intermolecular hydrogen bonding with both the monomer and propagating species [36]. A series of organic bases including amines [37], N-heterocyclic carbenes [38], 1,8-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]undec-7-ene [39], alkoxides [40, 41], phosphazenes [42-44] and cyclopropenimines [45] have been successfully employed as cooperative catalysts with (thio)urea derivatives. Notably, the combination of alkoxides and (thio)urea exhibits both hyperactive and selective characteristics in polymerizing diverse monomers including LA, δ-VL, ε-CL and cyclic carbonates [40, 41]. Despite the existence of numerous (thio)ureas catalysts, cyclic (thio)ureas have not yet been exploited in ROPs.', 'Currently, the synthesis methods of PLA mainly include direct condensation of lactic acid and ring-opening polymerization of lactide. Lactic acid reacts by condensation to yield a low-molecular weight polymer, which, for the most cases, is unusable for any applications unless external coupling agents are used to increase the molecular weight of the PLA.25 The PLA prepared by ring-opening polymerization of lactide has high molecular weight and purity. It was found that PLA with high molecular weight was easy to polymerize in the presence of tin, zinc, aluminum, and other heavy metal catalysts, furthermore, tin (II) and zinc yielding the purest polymers. These catalysts were applied extensively by researchers due to their covalent metal-oxygen bonds and free p or d orbitals.26 Nowadays, nano-ZnO was used as a green catalyst to avoid cytotoxicity of many organometallic compounds, including Sn (Oct)2.27 Zhen et al28 synthesized PLA by ring-opening polymerization with D, L-lactide as monomer, and zinc oxide pillared organic saponite as green catalyst. Zheng et al29 prepared PLA/amidated graphene oxide (AGO) nanocomposites by reactive extrusion process with L-lactide as raw material, zinc lactate as catalyst, hexamethylene diisocyanate as chain extender, and AGO as nano-nucleating agent prepared by amidation. The results showed that the AGO could significantly improve the crystallinity, mechanical properties, and thermal stability of PLA; furthermore, kinetics studies revealed that the polymerization reaction model presented the second-order reaction, and the apparent rate constant of PLA/AGO nanocomposites was 7.612 × 103 g/mol/min. In the current work, the difference from the previous work was to graft PLA molecules on the surface of phosphorylated graphene oxide (PGO) at a large density, which enhanced interfacial compatibility and dispersibility of GO in PLA composites. The novelty of this work was that PGO was prepared by in-situ phosphorylation method, and phosphorylated graphene oxide-poly (lactic acid) (PGO-PLLA) was synthesized via lactide ring-opening polymerization with nano-ZnO as catalyst. In order to improve the toughness of PLA, PGO-PLLA was applied in PLA as the fillers. The effect of PGO-PLLA on the crystallization, rheological behavior, and performance of PLA was investigated, respectively. Proteinase K was purchased from Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany.', 'These new complexes do not require PPNCl or excess epoxide for efficient initiation. Aliphatic polyesters are essential as biodegradable materials with a broad range of applications including packaging [1], [2], electronics [3] and medical devices [4], [5]. In particular, poly(lactic acid) (PLA) has many commercial applications due to its physical and mechanical properties. Ring-opening polymerisation (ROP) is one of the most efficient routes to prepare PLA with targeted material properties, which is achieved through careful control of the polymer microstructure. Some of the most powerful catalyst systems are homogeneous organometallic complexes, and aluminium-salen catalysts have garnered particular focus thanks to high catalyst activities, the low toxicity of the metal and a high level of control over the polymer microstructure [6], [7]. Most of the highly effective aluminium catalysts for rac-lactide (rac-LA) ROP feature alkoxide initiating groups. However, recent studies by Thomas, Maron et al. revealed that salen-AlCl catalysts, which are generally poor initiators for ROP [8], could achieve high catalyst activities when combined with an epoxide and an onium salt co-catalyst to generate an Al-alkoxide in situ (Fig. 1) [9]. This method of initiating ROP and ring-opening copolymerisations has gathered attention [10], [11], [12], and epoxides have been utilised as in situ activators for rac-LA ROP with porphyrin-AlCl [13], Sn(octanoate)2 [14], and salen-FeCl systems [15], [16], [17]. The homogeneous Al-Cl catalysts generally require the presence of a co-catalyst such as bis(triphenylphosphoranylidene)ammonium chloride (PPNCl) for efficient ROP initiation. These onium salts are proposed to enhance initiation through Lewis base coordination to the metal centre (Fig. 1, Step A), increasing the nucleophilicity of the metal-chloride bond towards epoxide ring-opening. This Lewis base coordination is also proposed to enhance the nucleophilicity of the metal-alkoxide bond towards the ring-opening of rac-LA, facilitating propagation [9]. The interaction between the catalyst and the co-catalyst is likely to occur through a reversible equilibrium (Step A), with the pentacoordinate Al complex providing a vacant site for epoxide coordination and activation towards nucleophilic attack (Fig. 1, Step B). On the basis of detailed mechanistic studies using a salen-AlCl/propylene oxide (PO)/PPNCl catalyst system based on the Jacobsen ligand, Thomas, Maron et al. proposed that initiation occurs through the formation of a highly nucleophilic hexacoordinate aluminate complex (Fig. 1, Step C) [9]. Notably, neutral aluminium chloride and aluminium alkoxide complexes were suggested to be inactive under the conditions investigated. The experimental set-up therefore involved overnight reaction of the Jacobsen-AlCl catalyst with PPNCl in PO solvent, to form the active initiator species prior to the addition of rac-LA. These insightful studies highlighted the ability of salen-AlCl species to efficiently polymerise rac-LA at ambient temperature. However, translation of this system to an industrial set-up may be limited by the need for excess epoxide (PO is highly toxic), an expensive PPNCl co-catalyst, and an overnight pre-activation of the catalyst components prior to the addition of rac-LA. Modification of the ligand scaffold offers the potential to alter the electronics at the metal centre and therefore influence the initiation mechanism and propagation rate.', 'The commercial manufacture of poly (L-lactic acid) relies heavily on organometallic catalysts. The most popular of them is stannous octanoate [Sn(Oct)2] [7], but the problem of trace metals is still a concern. Recent years have seen a lot of research on enzyme-catalysed ring-opening polymerisation of lactide, but so far the findings have been less than ideal from a yield and reaction time perspective. Mena et al. [8] employed immobilised Candida antarctica lipase as a catalyst and [BMIM] [PF6] ion solution as a solvent to produce low polymerisation PLLA at 65 ℃ for 11 days with a yield of only 29.1%. Clearly, this does not satisfy the production requirements. In addition, the majority of organic solvents are used in the traditional polymerisation process, which is neither conducive to human assimilation nor consistent with the concept of green chemistry in the preparation of drug carriers. In recent years, supercritical carbon dioxide (Sc-CO2) has replaced organic solvents in an increasing number of polymerisation reactions. This is because Sc-CO2 is inexpensive, nontoxic, and noncombustible, and it can be easily separated from the final product by systematic decompression [9]. This opens up new processing routes for the preparation of polymeric drug composites and is thus widely used in polymerisation reactions. In this study, Sc-CO2 was used as the solvent and erythritol as the initiator for the enzymatic synthesis of PLLA and its copolymers. About 80% of poly (L-lactic acid) with a porous structure was obtained after 24 hours of reaction time. By co-polymerisation modification with GA, 4s-PLGA with a faster degradation rate and enhanced hydrophilicity was subsequently synthesised while retaining its porous structure. However, PLGA derived through commercial random copolymerization still has issues such as inadequate mechanical strength and a rapid degradation rate. Several studies have demonstrated that the mechanical properties and degradation rate of the block copolymerization product PLLA-PGA are superior to those of the random copolymerization product PLGA [10]. Using the aforementioned eco-friendly method, the block copolymerization product 4s-PLLA-PGA, which is more suitable for medical implants, was synthesised in this study. Experimental materials', 'DFT investigation of the ROP of cyclic esters. Polylactic acid (PLA) has a unique combination of properties that make it suitable for various applications ranging from single use plastics to agricultural commodities, up to biomedical materials and a circular economy [[1], [2], [3]]. Indeed, PLA is produced from renewable feedstocks, it is biodegradable, and it exhibits interesting physical and mechanical properties comparable to traditional olefin-based polymers [[4], [5], [6], [7]]. The ring opening polymerization (ROP) is the widest used method for PLA synthesis, employing lactide (LA) monomers as starting materials. Given the chiral nature of lactic acid, LAs can exist as three different diastereoisomers: D-LA (R,R), L-LA (S,S) and meso-LA (R,S) and the stereoselectivity plays a crucial role in the ROP of cyclic monomers for the synthesis of polymers because the tacticity of the polymer determines its crystallinity, mechanical and rheological properties [8,9]. Depending on the starting monomer, several microstructures of PLA can be obtained ranging from isotactic PDLA and PLLA, isotactic stereoblock PLA, to atactic, heterotactic and syndiotactic PLA. The first two microstructures can be produced starting from the enantiopure D- and L-LA monomers [10,11] or from their racemic mixture (rac-LA) by using a stereoselective polymerization [12,13]. The isotactic stereoblock PLA is particularly interesting because the stereocomplexation of the enantiomeric blocks [1] affords higher Tm (up to 30-50 °C) compared to the enantiopure PLLA and PDLA. Although this microstructure may be achieved by the sequential addition of the enantiopure L-LA and D-LA employing a fast and living catalyst, the use of stereoselective catalyst starting from rac-LA feed [[14], [15], [16]] would be preferable although it imposes a non-trivial chemical challenge. Finally, the syndiotactic microstructure results in a semicrystalline polymer [17] and can be synthesized from meso-LA still adopting stereoselective catalysis [18]. In the last two decades, hundreds of homogenous metal-based catalysts have been synthesized to afford stereocontrolled ROP of rac-LA. To date, Salen based catalysts (Scheme 1, A) represent a worldwide recognized platform offering several advantages in controlling the stereoselectivity during ROP of lactides [19]. Their success mainly resides in two factors: a) the simple and cheap synthesis, reflecting also in an easy tunability due to a wide range of variously substituted commercial precursors; b) the great compatibility with various metal centres because these ligands consist of two salicylaldimine moieties connected by a bridge, which provides a unique chiral environment around the metal centre. Their most important characteristics are the steric and electronic properties achieved by modifying the substituents on the salicylaldimine moieties or the bridge (see R1, R2, R3, R4 and X, in Scheme 1, A). This tuning enables the control of the reactivity and selectivity of the catalyst, leading to precise control over the formation of stereoisomeric configurations in the resulting polymers [19,20]. The term “bridge” refers to the part of the Salen ligands that connects the two nitrogen atoms and several Salen based catalysts with the central metal (M) = Al resulted to be very stereoselective. As a matter of fact, the first stereoselective catalyst in the rac-LA ROP was synthesized by Spassky [21] by using the enantiopure chiral SalenBinaphtyl-Al catalyst (B, Scheme 1) that polymerizes primarily the d-lactide (88 % of optical purity at the 19 % of conversion). Then, Feijen reported a prevalence of l-lactide polymerization in the rac-LA mixture just varying the bridge of Al based Salen catalysts (C, Scheme 1) [22]. Finally, the effect of the ortho substituents (see R2 and R3 in A, Scheme 1) was crucial in inferring stereoselectivity to the catalyst, starting with the pioneering works of Nomura [23] (D, Scheme 1), up to recent machine-learning driven studies of Tong (E, Scheme 1) [20]. Despite this, aluminium based Salen catalysts suffer from severe problems of activity. Indeed, reactions are often conducted over several hours at high temperatures. For this reason, other trivalent transition metals have been incorporated into Salen ligands affording catalysts more active in lactide ROP. Each metal centre imparts distinct reactivity and selectivity, allowing for fine-tuning of the polymerization process and the resulting polymer properties. For example, the use of different metal centres with the same Salen ligands has been shown to promote in different ways the formation of isotactic PLA. Williams explored the stereoselective polymerization of lactide using La, Y and Lu-based phosphasalen catalysts demonstrating how the differences in the metal dimensions are crucial in determining the stereocontrol [24]. In addition, the corresponding order of reaction rates is inversely related to metallic covalent radius (La = 2.07 Å > Y = 1.90 Å > Lu = 1.87 Å) that, therefore, affects both catalyst stereoselectivity and activity. However, despite several efforts, and the development of different catalysts able to achieve full lactide conversion in minutes rather than days, enantiopure Salen aluminium based catalysts still remain the most stereoselective in the rac-LA ROP by enantiomorphic-site control (ES) [16,25]. The objective of this work is to investigate, by Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations, the origin of stereoselectivity in the ROP of rac-lactide promoted by enantiopure complexes to produce isotactic polylactic acid (PLA) with the aim of understanding the role played by the central metal atom on the stereoselectivity of this reaction. Considering the aforementioned discussion and the previously reported experimental data, the chiral (R,R)-cyclohexylsalen based catalyst [22] (C, Scheme 1) was selected as the ligand to investigate the stereoselectivity of rac-LA ROP. The ligands and metals chosen were preferred over others due to the abundant experimental data available in the literature on ROP of LA catalysed by Y [25] and Al-based systems. In addition, the inclusion of Sc and La-based catalysts, despite the lack of experimental data, was chosen to further evaluate the effect of central metal size (M). We focused on the LA polymerization on the LM-OCH3 bond in order to distinguish the net effect of the ligand/metal combination on the ES model cleaned up from the growing chain effects. Details of computational approach used here are reported in the Supporting Information and the whole methodology has been already tested in stereoselective rac-LA, meso-LA and methyl glycolide polymerization [[26], [27], [28]] as well as olefin polymerization metal catalysed [29]. The origin of the activities and enantioselectivities depending on the M atoms has been further investigated by using a molecular descriptor based on the buried volume percentage (%VBur) [30,31] and a non-covalent interaction (NCI) analysis [32], matched with the calculation of significant electronic parameters, including HOMO (Highest Occupied Molecular Orbital), LUMO (Lowest Unoccupied Molecular Orbital), chemical potential, chemical hardness and electrophilicity.', 'Crystallization behavior of fully biodegradable poly(lactic acid)/poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) blends Enhanced crystallization rate and mechanical properties of poly(l-lactic acid) by stereocomplexation with four-armed poly(ϵ-caprolactone)-block-poly(d-lactic acid) diblock copolymer Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is one of the most extensively investigated and utilized bio-based polymers due to its ideal attractive properties such as thermoplasticity, processability, renewability, biocompatibility, good mechanical properties, and low environmental impact.1-4 PLA, a kind of linear aliphatic thermoplastic polyester derived from renewable resources, is considered as a solution to relieve the dependence on traditional petroleum-based plastics. It can be produced either by catalytic ring opening polymerization of lactides (lactic acid dimers) or by condensation polymerization of lactic acid monomers which are obtained from the fermentation of sugar feed stocks.5-7 Lactic acid exists as two enantiomeric forms, the naturally occurring L (−) configuration and the D (+) configuration. Therefore, the corresponding enantiomeric polymers are produced by the conservation of the chiral centers.8 PLA with high strength and high modulus can be easily processed by a number of processing methods (e.g., foaming, extrusion, injection molding, blow molding, fiber spinning, film forming, and compression molding)9-11 to yield articles to be used in biocompatible/bioabsorbable market, for example, surgical implants, sutures drug delivery systems, and dentistry.12, 13 Moreover, lots of efforts have been currently made to use PLA as engineering material, for example, automobile components, building materials, and electric appliance bodies.11, 14 However, the high price, inherent brittleness and thermal instability of PLA currently limit its application.15-17 Considerable efforts have been made to improve these shortcomings of PLA.18-21', "Poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) is a biocompatible, biodegradable, aliphatic polyester derived from renewable resources with rigidity and clarity similar to poly(ethylene terephthalate), which has been widely used in the fields of biomedicine.1-3 Despite its excellent balance of properties, the broad application of PLLA as a commodity polymer material has been restricted significantly by the long and expensive synthesis process.4 Until now, industrial high molecular weight PLLA has been synthesized via a two-step route: The first one is condensation of lactic acid leading to oligomers, followed by depolymerization of the oligomers leading to lactide. The second is ring-opening polymerization of lactide to obtain PLLA.5, 6 To reduce the cost of PLLA, many approaches, such as solution polymerization,7, 8 melt polymerization,9 solid state polymerization,10, 11 chain extension of PLLA with low molecular weights (1-3 × 104 g/mol),12, 13 have been developed to synthesize PLLA. Recently, Dusselier et al.4 have developed a direct zeolite-based catalytic process, which converted lactic acid into lactide directly. This method can avoid both racemization and side-product formation during synthesizing lactide. Unfortunately, organic solvents or catalyst might be used or the energy consumption was high in those strategies. Therefore, there are still challenges in the large-scale production of PLLA economically and environmentally friendly. In addition, the inherently brittleness, as evidenced by short elongation at break, also greatly limits the widespread applications of PLLA.14-18 Many strategies, such as copolymerization19, 20 and blending21, 22 have been developed to improve PLLA's ductile properties. Blending PLLA with other flexible polymers provides a practical and economic way of toughening PLLA,23 however, sometimes, PLLA might not be miscible with some of these polymers, with their blends resulting in phase-separated morphologies that eventually lead to the deterioration of properties.24, 25 Copolymerization is the approach that mixes the polymer in molecular level leading to a good compatibility. Therefore, copolymerization with other monomer and soft polymer might be an alternative approach. Various biobased and petroleum-based monomers or polymers, such as polyethylene glycol26, 27 and caprolactone28, 29 have been introduced to PLLA backbone to improve its toughness. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, low cost and large-scale production of PLLA copolymers are not commercially available up to now. So, it is significant to explore ductile PLLA copolymers with the potential prospect of low cost.", 'Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is well-known biodegradable polyester that has been studied extensively for tissue engineering and drug delivery system and has been widely used in human medicine. Many of the PLA properties are compared to those polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), polystyrene (PS), and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) (such as stiffness, tensile strength, and gas permeability), turning PLA into a potential substitutes to petroleum-based products such as trash bags, table utensils, films, paper coating, fiber, and cloth [1]. PLA is made from lactic acid produced via fermentation of carbohydrate crops such as corn, wheat, barley, cassava, and sugar cane [2]. It is made from L- or D-lactic acid through two procedures: (a) ring-opening polymerization, a solvent free process where lactic acid is first transferred to a low-molecular weight poly(lactic acid), followed by depolymerization to lactide (fluctuating dimer), and then polymerized continuously to a controlled high-molecular weight polymer through a catalytic ring-opening process [3]; (b) direct condensation polymerization, a catalyzed process where the water generated during the polymerization is removed by an azeotropic dehydration process, producing a high-molecular weight polymer [4]. The products from both procedures present similar properties. PLA-based polymer is completely degraded under compost conditions. Although it has a hydrophobic characteristic (non-water soluble), microbes in marine environments can degrade it into water and carbon dioxide [5], and hydrolyzes more promptly than polyhydroxyalkanoates in anaerobic condition [6]. The first step of PLA degradation does not require microbial action and is characterized by the cleavage of the ester linkages to lactic acid by a temperature and humidity-enhanced process. Then lactic acid is biodegraded by microbes into carbon dioxide, methane, and water. The complete degradation of PLA by hydrolysis in the environment takes from several months to 2 years, which is relatively fast compared to 500 to 1,000 years for petroleum-based polymers such as PE, PP and PS. However, for some specific applications, PLA is still more expensive than petroleum-based products and other properties such as, low melt viscosity (for extrusion process), impact strength, and heat distortion temperature are frequently inadequate for various end-user applications. Properties of PLA can be modified by polymer blending techniques, acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS) was incorporated into PLA to improve PLA’s impact properties [7], thermoplastic starch (TPS) to enhance PLA’s biodegradability [8-13], poly (butylene succinate) (PBS) to improve PLA’s flexural properties [14], PS to reduce PLA’s cost [15, 16], and poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) [17-19] to improve PLA’s melt properties.', 'Poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) is a synthetic and biodegradable aliphatic polyester. Increasing concerns regarding sustainability of polymer materials have resulted in greater focus on renewable and biodegradable polymers derived from biomass. PLLA is a thermoplastic which has useful properties and is derived from sugars. PLLA is being explored as a potential alternative to petroleum derived polymers, such as poly(olefin)s, poly(ester)s and poly(styrene) [1-5]. PLLA has good mechanical properties and can be either rigid or elastic in nature. The polymer finds many applications, especially, as fibers, films and transparent thermoplastics in packaging, consumer goods and many articles of short life-cycle use. Synthesis of high molecular weight PLLA can be accomplished by two methods, namely, (1) dehydrative melt-polycondensation of l(+)-lactic acid (LA) [6-9] and (2) ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of a cyclic dimer (lactide) [10]. The method of choice is ROP of cyclic lactide and is used for the large-scale production of PLLA [11, 12]. This method involves the polymerization of LA to low molecular weight oligomers which is then depolymerized to a cyclic dimer (lactide), purified by melt crystallization followed by ROP to PLLA (M w > 50,000) using a suitable catalyst. Melt phase polycondensation of LA has been widely studied [13-16]. Melt phase polycondensation methods have several drawbacks, such as inability to achieve high molecular weights due to competitive formation of cyclic oligomers at higher temperatures, undesirable side reactions leading to broad polydispersity color, racemization and difficulties in removal of water effectively from a high viscosity melt. Solid-state polycondensation is another alternative method for the synthesis of high molecular weight PLLA. However, the low melting point of lactic acid oligomers and the slow reaction rate have limited the scope of this method for the synthesis of PLLA [17-19].', 'PLA can be synthesized by two reaction mechanisms: The first is a commonly commercialized one to ring-open polymerization of the intermediate lactide by step-growth condensation polymerization.8 The second one is also a commercialized route, established by Mitsui Chemicals Co. (Japan), wherein lactic acid and catalyst are azeotropically dehydrated in a refluxing, high boiling point, aprotic solvent such as diphenyl ether, under reduced pressure9 to obtain PLA with weight-average molecular weight (Mw) greater than 3.0 × 105. Kazuhiko et al.10 reported rapid synthesis of PLA by direct polycondensation of lactic acid (LA) using microwave irradiation at 200°C, 30 mmHg for 30 min with various catalysts such as Bronsted/Lewis acids/metals/metal triflates. Among the catalysts, SnCl2/p-TsOH binary catalyst system gave PLA with molecular weight of 16,000. Bharatkumar et al.11 synthesized PLA with molecular weight of 14,875 using cellulose sulfuric acid in m-xylene at 180°C for 24 h. Low-molecular weight PLA has substandard mechanical properties and even the low molecular weight precondensates is of interest for the preparation of biodegradable glues or lacquers, because the \uf8ffOH and \uf8ffCOOH end groups allow crosslinking with suitable inorganic or organic multivalent additives.12 Our aim is to prepare low-molecular weight polylactic acid. Since polyaniline (PANI) salts are mild polymer-based acid catalyst, in this work, lactic acid is polymerized to low-molecular weight polylactic acid using PANI salts.', 'FTIR, NMR and SEC methodologies have been applied for yield monitoring and molecular weight estimations. Polylactic acid (PLA) is one of the most promising biodegradable polymers due to its processability, origin of renewable sources, biodegradability and mechanical behavior. PLA can be polymerized by via direct polycondensation of lactic acid or via ring-opening polymerization (ROP). Raquez et al. have nicely reviewed the chemical aspects of reactive extrusion (REX) processes applied to the synthesis and modification of PLA-based materials [1]. In this regard, REX combines thermal, mechanical and chemical variables in a single equipment, considering a cost-effective technology. Jacobsen et al. explored the combination of a twin screw extruder and static mixer for the synthesis of high molecular weight PLA showing it was possible to reduce the time of synthesis up to 80% [2]. Furthermore, Liu et al. have also studied the use of twin-screw extruders for the synthesis of PLA, despite molecular weight obtained has been of intermediate size [3]. Dubey et al. have combined alternative energies such as ultrasound and microwave obtaining an increase in the number-average molecular weight of up to 119.7%, showing the benefits of using ultrasound during the reactive extrusion process to also accelerate the kinetics of the reaction [4]. Since polyaniline (PANI) salts are mild polymer-based acid catalyst, in this work, lactic acid is polymerized to low-molecular weight polylactic acid using PANI salts.', 'Biopolymers have attracted great attention as substitute materials for petrochemical-based products because of their unique advantages like biodegradability and origin from renewable feedstock [1-3]. Polylactic acid (PLA) is a biodegradable, recyclable, biocompatible and thermoplastic material. It is aliphatic polyester derived from renewable resources (i.e., corn starch or sugarcanes) by bacterial fermentation used to produce lactic acid [4]. PLA and its derivatives have the potentiality to be used in the field of pharmacology and textile industries [5, 6]. PLA can be synthesized by two ways. Most frequently, ring-opening polymerization of lactide is a suitable way to obtain polylactic acid with high molecular weights [7]. But lactide is expensive since it is difficult to be manufactured. As an alternative synthetic route, a direct polycondensation can be employed for preparation of PLA. However, only low molecular weights of the PLA product can be obtained in directly polycondensation, as a result, little use of the product can be found.', 'Nowadays, most of the raw materials used in the manufacture of polymer materials come from petrochemicals. The gradual replacement of petroleum-based materials with renewable resources ones is part of the society major concerns: national independence with regard to the supply of raw materials, preservation of the environment, reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. Among the different biobased materials available on the market, poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is becoming more and more competitive and accounts for about a quarter of biodegradable bioplastic production. Indeed, the industry has made many investments in this sector, leading to a reduction in its production and implementation costs. This biodegradable and biocompatible polyester is synthesized either by direct polycondensation of lactic acid, resulting from the fermentation of agroresources, or by Ring Opening Polymerization (ROP) of lactide, a cyclic ester derived from oligomerization-cyclization of lactic acid. Although the second synthetic route requires an additional step, it allows the formation of poly(lactic acid) of higher molar masses and is most commonly employed in industry [1]. The ROP requires the use of a catalyst which ring-opens the lactide and initiates its polymerization. Among ROP methods, coordination-insertion polymerization monitored by metal-based catalysts is a powerful and versatile technique, allowing access to well-defined high molar mass polymers. A wide range of metals are well-known to afford highly active catalytic systems for this reaction, such as tin [2], aluminium and group 13 metals [3], zinc and main group metals [4], group 4 [5], group 3 and lanthanides [6]. Among the commercial lactides, l-lactide (l-LA), resulting from the cyclization of the l- isomer of lactic acid, is particularly interesting since it leads, regardless of the type of polymerization initiator used, to 100% isotactic poly(lactic acid) (PLLA). Finally, the dimensional stability of these new PLLA hybrid materials under heat was herein qualitatively evaluated.', 'Poly(l-lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), approved by US Food and Drug Administration for medical use, for example, implants for interior bone fixation, artificial skin, tissue scaffolds, and drug delivery,1 is the most widely employed biodegradable and bioassimilable polymers both experimentally and clinically.2-4 The control to its structure and composition is a permanent topic for meeting various needs, especially sequence and/or stereo-control, which is a powerful tool for creating PLGAs with the precisely tuned behavior and became an exciting new frontier recently. The primary mechanism for synthesizing high molecular weight polylactic acid (PLA) via ring-opening polymerization (ROP) is the **coordination-insertion mechanism**, mediated by metal-based catalysts such as tin (Sn), zinc (Zn), aluminum (Al), or titanium (Ti) complexes. This mechanism involves:  
1. **Coordination** of the cyclic ester monomer (e.g., lactide) to the metal center of the catalyst, activating the monomer for nucleophilic attack.  
2. **Insertion** of the monomer into the metal-oxygen bond (e.g., M–OR), followed by chain propagation through repeated monomer insertion.  

The **coordination-insertion mechanism is preferred** because it enables:  
- **Controlled polymerization**: Precise regulation of molecular weight, low polydispersity (Đ), and well-defined chain microstructures (e.g., stereochemical regularity), critical for tailoring PLA’s mechanical and thermal properties.  
- **High efficiency**: Metal catalysts (e.g., Sn(Oct)₂, Al-salen complexes) exhibit exceptional activity, enabling rapid polymerization under mild conditions.  
- **Stereoselectivity**: Metal centers (e.g., chiral Al or Ti complexes) enforce enantiomorphic-site control, producing isotactic or stereoblock PLA with enhanced crystallinity and performance.  
- **Avoidance of side reactions**: Unlike direct polycondensation, which often yields low-molecular-weight PLA due to competing cyclization or racemization, coordination-insertion minimizes undesired side processes.  
- **Scalability**: Compatibility with industrial processes like reactive extrusion, where metal catalysts (e.g., Ti oxo-clusters) facilitate solvent-free, continuous production of high-molecular-weight PLA.  

This mechanism’s superiority over organocatalytic or enzymatic ROP lies in its unparalleled ability to balance catalytic efficiency, structural control, and scalability, making it indispensable for synthesizing high-performance PLA.

This route is preferred because it avoids the formation of water byproducts associated with polycondensation, allowing for the synthesis of high molecular weight polymers (Mn > 100,000 Da) with controlled stereochemistry and narrow polydispersity.

IntroductionWithin the frame of sustainable development, aliphatic polyesters based on lactic or glycolic acid and their copolymers have been extensively investigated due to their biocompatibility and biodegradability [1]. It is generally accepted that PLGA demonstrates desirable mechanical properties, good toxicological safety and tuneable degradation rates which are affected by several physical and chemical parameters, such as initial pH, ionic strength and temperature of external medium, the molar ratio of monomers, enantiomeric form, initial molecular weight, crystallinity and specimen size [3], [4]. This would suggest the involvement of either intracellular enzymes or enzymes secreted from bacteria, yeast or fungi [7]. The biodegradation rate of Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) copolymers **inversely correlates with the lactide-to-glycolide (L/G) ratio**. Specifically:  

1. **Higher Glycolide Content (Lower L/G Ratio)**:  
   - Accelerates degradation due to increased hydrophilicity, reduced steric hindrance (glycolate ester bonds are less hindered than lactate esters), and enhanced susceptibility to hydrolysis.  
   - Example: PLGA 50/50 (L/G) degrades in 1–2 months, while PLGA 75/25 degrades in 4–5 months, and PLGA 85/15 in 5–6 months (Context 2).  
   - Enzymes like *Candida antarctica* lipase exhibit substrate specificity, with degradation rates directly proportional to glycolic acid content (Context 1).  

2. **Crystallinity and Hydrophobicity**:  
   - Higher lactide content (higher L/G ratio) increases hydrophobicity and crystallinity, slowing water penetration and hydrolysis (Context 3). However, in later stages, crystalline regions with high glycolide content may paradoxically decelerate degradation (Context 3).  

3. **Enzymatic Influence**:  
   - Microbial/enzymatic degradation (e.g., lipases, esterases) significantly accelerates PLGA breakdown, with enzymes like *C. antarctica* lipase showing up to **25-fold faster ester cleavage** compared to abiotic hydrolysis (Context 1).  

4. **Acidic By-Products**:  
   - Faster degradation at lower L/G ratios releases acidic by-products (e.g., glycolic acid), which can autocatalyze hydrolysis but may also provoke inflammatory responses in biomedical applications (Contexts 2, 12).  

In summary, **PLGA degradation rate increases as glycolide content rises (lower L/G ratio)**, driven by enhanced hydrophilicity, reduced steric effects, and enzymatic activity, though crystallinity and by-product accumulation may modulate this trend.

The 'supercooling window' in the context of Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) of Polycaprolactone (PCL) refers to the temperature range between PCL's melting point (Tm ≈ 60°C) and its crystallization temperature during cooling. This window is critical because PCL, being semi-crystalline, requires precise thermal control to avoid incomplete crystallization or partial melting during SLS processing. 

In SLS, rapid cooling can trap the polymer in a supercooled state, leading to insufficient crystallization and weak, porous microstructures. Proper management of the supercooling window ensures adequate time for molecular reorganization and crystallization, which is essential for achieving dense, mechanically robust scaffolds. Context [4] highlights that post-treatment (re-melting at 65°C followed by controlled re-solidification) mitigates these issues by allowing complete melting and recrystallization within this window, thereby improving filament quality and mechanical stability. Thus, optimizing the supercooling window is vital to prevent structural defects and enhance the performance of SLS-fabricated PCL scaffolds.
reference: The supercooling window is the temperature difference between the melting point (Tm) and the crystallization temperature (Tc). For PCL in SLS, a wide window is critical to prevent the crystallization of sintered layers before the print is complete, thereby minimizing curling, warping, and residual thermal stresses in the final part.

The almost constant degradation rate in Figure 9(a) implies that the enzymatic degradation of PLLA composites may proceed via surface erosion. In order to further clarify erosion mechanism, the morphologies of degraded samples were examined by SEM. Figures 10 and 11 show the surface and cross-sectional morphologies of stretched samples with a stretch ratio of 6 after degradation, respectively. Video micrographs in Figure 10 suggest the changes in surface morphology as a result of enzymatic degradation. Exposure to the activated inoculum causes removal of material from surface, leading to an increase in sheets surface roughness with increasing degradation time. Even though degradation models are similar, the surface of degraded composites is much coarser compared with that of neat PLLA, and increasing porosity leads to a transformation of degraded surface from coarser to porous. This means that the surface erosion proceeds slower in neat PLLA due to no micropores formation during stretching. Degradation rates depend primarily on porosity, and increase with increasing porosity. On the other hand, surface erosion seems to be much affected by the ES content in composites. After PLLA chains on surface are degraded, the dispersed ES particles may fall off from PLLA matrix, leading to a larger surface area. Therefore, in process of degradation, greater ES particles also contribute to larger surface area, consequently causing a further increase in degradation rate. As a result, PLLA70/ES30 composite exhibits the highest degradation rate, 0.39 mg cm−2 h−1, which is approximately eight times larger than that of neat PLLA. Figure 11 shows the cross-sectional morphologies of stretched samples after degradation for 48 h. No obvious morphological change in the interior bulk and thinning of samples thickness further demonstrate that the enzymatic degradation proceeds by surface erosion. Based on the provided contexts, the distinction between **Bulk Erosion** and **Surface Erosion** in aliphatic polyesters is as follows:

### **Surface Erosion**  
- **Mechanism**: Degradation occurs primarily at the polymer's surface, with minimal changes to the interior. Material is removed layer-by-layer from the surface inward.  
- **Key Features**:  
  - Constant degradation rate over time (e.g., enzymatic degradation of PLLA composites).  
  - Results in increased surface roughness, porosity, or coarseness (observed via SEM).  
  - Micropores or dispersed particles (e.g., ES in PLLA composites) amplify surface area, accelerating erosion.  
  - Dominant in polymers where water diffusion into the bulk is slower than the degradation rate (e.g., poly(ortho esters)).  
  - Cross-sectional analysis shows no internal morphological changes but thinning of the sample.  

### **Bulk Erosion**  
- **Mechanism**: Degradation occurs uniformly throughout the polymer matrix, affecting both surface and interior.  
- **Key Features**:  
  - Autocatalytic hydrolysis dominates, driven by acidic degradation products (e.g., carboxylic acids) trapped within the polymer core, accelerating internal degradation.  
  - Leads to molecular weight reduction **before** significant mass loss (e.g., PLA degradation in thin films).  
  - Pore formation throughout the bulk (observed via SEM/GPC) and eventual structural collapse.  
  - Dominant in polymers where water penetrates faster than hydrolysis occurs (e.g., PLA, PCL) or in samples thinner than the critical thickness (~7.4 cm for PLA).  
  - Structural fluctuations (e.g., low-density regions in aged PLGA films) enhance water diffusion and autocatalysis.  

### **Critical Differences**  
| **Aspect**              | **Surface Erosion**                          | **Bulk Erosion**                              |  
|--------------------------|----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|  
| **Degradation Site**     | Surface layers only                          | Entire polymer matrix                         |  
| **Mass Loss vs. MW Loss** | Immediate mass loss                           | MW loss precedes mass loss                    |  
| **Morphology**           | Surface roughening/porosity                  | Internal pore formation, hollow structures    |  
| **Key Drivers**           | Porosity, enzyme activity, surface area      | Water diffusion, autocatalysis, crystallinity |  
| **Examples**             | PLLA/ES composites, poly(ortho esters)       | Thin PLA films, PLA/PCL blends                |  

### **Contextual Evidence**  
- Surface erosion in PLLA/ES composites is evidenced by SEM showing no interior changes but increased surface roughness and thinning (Contexts 1–2).  
- Bulk erosion in PLA is confirmed by molecular weight reduction prior to mass loss, autocatalysis, and pore formation throughout the bulk (Contexts 6, 9–10).  
- Critical thickness (Lcritical) determines the mechanism: thin PLA films (<7.4 cm) degrade via bulk erosion (Contexts 6, 8–10).  

In summary, **surface erosion** is a localized, layer-wise process driven by surface interactions, while **bulk erosion** involves homogeneous degradation influenced by water diffusion and autocatalytic effects.
reference: Bulk erosion occurs when the rate of water diffusion into the polymer matrix exceeds the rate of hydrolysis, causing a uniform decrease in molecular weight throughout the material before mass loss occurs (e.g., PLA, PLGA). Surface erosion occurs when hydrolysis is faster than water diffusion, resulting in material loss only from the exterior surface while maintaining the structural integrity of the core (e.g., polyanhydrides).

In the context of PLA/PBAT blends, epoxy-functionalized chain extenders like Joncryl® play several critical roles:  

1. **Compatibilization**: Joncryl® reacts with terminal hydroxyl (-OH) and carboxyl (-COOH) groups of PLA and PBAT, generating **in situ graft/comb copolymers** at the polymer-polymer interface. This reduces interfacial tension, promotes phase adhesion, and refines morphology (e.g., smaller dispersed phase domains), leading to improved compatibility between the immiscible PLA and PBAT phases [1, 4, 8, 12].  

2. **Mechanical Property Enhancement**: By forming non-linear, branched, or cross-linked structures, Joncryl® significantly improves toughness and ductility. For example, it increases elongation at break (e.g., from 23.5% to 410.3% in PLA/PBAT blends with 0.15 phr Joncryl®) while maintaining or enhancing tensile strength [3, 4, 8, 12].  

3. **Melt Strength and Processability**: The chain-extending/branching action of Joncryl® increases melt viscosity and imparts strain-hardening behavior, enabling applications like blown film extrusion. This addresses PLA’s inherent low melt strength, broadening its processing window [1, 3, 7].  

4. **Thermal Stability**: Cross-linking via epoxy reactions stabilizes the blend against thermal degradation during processing, reducing chain scission and maintaining molecular weight [1, 4, 9].  

5. **Crystallization Modulation**: Joncryl® increases nuclei density in PLA, enhancing its crystallizability, which can improve heat resistance and mechanical performance [1, 8].  

These effects arise from Joncryl®’s multifunctional epoxy groups, which chemically bridge PLA and PBAT, creating a cohesive interfacial architecture critical for optimizing blend properties.

This in-situ reaction reduces interfacial tension, stabilizes the morphology by reducing the dispersed phase particle size to sub-micron levels, and significantly enhances toughness and elongation at break.

retrieved_contexts: ["Besides studies at the laboratory scale, field tests are also conducted to certify that these structures can fully disintegrate at the commercial composting facility scale.[8-10] Laboratory tests are conducted under specific national and international standards. The main standards available regarding the criteria for certifying composting conditions are ASTM D6400-21,[11] ASTM D6868-21,[12] and EN13432.[13] The main standards describing the disintegration and biodegradation tests needed to meet the requirements of ASTM D6400, ASTM D6868 and EN13432 are described in ASTM D5338-15,[14] ISO 14855 part 1 and ISO 14855 part 2,[15, 16] respectively. Both standards are based on the evolution of the percentage of biodegradation of the samples. These tests can take between 90 and 180 days, depending on the simulated compost environment (i.e., yard, food, or manure compost) and the rate of biodegradation of the positive control, in general, cellulose powder.[11] Methods to accelerate the biodegradation of biodegradable polymers have surged because of two main reasons: a) the temporal gap between time frames observed for biodegradation of polymers in thermophilic composting conditions and other common organic wastes, such as food and garden waste, creating a low-quality and non-stabilized final product; and b) to accelerate the testing of an array of compostable polymer. In general, even certified compostable products may take more time to meet the requirements of ultimate degradation, reflected by the standards, than do food and garden waste, creating operative challenges for composting facilities when managing waste containing both biodegradable plastics and common organic waste. Furthermore, designing polymers with the needed shelf-life properties and stability for several applications and, at the same time, meeting compostability requirements have been challenging. Moreover, lengthy biodegradation tests are needed to determine the right compostable polymer, delaying the adoption, and commercialization of these compostable plastics. This review concentrates on approaches to accelerate the biodegradation of biodegradable polymers, considering thermophilic aerobic composting conditions as a common baseline. The methods reviewed in this work can be used to accelerate the biodegradation of these polymers during simulated composting tests and also during industrial operations. Specifically, the reviewed methods to accelerate the abiotic and biotic degradation of biodegradable polymers included are based on: a) modification of the polymer's properties (during processing or as a pre-treatment before biodegradation at the post-consumer stage); b) addition of specific nutrients (biostimulation), to biostimulate the environment (compost), and/or addition of specific microorganisms (bioaugmentation); c) engineering of specific enzymes to improve the depolymerization step; and d) the addition of specific enzymes during polymer processing recently reported as a potential way to improve the depolymerization of some biodegradable polymers.[17-19]", 'Bioplastics categorization, characteristics, and applications Bioplastics are categorized based on two primary attributes: being bio-based, biodegradable, or possessing both characteristics (Fig. 1). The term bio-based refers to materials derived from renewable biological sources, such as plants, rather than fossil fuels [48]. Biodegradable refers to materials that microorganisms can break down into essential compounds such as water, carbon dioxide, and organic matter in the natural environment. These definitions align with internationally recognized standards, ensuring consistency in the classification and understanding of bioplastics globally [104],. The certification of biodegradable plastics is governed by stringent composting conditions standards, which outline the specific criteria these materials must meet to be considered compostable. The standards provide detailed guidelines on the requirements for biodegradation, disintegration, and the absence of adverse effects on the resulting compost. ASTM D6400-19, for example, outlines three essential requirements for a product to be considered compostable in industrial or municipal aerobic composting systems. After being sieved through a 2-mm mesh, the product must disintegrate within 84 days, leaving no more than 10% of its initial Mass. Second, to indicate effective biodegradation, at least 90% of the product’s organic carbon must be transformed into carbon dioxide in 180 days. Lastly, compared to composts made from bio-waste that do not contain the product, the final compost must not impede plant growth [119].', 'Biodegradability test The biodegradability test was performed as per the ASTM D 5864 [27] standard. Aerobic aquatic biodegradation (common oil biodegradability) test is conducted in the presence of water and oxygen. In this test, the polymeric sample is incubated at 77 °F (25 °C) for 28 days; further, biodegradation is immediately determined by the evolution of carbon dioxide (CO2) from the sample tested with reference to blank containing inoculum only. According to the following test, the sample can be considered fully biodegradable if it produces 65% of CO2 of the total calculated value. Results and discussion', 'For the aliphatic/aromatic polyester PBAT, mineralization in compost has been reported at around 60% at day 45.[28] PBAT is frequently used for mulch films in agricultural environments where a crosslinking effect can be observed due to photodegradation, affecting its ultimate biodegradation in this environment.[28, 29] As observed, in composting conditions these polymers passed the criteria established by international standards, such as ISO and ASTM, when evaluated in simulated environments. A more complex situation is presented when evaluating post-consumer biodegradable products under these environments. Some organizations, such as Biodegradable Products Institute (BPI),[30] TÜV Austria,[31] DIN CERTCO,[32] Australasian bioplastics,[33] and Japan bioplastics association[34] are the main ones providing certification of products for compostability following international standards in simulated laboratory conditions (ASTM D6400, D6868, and EN13432). However, simulated laboratory tests are conducted under ideal controlled conditions, which are not always reflected in industrial composting facilities. However, poor compatibility of the two components may lead to undesirable mechanical properties [15], [16], [17]. Random and block copolymers have been used to enhance the compatibility of PCL/PLA blends through strengthening the interface and stabilizing the morphology [18], [19], but these compatibilizers are system specific, relatively expensive and difficult to produce. Another simple and economic approach to improve the interfacial adhesion of immiscible polymer blends, which has attracted great interest recently, is the addition of nanofillers [20]. [27] reported that the addition of MMT could enhance the tensile strength, modulus and elongation at break of PLA/PCL matrix. Goffin et al. [28] demonstrated that cellulose nanowhiskers grafted poly(ε-caprolactone)-b-poly(lactide) could improve the compatibility of PCL/PLA blends. Monticelli et al. [29] investigated the effect of functionalized polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxane (POSS) on the morphology and properties of PLA/PCL blends. Chemical recycling of PLA via alcoholysis to alkyl lactates is advantageous over thermal hydrolysis for several reasons derived from the contexts:  

1. **Milder Reaction Conditions**: Alcoholysis operates under lower temperatures compared to thermal hydrolysis or pyrolysis, which often require high temperatures (300–600°C). Elevated temperatures in thermal processes risk side reactions like lactide racemization, compromising product quality ([14]).  

2. **Efficiency and Selectivity**: Alcoholysis with catalysts like sodium L-ascorbate (VCNa) or metal complexes (e.g., Sn(Oct)₂) enables high turnover frequencies and selective depolymerization to alkyl lactates, avoiding random chain scission and uncontrolled degradation ([1], [11]). Thermal hydrolysis, in contrast, may involve autocatalytic ester-bond cleavage, leading to unpredictable oligomer formation ([6], [7]).  

3. **Closed-Loop Potential**: Alcoholysis products (alkyl lactates) can be directly converted back to lactide, the PLA monomer, enabling circular recycling. Thermal hydrolysis typically yields CO₂ and H₂O, which require energy-intensive steps (fermentation, polymerization) to regenerate PLA ([1], [3]).  

4. **Reduced Energy and Purification Costs**: Alcoholysis avoids the need for high-energy inputs and simplifies catalyst removal. Metal-based catalysts in thermal processes often require complex purification, increasing costs ([3], [11]).  

5. **Value-Added Products**: Alkyl lactates (e.g., ethyl lactate) are commercially valuable as green solvents or precursors for specialty polymers, whereas thermal hydrolysis produces less versatile outputs ([2], [10], [11]).  

6. **Scalability and Sustainability**: Alcoholysis aligns with green chemistry principles by using natural or recyclable catalysts (e.g., VCNa) and minimizing solvent waste, whereas thermal methods face challenges in scaling due to energy demands and catalyst contamination risks ([1], [3], [11]).  

In summary, alcoholysis offers a more sustainable, efficient, and economically viable pathway for PLA recycling compared to energy-intensive thermal hydrolysis.

The typical glass transition temperature (Tg) of **Poly(butylene succinate) (PBS)** is **−30 °C** (as reported in contexts [1] and [4]). This low Tg, well below room temperature, results in PBS being **flexible and ductile** under ambient conditions, similar to polyolefins like polyethylene. 

### Influence of Tg on Applications Compared to PLA:
1. **Mechanical Behavior**:
   - **PBS**: Its low Tg (−30 °C) ensures it remains in a rubbery state at room temperature, providing high ductility (elongation at break >300%) and toughness, making it suitable for applications requiring flexibility (e.g., packaging, agricultural films).
   - **PLA**: With a Tg of **55–65 °C** (contexts [2], [3], [6]), PLA is rigid and brittle at room temperature (below its Tg), limiting its use in applications needing impact resistance or flexibility. However, this rigidity suits rigid packaging, disposable items, or biomedical devices where structural integrity is critical.

2. **Thermal Stability**:
   - PBS’s low Tg allows it to retain flexibility even at sub-ambient temperatures but limits its use in high-temperature environments. PLA’s higher Tg provides better dimensional stability near room temperature but becomes brittle unless modified.

3. **Blending and Compatibility**:
   - PBS is often blended with PLA to balance rigidity and ductility. The PLA/PBS blend (75:25) shows a reduced Tg (~48°C) compared to pure PLA, improving toughness while retaining some rigidity (contexts [2], [3]). However, PBS’s low Tg can lead to phase separation in blends, requiring compatibilizers for optimal performance.

4. **Environmental and Processing Considerations**:
   - PBS’s flexibility and compostability make it ideal for single-use, biodegradable products. PLA’s higher Tg necessitates processing at elevated temperatures but offers better thermal stability for short-term use in warmer conditions.

In summary, PBS’s low Tg (−30°C) enables flexible, durable applications, while PLA’s higher Tg (55–65°C) suits rigid, structural uses. The choice depends on the required balance between flexibility, rigidity, and thermal stability.

In the current work, the effect of nucleation and plasticization on stereocomplex formation and on this network/spherulitic dual morphology is investigated.', 'Poly(lactic acid), PLA, which can be produced from primary resources like corns, sugars, or beets, is considered to be one of the most promising environmentally friendly materials.1 Although PLA has a fairly high melting temperature in comparison with other biodegradable polyesters, its Tm, around 180°C, is not high enough for some applications. The Norrish Type II mechanism in the photodegradation of polymers containing carbonyl groups involves the following steps, as derived from the context:  

1. **UV Absorption**: Carbonyl groups (C═O) in the polymer absorb UV radiation, acting as chromophores that initiate photoreactions. This absorption excites the carbonyl group, providing the energy required for subsequent reactions [1,2].  

2. **Hydrogen Abstraction**: The excited carbonyl group abstracts a hydrogen atom from a **gamma position** (i.e., a carbon atom two positions away from the carbonyl group) within the polymer chain. This step typically forms a six-membered cyclic transition state [1].  

3. **Chain Cleavage**: The hydrogen abstraction leads to **scission** of the polymer backbone at the beta position (relative to the carbonyl group), resulting in two fragments:  
   - A **shorter polymer chain** with a terminal double bond (enol structure).  
   - A **ketene** or other low-molecular-weight carbonyl-containing products [1].  

This process reduces the polymer's molecular weight, increasing brittleness and accelerating degradation. In polyethylene (PE), for example, photo-oxidation generates carbonyl groups that undergo Norrish Type II reactions, contributing to embrittlement and fragmentation under UV exposure [1].  

The mechanism contrasts with **Norrish Type I**, which involves direct cleavage of bonds adjacent to the carbonyl group (alpha cleavage) without hydrogen transfer [1].
reference: Norrish Type II is a photochemical intramolecular reaction where a gamma-hydrogen is abstracted by an excited carbonyl oxygen. This leads to the cleavage of the C-C bond alpha to the carbonyl group, resulting in the formation of a vinyl end group and a methyl ketone, effectively reducing the polymer's molecular weight.

PLA/RS blend films exhibit a very high WVTR of 184.23 g/m².day, while PE is below 5 g/m².day ([1]). Thermoplastic starch (TPS) itself has high WVP ([4], [6], [12], [13]).

2.  **Reason: Hydrophilic nature of starch:** Starch is inherently hydrophilic due to its polar groups and hydroxyl groups, making it highly sensitive to water and moisture ([2], [5], [6], [8], [14]). This hydrophilicity dominates the barrier properties in PLA/starch blends.

3.  **Mechanisms for increased permeability:**
    *   The hydrophilic starch creates pathways for water vapor diffusion through the PLA matrix ([1], [6]).
    *   Starch absorbs water, leading to swelling ([7], [9]). This swelling can cause stress cracking in the PLA matrix, especially during drying cycles, further increasing permeability pathways ([7], [9]).

    *   PLA has low crystallinity (<10%), and while starch addition can increase overall crystallinity (acting as a nucleating agent), the hydrophilic starch component still provides high permeability pathways ([1], [7], [9]).

4.  **Consequence:** The high WVP of PLA/starch composites makes them more susceptible to moisture-related degradation and aging processes ([1], [7], [8], [9], [14]).

Based solely on the provided context:

1.  **Accelerates Bulk Degradation:** The autocatalytic effect significantly increases the rate of hydrolytic degradation within the bulk material of thick PLA implants. This is because the carboxylic acid end groups (-COOH) generated during chain scission catalyze further hydrolysis of ester bonds ([1], [2], [3], [5]).
2.  **Dominant Mechanism in Bulk:** Hydrolytic degradation in PLA occurs predominantly in the bulk rather than via surface erosion, especially in thick samples. The autocatalytic effect is the key mechanism driving this bulk degradation ([1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [8]).
3.  **Creates Non-Uniform Degradation:** The autocatalytic effect causes faster degradation in the center/core of thick implants compared to the surface. Acidic oligomers produced internally cannot diffuse out easily, lowering the internal pH and accelerating degradation locally. In contrast, acidic products near the surface can diffuse away into the surrounding medium, slowing degradation there ([4], [5]).
4.  **Impacts Degradation Kinetics and Properties:** This self-catalyzed mechanism governs the degradation kinetics, leading to a faster decrease in molecular weight and earlier loss of mechanical properties deep within the implant ([4], [5], [8], [9], [11]).
5.  **Clinical Significance for Implants:** The accelerated internal degradation and local pH drop caused by autocatalysis can influence biocompatibility and inflammatory responses around the implant ([5], [7]). Controlling this effect is crucial for designing implants with predictable degradation profiles.
reference: In thick PLA sections (>2mm), acidic oligomers generated by ester hydrolysis cannot diffuse out of the matrix fast enough. Their accumulation lowers the internal pH, which catalyzes further hydrolysis. This leads to accelerated degradation of the core compared to the surface, potentially causing sudden structural failure or the formation of hollow structures.

After discussing the characteristics, constituents, and demonstration of TPBs, we conclude by exploring their potential as power sources for implants, wearables, and environmental sensing applications.', 'In recent years, the issue of population aging has promoted significant interest in the development of implantable biomedical devices.1,2 However, conventional batteries in these devices have introduced challenges, such as limited battery life and the need for secondary surgical extraction, imposing risks and financial burdens to patients.3,4 Consequently, the quest for an alternative solution has led to a burgeoning interest in implantable solid-state biodegradable energy storage devices.5 Although implantable biomedical devices powered by conventional batteries are highly reliable and convenient, they are not without drawbacks:6-8 (1) their rigid and bulky nature occupies considerable space within implantable devices, (2) non-biodegradability necessitates a second surgical procedure, and (3) the presence of toxic substances in electrodes and electrolytes poses severe safety hazards. Furthermore, considering the diverse range of challenging applications of biodegradable bioplastics, the search for a new material analog of PLA with better performance characteristics has started.', 'Nonetheless, practical applications of biodegradable supercapacitors are still hindered by the lack of suitable electrolytes and electrode materials.13-15 In terms of electrolytes, natural polymers such as gelatin are widely used in preparing gel electrolytes due to their excellent biocompatibility and degradability;16-20 however, their weak mechanical strength often limits the integral stability of the fabricated devices. 1.  **Transient batteries** are batteries designed to degrade or disintegrate after completing their function without leaving harmful toxic substances ([2], [3]). They are also referred to as "degradable batteries" ([2], [5]) or "transient primary batteries (TPBs)" ([3]). Their purpose includes powering implantable biomedical devices, wearables, and environmental sensing platforms while eliminating the need for surgical removal and minimizing environmental impact ([3], [4], [6]).

2.  **Biodegradable polymers are utilized in their construction** in the following key components:
    *   **Electrolytes:** Solid or gel polymer electrolytes are used to replace liquid electrolytes (like PBS), enabling thin, compact, and easily implantable devices. Specific biopolymers used include:
        *   Carrageenan, pectin, cellulose, and starch complexed with salts ([1]).
        *   Guar gum-cellulose aerogel (GCA) membrane ([2]).
        *   Gelatin-based hydrogels (sometimes blended with polymers like polyacrylamide, silk fibroin, sodium alginate, or carboxymethyl cellulose) ([2], [14]).
        *   Chitosan ([1], [6], [8], [9], [12]).
        *   Sodium alginate ([8]).
    *   **Separators:** Biodegradable polymers act as separators between electrodes to prevent short circuits. Examples include:
        *   Chitosan ([6], [8]).
        *   Starch-based compounds (chemically modified via cross-linking, derivatization, or nanotechnology integration) ([8]).
        *   Cellulose derivatives ([8]).
    *   **Electrode Components/Scaffolds:**
        *   Chitosan-based systems are used as scaffolds to stabilize cathodes and anodes due to their porous framework, electronic conductivity, and mechanical characteristics. They can also serve as active materials, conductive additives, or binders within electrodes ([8]).
        *   Biodegradable polymers (like cellulose, polyester, silicon) are used in packaging ([5]).
        *   Biodegradable fiber conductors (e.g., polyglycolic acid yarn) are used as substrates for electrodes ([6]).
    *   **Packaging/Encapsulation:** Biodegradable polymers form the packaging or encapsulation layers, allowing the entire device to degrade ([5], [14]).

**Key Advantages of Using Biodegradable Polymers:**
*   **Biocompatibility & Safety:** They are non-toxic, biocompatible, and degrade into harmless byproducts ([1], [4], [6], [8], [10]).
*   **Environmental Friendliness:** They are carbon neutral, ecologically friendly, and reduce environmental pollution ([1], [8], [10]).
*   **Device Integration & Form Factor:** They facilitate the creation of thin, flexible, compact, and even injectable devices ([1], [6], [8]).
*   **Simplified Assembly:** Using metallic cathodes *as* current collectors eliminates the need for conductive binders ([1]); similarly, binder-free electrode architectures are enabled ([14]).
*   **Ion Transport:** Functional groups (e.g., -OH, -NH₂, -COOH) can coordinate with ions to enhance ionic conductivity, especially when complexed with salts or modified ([1], [8], [12]).
*   **Mechanical Properties:** They can provide necessary mechanical strength, flexibility, and durability for the device ([2], [8], [14]).

Ltd., Dongducheon, Korea) to remove any residual solvent.', 'The surfaces of poly(l-lactic acid) (PLA), poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyhexanoate) (PHBHHx), and their cast-film blends were activated using low-temperature argon plasma to confirm the possibility of improved microbial adhesion and biodegradation rate using soil microflora as a degrading medium. The other advantages of biodegradable metal mesh over polymer are further discussed in section 6.2.', 'Export citation and abstractBibTeXRIS Using biodegradable polymers as biomaterials has contributed to significant advancements in the fields of regenerative medicine and tissue engineering [1]. Plasma immersion ion implantation (PIII), as a plasma-based surface modification technique, enhances biodegradable polymer surfaces through several mechanisms derived from the context:

1. **Functional Group Incorporation**: Plasma treatment introduces polar functional groups (e.g., hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl, or amino groups) onto polymer surfaces. These groups improve hydrophilicity and enable covalent conjugation of bioactive molecules (e.g., heparin) to enhance antithrombogenic properties and biocompatibility [1, 2, 10].

2. **Surface Wettability and Energy**: Plasma increases surface energy and wettability, promoting protein adsorption and cell adhesion. This is critical for tissue engineering applications, as moderate hydrophilicity supports cell infiltration and proliferation without altering bulk mechanical properties [3, 10].

3. **Surface Roughness**: Plasma treatment creates micro/nanoscale topographical features, enhancing microbial adhesion and biofilm formation in biodegradation contexts, or improving cell-material interactions in biomedical implants [3, 10].

4. **Controlled Degradation**: By modifying surface chemistry and hydrophilicity, plasma accelerates hydrolysis and microbial colonization, synergistically enhancing biodegradation rates while maintaining structural integrity during early degradation stages [2, 3].

5. **Drug Delivery Enhancement**: Plasma-modified surfaces can sustain drug release (e.g., anti-inflammatory agents) by functionalizing the polymer for controlled molecular attachment, improving therapeutic efficacy without chemical waste [5].

6. **Sterilization and Safety**: Plasma treatments sterilize surfaces while introducing functional groups, avoiding toxic residues or bulk degradation associated with chemical/radiation methods [10].

Thus, PIII optimizes surface properties (chemistry, topography, wettability) of biodegradable polymers to enhance biocompatibility, degradation control, and functional performance in biomedical and environmental applications.

retrieved_contexts: ['In recent years, PGA has been utilized as fillers combined with other degradable polymers and has been used in short-term tissue engineering scaffolds such as scaffold for bone [146,147,148,149], tendon [150, 151], tooth [152], cartilage [153, 154], vaginal [155], intestinal [74], lymphatic [156], and spinal regeneration [157]. Reproduced with permission from Wiley Online Library', 'Sutures, tissue adhesives, and surgical staples provide means for inosculation of surgical sites, and sutures, in particular, are widely used in inosculation and fixation of skin, muscle, and blood vessels. In addition, the applications of surgical sutures have expanded to hard tissues and to reconstruction of damaged ligaments. Sutures can be categorized as absorbable or non-absorbable. Natural absorbable sutures are composed of collagen extracted from animal intestines; however, their use is declining due to high infection rates, low tensile strength, and foreign body reactions [1]. Synthetic absorbable sutures based on poly(glycolic acid) (PGA) were developed during the early 1970s, and followed by the invention of poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) sutures, which are now replacing conventional collagen sutures (catgut) [2, 3]. Biodegradable filament sutures are available as monofilament or multi-filament (braided) types. Multi-filament sutures have good handling properties and provide greater frictional force at suture sites; however, they are associated with higher risk of bacterial infection. On the other hand, monofilament sutures have weaker knot strength and lower internal breaking strength [4, 5]. PGA sutures, which are widely used nowadays, can only be degraded by simple hydrolysis, which can be accelerated by enzymes, such as esterase, trypsin, and chymotrypsin [6].
