However, its low melting point, plasticity, and pyrolysis during the spinning process leave room for improvement [9].', 'A poly(lactide-co-glycolide)/hydroxyapatite composite scaffold with enhanced osteoconductivity Tissue engineering represents a powerful approach toward bone regeneration through the surgical implantation of a biodegradable scaffold, i.e., a porous structure mimicking the properties of the native extracellular matrix. The scaffold can be either directly implanted in the tissue defect site or previously cultured with the appropriate cell type and combined with bioactive substances promoting tissue regeneration, such as growth factors and signaling molecules.[1] Poly(α-hydroxy acids) are among the most widely investigated synthetic polymers for tissue engineering since they are approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for drug delivery and other clinical applications.[2] They include poly(lactide) (PLA), poly(glycolide) (PGA), and their copolymers poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA), linear aliphatic polyesters degraded in physiological environments through the hydrolysis of their ester linkages into non-toxic molecules removed by natural metabolic pathways.[3] Depending on the application, PLGA can be preferred to the two relevant homopolymers (i.e., PLA and PGA), since its hydrophobic/hydrophilic balance and the resulting degradation kinetics can be tailored by varying the molar ratio between the two comonomer units.[4] Indeed, PLGA has been studied for tissue engineering applications since the 1990s.[5, 6] However, even though the mechanical properties of PLGA scaffolds can be engineered to be comparable to those of trabecular bone, their stiffness is much lower than that of cortical bone. For this reason and to enhance their osteoinductive properties,[4] PLGA is often loaded with bioactive calcium phosphate ceramics, including hydroxyapatite (HA)[7-11] and β-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP).[12-16] Increasing the compatibility between a polymer phase and an inorganic filler represents one of the main challenging issues in composite material development and mechanical properties optimization.[17] In particular, the interface adhesion strength between HA and poly(α-hydroxy acid) matrices is typically low, compromising the structural stability of the resulting composite material.[18] HA particle surface modification through polymer grafting can be exploited to increase compatibility and achieve effective mechanical stress transfer between the two phases. In this way, it is possible to reduce inter-phase stress concentration and improve material mechanical properties.[19] “Grafting from” approaches involve polymer synthesis directly on the surface of HA particles,[15] often after ceramic functionalization through covalent linking monomers that act as initiators.[20, 21] These methods have some disadvantages, including poor control over PLGA comonomeric unit ratio and the possibility of grafting only short polymeric chains.[22] For this reason, a “grafting to” approach based on covalent bonding of preformed aliphatic polyesters on the surface of HA particles, was explored in this study to develop additively manufactured composite materials.', "Export citation and abstractBibTeXRIS Various materials have been developed as ‘scaffolds’ for regenerative medicine. A typical scaffold of synthetic polymers may contain poly-glycolic acid (PGA), poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) and poly-lactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA), and scaffolds of natural polymers contain collagen and gelatin. These scaffolds have been used in clinical practice and yield adequate results [1-7]. However, PGA, PLLA and PLGA scaffolds may cause needless adhesion or toxicity because they may reduce the pH of the surrounding tissue [8-10]. We found that a collagen fiber scaffold manufactured at physiological pH was biocompatible and yielded no adhesion. However, it dissolved before tissue regeneration was complete. Various modifications may therefore be needed [11-14]. Glutaraldehyde (GA) and N-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)-N’-ethylcarbodiimide hydrochloride (EDC) are well-known chemical cross-linkers. Although defects may make chemical cross-linkers cytotoxic [15], EDC has a relatively low cytotoxicity and is useful as a cross-linker [12, 14, 16]. UV is used for physical cross-linking; it does not involve toxic chemicals [15], but cannot provide sufficient stiffness in a collagen scaffold [16]. We examined thermal processing as a simple physical cross-linking method. We made a collagen fiber scaffold by freeze drying a collagen fiber suspension with a physiological pH of 7.4. This was followed by heating under negative pressure. Heating formed cross-links between the collagen fibers, providing sufficient strength to maintain a space for tissue regeneration against the pressure of surrounding tissue or collagenase [17]. In this study, mechanical strength is defined as the ability to maintain space for tissue regeneration, rather than mere physical strength; this characteristic is important for regenerative medicine. The scaffold was embedded under the back skin of a rat to determine if it had sufficient biocompatibility and space maintenance ability to be used as a scaffold for regenerative medicine. Collagen forms a molecular structure under acidic conditions, but forms fibers under neutral conditions, and the modes shift reversibly. Furthermore, it can be denatured by exposure to heat (denatured collagen, which contains 0% superhelix structure, is called gelatin). The temperature by which half of the collagen molecules have lost their superhelix structure is called the ‘denaturation temperature’. The denaturation temperature in the dehydrated state is around 112 °C [18]. The collagen fiber scaffold evaluated in this study was freeze dried and heated under negative pressure. Thermal processing above the denaturation temperature introduced various chemical changes including cross-linking [19, 20] and provided mechanical strength [21, 22]. However, as denaturation and mechanical strength of the scaffold increases, the host's foreign-body reaction also increases. As a result, the scaffold is no longer suitable for use in the body. Therefore, it is important to create a scaffold with moderate mechanical strength to minimize foreign-body reaction. In addition, collagen fiber becomes a barrier with increased mechanical strength, and the number of cells invading the scaffold decreases (figure 1(a)). Therefore, our scaffold was designed to promote cell infiltration by orienting the collagen fibers (figure 1(b)). As an icy crystal is formed perpendicular to a cooling surface, orientation was achieved by cooling a collagen fiber suspension only from the bottom of the container.", 'Surgical sutures are wound closure filaments manufactured in different shapes. These sutures secure tissues in position until the wound naturally heals and gives enough tissue strength. The U.S. Federal Drug Administration (FDA) has approved PLA for utilizing as a suture material due to its advantageous features such as biocompatibility, bioresorbability, and biodegradability with non-toxic degradation products. But, the inherent properties of PLA like high crystallinity (around 40%), and slow rate of degradation, impose restrictions on its application as material for suture. Because of this, copolymerization of lactic acid (LA) with biodegradable monomers, like glycolic acid (GA), is done to obtain the PGA/PLA copolymer, which has better properties than PLA for suture applications. This amorphous copolymer has lower glass transition temperature (Tg) and higher degradation rate than that of PLA and has been found very much useful as a suture material [111, 139]. A stent is a small mesh tube used to hold open passages in the human body, such as weak or narrowed arteries. There exist three major kinds of stents: (a) bare-metal stents, (b) drug-eluting stents, and (c) biodegradable / bioresorbable stents. Bare-metal stents and drug-eluting stents may leave residues in the body that can affect further treatment and recovery process, whereas bioresorbable stents, providing both mechanical support and drug delivery to the vessel wall, can be fully absorbed by the body, and therefore, permits better vascular remodeling and decreases the triggering of persistent inflammation. The mechanical tests demonstrated that the alignment of scaffolds could enhance the mechanical properties in vitro and increase the biomechanical properties of the neotendon in vivo.", 'The use of polymers in tissue engineering has been growing in the last decades. Temporary grafts must be prepared as porous scaffolds to allow bone growth, and nutrients and waste exchange through the pores promoting the healing process.[21-25] But porosity weakens scaffolds,[26] which is critical when using a rigid and brittle polymer such as PLA.', 'In reconstructive medicine there is a tremendous need for suitable biomaterials to allow the repair and regeneration of damaged or diseased tissue [1]. We propose that the presence of numerous hydroxyl groups in HBPG will be therefore able to promote the cellular attachment and differentiation without exogenous biological stimuli.', 'Synthetic biomaterials such as PCL, poly lactic acid, poly glycolic acid, and PLGA have been used to prepare the scaffolds for enhanced tissue regeneration [36]. In particular, PLGA is used for the reconstruction of various tissues owing to its high cytocompatibility [36, 48, 49]. However, scaffolds composed only of PLGA do not maintain their shapes either in the in vitro or in vivo environments owing to their brittle property and rapid resorption [34, 50]. In contrast, PCL has comparatively less cell affinity than PLGA, but it has excellent mechanical properties that prevent early fractures of the scaffold [39] and its degradation rate is slower than the rate of bone regeneration [51]. Thus, blended PCL/PLGA scaffolds exhibit biological and mechanical advantages obtained during the PCL and PLGA mixing processes that complement their respective weaknesses [36]. In addition, as β-TCP was added to the blended PCL/PLGA for the fabrication of the PCL/PLGA/β-TCP membrane, their elastic modulus was enhanced and their surface roughness was increased [1, 52, 53]. In the SEM images of the PCL/PLGA/β-TCP membranes prepared in this study, the rough surfaces generated by the incorporated β-TCP were confirmed (figure 7). During cellular testing with fibroblasts and preosteoblasts, early cell attachment and differentiation were higher in collagen, but the difference of proliferation and differentiation had disappeared when examined on day 7 and day 14, respectively. In contrast, fibroblasts aggregated and were detached from the membrane when maintained until day 14 (data not shown). This was in line with the results of a previous paper [40] and is an indication of the membrane’s ability to inhibit the ingrowth of soft tissues. We next applied the GBR to an in vivo implant model utilizing beagle dogs and performed histological analyses after sacrifice at 8 weeks. The histologic and histomorphometric analyses in this study showed that the PCL/PLGA/β-TCP group did not differ significantly from the collagen group; furthermore, in particular among the histometric measurements, the new bone area (%) and bone-to implant contact (%) of the PCL/PLGA/β-TCP group were significantly higher than those of the collagen group (P < 0.05). These findings indicated that the group receiving PCL/PLGA/β-TCP membranes showed levels of new bone formation and regeneration in the defect area comparable with those induced by collagen membranes, confirming that the biocompatibility of the PCL/PLGA/β-TCP membranes as well as their ability to maintain migration and proliferation of surrounding tissue and to support osteogenic differentiation to ultimately induce bone formation are comparable to those of collagen.', 'To address these limitations, tissue engineering has emerged as a promising solution, focusing on the design of biomimetic scaffolds that promote tissue regeneration and provide durable, functional conduits [11]. An ideal graft for in situ tissue engineering should be readily available for implantation, compliant, durable, and biologically active to support arterial regeneration and ensure long-term patency [12]. However, significant challenges remain in creating grafts that satisfy all these critical requirements while addressing biomanufacturing considerations, including aseptic processing and logistical constraints related to time and cost [13]. A critical aspect of graft development for in situ tissue engineering is the selection of scaffolding polymers, which provide structural support and mechanical stability [14]. The mechanical properties of these polymers are essential for maintaining scaffold integrity under physiological conditions, while their degradation behavior significantly impacts the scaffold’s capacity to support tissue regeneration over time [14]. Polycaprolactone (PCL) has been widely studied for its strength and slow degradation properties [15],whereas PCL-co-lactic acid (PLCL) is gaining attention as an alternative due to its faster degradation rate and higher elasticity, aimed at accelerating the in situ tissue remodeling process [16]. However, both polymers lack inherent bioactivity. To overcome this limitation, our previous studies have utilized a versatile hydrogel material, 4-arm, end-functionalized polyethylene glycol-norbornene (PEG-NB) [17]. This material’s ability to bind various cell-adhesive and functional ligands via photoclickable ‘thiol-ene’ chemistry makes it an excellent candidate for bioengineered scaffolds that regulate cellular activities. We employed coaxial electrospinning to combine PCL with PEG-NB, creating nanostructured fibers that form a porous hybrid graft scaffold [17]. While these scaffolds are mechanically strong enough to function as native arteries, further advancements in graft degradation, compliance, and cell penetration are necessary to progress such hybrid grafts into vascular surgery.', 'Many synthetic polymers, such as poly(lactic-co-glycolic) acid and polycaprolactone (PCL), have been extensively studied as potential scaffold materials for tissue engineering. The use of a well characterized synthetic material has potential advantages for such applications including avoiding the need for donor tissue with autografts and immunological rejection with allografts, as well as supply and reproducibility challenges that can occur in using natural polymers. For skin tissue engineering, these polymers serve as the scaffold supporting cell functions and resisting contraction to allow the tissue to regenerate. Ideally, natural tissue is formed and fills the space and function of the polymer matrices that eventually degrade under the environment created by biological processes. Therefore, the matrices need to support functions (such as adhesion, proliferation and differentiation) of appropriate cells (such as fibroblasts) and have mechanical and degradation characteristics suitable for skin regeneration applications. However, the hydrophobic nature of many polymers such as PCL makes them non-ideal for adsorption of important adhesive proteins (such as fibronectin, vitronectin) in their native conformation. The hydrophobic surfaces tend to cause protein denaturation and subsequent foreign body reactions to the implants in vivo. This in turn limits the functions of adherent cells including fibroblasts [1-4]. This hydrophobic nature of polymers such as PCL also results in very slow degradation, often requiring 1 year or more for complete degradation in the case of PCL [5-7]. In skin tissue engineering applications where tissue formation takes place in the first several months following the surgery, a faster degradation rate is desirable. Therefore, in this study, we demonstrated that by simply altering the wetting properties of the model polymer PCL, we have (1) enhanced its interaction with fibroblasts and (2) accelerated its degradation. PCL is a biodegradable polyester polymer synthesized by ring-opening polymerization reaction of ε-caprolactone [8]. Its biodegradability is attributed to non-enzymatic hydrolysis of the ester bonds in the polymer chains in the physiological environment [5, 9, 10]. Reports in the literature have demonstrated methods such as hydrolysis using concentrated NaOH to make polymers such as PCL more hydrophilic for cell interactions [11-13]. However, these methods tend to only alter the wetting properties of the surface of the materials and can lead to etching; therefore, they may not be ideal.', '© 2023 Wiley Periodicals LLC. Tissue engineering which aims to bring together cells, scaffolds, and chemical factors has been proposed as a potential strategy to fabricate tissue and organ substitutes for sustaining, reestablishing or augmenting functions of their damaged or diseased counterparts in vivo.1, 2 The scaffold is a pivotal structure that is convenient for chemical cues, like nutrients and waste, to penetrate and diffuse. Meanwhile, it provides mechanical integrity for the tissue engineering construct and promotes cell growth.3, 4 A major focus in tissue scaffolds is to find biomaterials with optimum performance that can lead to fabrication of better biomimetic tissues. For example, it is essential for the scaffold materials to be elastic to develop flexible tissues such as blood vessels and heart valves which experienced dynamic deformation.5 Many kinds of biodegradable polymers such as poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), polycaprolactone (PCL), poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) and polylactic acid (PLA) have been extensively explored to meet demands of various tissue engineering applications. However, the applications of these polymers are limited for their heterogeneous degradation properties and inferior mechanical properties. Specifically, PCL has slow degradation rate up to 3-4 years in vivo.6, 7 PLGA degrades by bulk degradation, which might cause sudden structure failure and inflammatory response.8, 9 PHB is a stiff and brittle polymer, which leads to difficulty in processing.10 PLA suffers from some significant drawbacks such as high brittleness, low melt strength and slow crystallization rate.11-13 Therefore, exploring new elastomeric materials has attracted more and more attention in recent years. As a new thermosetting elastomer, the successful synthesis of poly (glycerol sebacate) (PGS) threw light on the application of elastic scaffold materials in regenerative medicine.14 PGS has excellent biocompatibility, tunable degradation behavior and mechanical properties.15-17 Besides, the surface degradation kinetic of PGS, which shows linear decline of strength and mass without sudden rupture, also makes it very suitable for scaffold material in tissue engineering.18 Degradation of PGS yields glycerol and sebacic acid which are bioabsorbable. The former is a component of lipids while the latter a natural intermediate of fatty acid metabolism.19 Although the properties and applications of PGS have aroused great interests of researchers, the effect of curing time on its properties is still ambiguous. To better understand and extend its potential applications, it is valuable to systematically explore the properties of PGS synthesized for different curing conditions. Jaafar et al. fabricated PGS with curing temperature at 120°C, 130°C, 140°C, 150°C, and 165°C for 24 h.20 They found that the elasticity of PGS enhanced with the increase of temperature. Based solely on the provided context, PGA is rarely used for long-term tissue scaffolds due to its degradation characteristics:  

1.  **Rapid Degradation**: PGA degrades quickly in vivo (e.g., completely degraded in 11 weeks in a vascular scaffold study [1]), which is too fast for the longer time frames required for tissue regeneration in many applications ([1], [10]).
2.  **Mechanical Instability**: The rapid degradation leads to a swift loss of mechanical properties (viscosity/strength). This is unsuitable for scaffolds needing to maintain structural integrity long-term to support tissue growth ([1], [7], [10]).
3.  **Degradation-Induced Toxicity**: PGA degradation lowers the local pH, causing damage to nearby cells and potentially inducing fibrosis and inflammation. This negative biological response is problematic for long-term implants ([1], [4], [6]).
4.  **Limitations for Scaffold Requirements**: Long-term scaffolds require degradation rates matched to tissue regeneration (often slower) and maintained mechanical strength – PGA's inherent properties conflict with these needs ([1], [3], [6], [10]).

In contrast, PGA is suitable for sutures because:  
*   Its degradation timeframe aligns with the shorter period needed for wound closure and healing ([2], [5]).  
*   Suture applications do not require long-term mechanical support of regenerating tissue ([2], [5]).
reference: PGA has high tensile strength (6–7 GPa modulus) but degrades rapidly via hydrolysis, losing ~50% of its strength within 2 weeks and resorbing completely in 6–12 months. This rapid degradation is ideal for sutures that need to hold tissue only until healing occurs but is too fast for scaffolds requiring long-term structural support.

Among the various types of nucleating agents, inorganic particles, such as talc and clay, have been widely used [1-3]. Mohammadreza et al. [4] reported that microsized talc particles effectively enhance the crystallization rate of PLA through fast nucleation and a high growth rate, leading to more perfect crystals. Majority of the previous studies reported the effect of talc as a nucleating agent for polypropylene or neat PLA [7-9]; however, the influence of talc on PLA and PBS (PLA/PBS) blends has not been reported. The isothermal crystallization kinetics results showed that the crystallization rate of PLLA with small amount of PPZn was much higher than that of neat PLLA, and the half-time (t1/2) of PLLA/PPZn sample is far less than that of neat PLLA. As an effective nucleating agent, PPZn particles had also some influence on nucleation mechanism and crystal growth of PLLA. © 2013 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. J. Appl. Polym. Sci. 130: 2744-2752, 2013 Poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) is a renewable, biodegradable, and biocompatible thermoplastic semicrystalline polymer with high tensile strength and high modulus, which has been widely used in the biomedical, agricultural, and package fields.1-10 However, its slow crystallization rate, relatively poor toughness, and low heat deflection temperature have restricted its further large-scale commercial application. However, the fact that PLA is brittle due to its slow crystallization behavior, the improvement of PLA-based product is still required. As the crystallization of PLA in terms of the rate and the extent of crystallization can be enhanced by nucleating agents, the mechanical properties can be improved whereas the cycle period in injection molding processes becomes shorten [1], [2]. Nucleating agents are typically either low molecular weight organic or inorganic additives. Talc is a good inorganic nucleating agent for crystallization of polycaprolactone [3], [4], poly(ethylene terephthalate) [5], and PLA [6], [7], [8], as evidenced from a decrease of crystallization temperature upon heating as well as a decrease in spherulite size. Jiang et al. [9] investigated the crystallization behavior of PLA nanocomposites with montmorillonite clay and found the crystallization temperature (Tc) was shifted to lower temperature leading to an enhanced crystallinity. For organic nucleating agents, Nam et al. [10] reported that aliphatic amide such as N,N′-ethylenebis(12-hydroxystearamide) increased an overall crystallization rate of PLA whereas the average spherulite size was found to decrease as the number of nuclei increased. Blending PLA with other polymers can also modify the crystallization behavior. For example poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) [11], poly(butylene succinate) [12], and poly(ethylene oxide) [13] shifted the cold crystallization temperature of PLA to lower temperature and increased the crystallization rate. Stereocomplexation between PLLA and PDLA is accepted as the most effective methods to enhance the thermal properties of PLA-based materials [14], [15], [16]. Dendritic hyperbranched polymer (DHP) was reported about its nucleation effect as it significantly increased crystallization rate and crystallinity of PLA and simultaneously improved mechanical properties [17]. Although various nucleating agents for PLA were reported, most still showed phase separation with PLA. In addition, the price is also the condition for the practical nucleating agents.It should be noted that the organic molecules with a certain chain length such as dibenzoylhydrazide compounds [18] or carboxylamide derivatives [19] were reported for enhancement of crystallization of PLA. This leads us to an idea of short chain polymer to initiate the crystallization of PLA. Here, we consider the multi-branched short chain PLLA (m-PLLAs) as an effective nucleating agent which not only can be expected for the acceleration of PLA crystallization in multi-directions but also the good miscibility with PLA. Up to the present, only few reports are about the synthesis of the m-PLLA. For example, Miao et al. [20] reported the preparation of m-PLLA in star form using carbohydrate derivatives as the multi-functional cores. Hao et al. studied the syntheses of 3- to 6-armed star PLLA with natural sugar alcohols of glycerol, erythritol, xylitol, and sorbitol as initiators [21]. It should be noted that all of those star PLLAs were prepared through a ring-opening polymerization of l-lactide. In this work, l-lactic acid was applied as the monomer to prepare poly(lactic acid) via polycondensation. We propose a simple preparation of m-PLLAs by using core molecules containing multi-functional groups for the functionalization with l-LA. The use of succinic acid (SA), malic acid (MA), and citric acid (CA) allows us to vary the branch number for two, three, and four, respectively (Scheme 1). The work also covers the studies on the blends between PLA and m-PLLAs in order to evaluate the miscibility and the crystallization behavior of PLA, as well as the related physico-chemical and thermal properties in terms of glass transition temperature (Tg), crystallization temperature (Tc) melting point (Tm) and degree of crystallinity (χc), including the mechanical properties. In fact, the inorganic nucleating agents have been used to improve the crystallization rate of PLLA-based polymers, including talc,16 nano-calcium carbonate (CaCO3),17 graphene oxide (GO),18 cellulose nanocrystals (CNC)19 and so on. Wu et al20 showed that the introduction of GO into star-shaped poly(d-lactide)-co-poly(l-lactide) stereoblock copolymers (s-PDLA-PLLA) matrix significantly increased the crystallization ability of s-PDLA-PLLA matrix. Moreover, in our previous published research, the sc-PLA crystals as nucleating agents significantly improved the crystallization rate of PLLA segments in the semi-crystalline PTLG matrix and enhanced mechanical properties of PTLG matrix. Due to the PLLA segment of the PTLG with PDLA chain constructed as stereocomplex structures and could growth to stereocomplex crystals, used it as nucleating agents, thus improving the crystallization ability of PLLA segments in the PTLG/PDLA blends and to understand the nucleating agents, crystallization behavior, the relationship between structure and properties of PTLG/PDLA blends. l-lactide (LLA), d-lactide (D-LA), glycolic acid (GA) and 1,3-trimethylene carbonate (TMC) were purchased from Daigang Biomaterial (China). In the past decade, the application of PLA has widened from the initial biomedical applications to packaging and molded articles.1, 2 Despite its good mechanical properties and processability, PLA has a lower heat resistance for its low glass-transition temperature and low crystallinity.3, 4 The solution for this problem has attracted more attention in recent years.5-7 Many attempts have been made to accelerate the crystallization rate of PLA and increase the crystallinity of PLA by the addition of nucleating agents8-10 or plasticizers.11-13 It is well known that the addition of a plasticizer to increase the chain mobility of PLA tends to increase crystallization rate and extend the crystallization temperature (Tc) window. The most popular plasticizers of PLA in the past decade have been poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)13 and triphenyl phosphate.11, 12 However, the prevailing approach for improving the crystallization ability of PLA has been the addition of a nucleating agent. In fact, there have been many publications reporting different nucleating agents in the past decade. These nucleating agents can be classified into three categories, including inorganic particles, organic compounds, and macromolecular agents.', 'As a highly effective nucleating agent, layered zinc phenylphosphonate (PPZn) is incorporated into polylactic acid (PLA) to investigate the epitaxial crystallization of PLA on PPZn in this study. The corresponding lattice spacing change, crystalline morphology, and crystalline structure are emphasized to reveal the epitaxial crystallization mechanism. As a result, with the increase of PPZn content and the annealing time, the increasing lattice spacing of PPZn and the formation of mutually perpendicular rodlike crystals are observed through x-ray diffraction (XRD) and polarized optical micrograph (POM) measurements, implying that the interlayer spacing of PPZn crystals is expanded as the PLA α-form crystals epitaxially grow on its surface, that is, epitaxial crystallization. To be specific, “edge on” lamellae epitaxial grow on the PPZn crystals along the [010] and [100] directions under two excellent lattice matchings, which possess acceptable mismatching of 0.347% and 7.5%, respectively. With the support of the epitaxial crystallization mechanism, the occurrence of the filamentous structure observed in the fracture morphology of PLA/PPZn composites suggests strong interfacial adhesion between PLA and PPZn, which makes the impact toughness of the PLA/PPZn composites increase by 53.6% compared with pure PLA. Polylactic acid (PLA) is regarded as the most promising substitute for traditional petroleum-based polymers, arising from its excellent biodegradable properties, superior processing properties, and sufficient tensile strength.1-3 However, the slow crystallization rate of PLA, which is driven by the low mobility restricted by the strong polarity of ester groups and the steric effect of side methyl groups, leads to inferior ductility, and extremely limits its feasibility in potential applications.4-6', 'Other inert fillers, such as talc and calcium carbonate, have also made their way into PLA-matrix composites for the above reasons, as well as to reduce cost and improve mechanical properties. Further, the nonpolar nature of PLA makes it difficult to react with reinforcements containing polar moieties such as natural fibers, talc and starch, resulting in poor dispersion, a lack of sufficient adhesion and a reduction in properties. This presents a major disadvantage to PLA matrix composites, providing that they are unable to reach their full performance potential. Consequently, the use of coupling agents or compatibilizers is essential to promote chemical bonding across the filler-matrix interface. Substantial experimental efforts have been made in an attempt to improve the phase interaction of PLA-based composites by reactive compatibilization. This is typically done by modifying either one or both of the composite constituents by grafting or by the incorporation of a third component (a coupling agent) that acts to reduce the interfacial tension between the phases and improves the dispersion of the filler within the PLA matrix. One commonly used coupling agent is maleic anhydride (MA), a polar monomer that has been extensively studied and shown to be quite effective in improving the adhesion between two or more phases due to its highly reactive nature.10-13 The dual reactivity of MA stems from the free radical reactivity of the double bond and the functional reactivity of the cyclic anhydride. Once grafted, an MA-based copolymer can preferentially reside at the interface and act as a bridge between binary phases to improve interfacial adhesion, and thereby result in a finer dispersion and more stable morphology.', 'Highly crystalline PLA exhibits excellent mechanical strength and heat resistance. Polylactide (PLA) is the most well-established biodegradable plastic, with the largest production and widespread utilization [1,2]. PLA exhibits comparable physical and mechanical properties to conventional petroleum-based polymers like polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and polystyrene (PS) [[3], [4], [5]]. It finds extensive in packaging, textile industry, agricultural mulch and biomedical polymer industries, making it an ideal alternative to traditional petroleum-based plastic products [[6], [7], [8], [9]]. However, the slow crystallization rate and low heat-resistance temperature restrict the further development of the PLA. The incorporation of nucleators can effectively reduce the surface free energy barrier required for PLA nucleation, thereby enhancing its crystallization rate [21]. This method currently represents the simplest and most efficient approach to improve the crystallization rate and low heat-resistance properties of PLA. The nucleators commonly employed for PLA include inorganic agents, organic agents, and polymeric nucleators[[10], [11], [12]]. Inorganic nucleators, such as talc, [13,14], montmorillonite (MMT) [15], carbon nanotubes [16], nanocalcium carbonate, nanoclay, silica (SiO2), and graphene oxide (GO), etc. have the advantages of low cost and high modulus [17]. For instance, talc is a very cheap and effective inorganic nucleating agent for PLA. Kolstad et al. [18] demonstrated that the addition of talc to increase the nucleation density of PLA by 500 times and reduce the semi-crystallization time (t1/2) by 7 times. Furthermore, the incorporation of graphene oxide can increase the crystallization temperature of PLA by about 5 °C and increase the crystallinity from 3.7 % to 38 %, while the tensile modulus of PLA composites is significantly increased [19]. However, the application of inorganic nucleators is mainly limited by their high loading requirements and poor compatibility with the PLA matrix, often necessitating complex surface modifications.', 'Nucleating agents are widely used to enhance the crystallisation rate and thus improve the properties of PHA. Many kinds of nucleating agents such as boron nitride (BN) [14], [15], talc [14], [15], lignin [16], orotic acid [17] and saccharine [18] have been proposed for PHBV, with BN being the most effective agent to date [15]. Apart from being used as a nucleating agent, talc has also been used alone or in combination with other fillers as reinforcement for PP [20], [21], [22] and poly(lactic acid) (PLA) [23], [24], to improve their melt strength and stiffness. It has also been used as an additive to aid processing [25] and as a post processing step to improve the surface quality of the final product [26]. Talc is a natural mineral with Mg3(Si4O10)-(OH)2 as the unit structure. Its low cost and ease of processing make it particularly attractive as a sub-filler in PHBV WPCs, to provide performance enhancement and as an additional cost benefit. It is reported that a PHBV/wood flour/talc 60%/20%/20% hybrid composite demonstrated enhanced stiffness and strength when compared to PHBV/wood flour 60%/40% [27]. In another study, 5 wt% of talc was added to every composite formulation in an investigation into the effect of compatibilisers in wood flour/PHB composites, in order to improve water resistance and processability. However, the impact of talc alone was not studied in this case so a conclusion cannot be drawn about its contribution in isolation of other factors [25]. In the present work, the effect of inclusion of both BN and talc on radiata pine wood flour/PHBV composites with a wood content similar to that of commercial WPCs was investigated. Samples were prepared using a single-step extrusion process. Based solely on the provided context, nucleating agents like talc and zinc phenylphosphonate (PPZn) play the following critical roles in the injection molding of PLA:

1.  **Acceleration of Crystallization Rate:** They significantly increase the speed of PLA crystallization during cooling in the mold.
    *   Talc: "effectively enhance the crystallization rate of PLA through fast nucleation and a high growth rate" [1], "dramatically decreased the crystallization half-time (t1/2) of PLLA" [2], "reduced the half-crystallization time (t1/2) by 7 times" [8], "the crystallization half-time of PLA was significantly reduced by more than one order of magnitude to less than 3 min" at 1 wt% [12].
    *   PPZn: "the crystallization rate of PLLA with small amount of PPZn was much higher than that of neat PLLA, and the half-time (t1/2) of PLLA/PPZn sample is far less than that of neat PLLA" [2].

2.  **Reduction of Cycle Time:** By accelerating crystallization, they directly shorten the required cooling/solidification time within the mold, increasing productivity.
    *   "Crystallization speed has a profound effect on the productivity of injection molding" [1].
    *   "the cycle period in injection molding processes becomes shorten" [3].

3.  **Improvement of Thermal Deformation Resistance:** Enhanced crystallization leads to higher crystallinity, which improves the heat resistance (Heat Deflection Temperature - HDT) of the final molded part.
    *   "the thermal deformation of the product is improved by crystallization" [1].
    *   "the heat distortion temperature values suggested that the modified PLA could resist the thermal deformation from 58 °C to a maximum value of 139 °C when 1 µm talc was added at 10 wt%" [10].
    *   "enhance the heat deflection temperature of PLLA matrix" [2].

4.  **Increase in Crystallinity:** They promote the formation of a higher degree of crystallinity in the PLA part.
    *   Talc: "leading to more perfect crystals" [1], "increased the degree of crystallinity" [10].
    *   PPZn: "increased the degree of crystallinity of PLLA" [2].

5.  **Modification of Crystal Morphology:** They influence nucleation density and spherulite size.

The rubber phase with smaller size can produce more small stress concentration-induced plastic deformation in the matrix, resulting in better toughness [[20], [21], [22]]. Ideally, the polymer is allowed and desired to biodegrade only at its end-of-use time, that is, after a minimum period of in-use time, while the expected time-in-use differs per application. In anticipation of a further tightening of regulatory requirements and as a consequence of the introduction of sustainability targets in industry, in the next decade or so, industry targets to replace the currently used and predominantly non-biodegradable high value water-soluble and water-dispersible polymers by biodegradable alternatives, wherever sustainably possible. To achieve this goal and deliver a contribution to a more sustainable way of life, it is key to recognize the challenges of the introduction of a biodegradable polymer in these applications.', 'Polymer degradation is defined as the “chemical changes in a polymeric material that usually result in undesirable changes in the in-use properties of the material” [184]. In spite of such definition and within the framework here discussed, the term degradation is considered an enormous asset instead of an undesirable property as many polymers should be degradable to avoid their accumulation in the environment. Polymer degradation is an irreversible phenomenon that takes place through scission of the main chain or side chain of the macromolecules. Under natural conditions, polymer degradation may be induced by processes such as photolysis, oxidation, radiolysis, thermal activation, hydrolysis or biological activity [185]. It should be taken into account that degradable does not necessarily mean biodegradable. A wide number of polymers which undergo fragmentation into smaller pieces and even degrade into invisible residues to the naked eye are available. Although these materials are eroded (or degraded) into microscopic pieces and several synthetic approaches are available to accelerate this process, such microgranules may accumulate in the oceans or landfills as they are not completely degraded within a reasonable period of time [186]. Henceforth, this fragmentation does not mean biodegradation per se. Accordingly, the American Society of Testing and Materials (ASTM), in its standard D6813 defines the term biodegradability as “capable of undergoing decomposition into carbon dioxide, methane, water, inorganic compounds, or biomass in which the predominant mechanism is the enzymatic action of microorganisms, that can be measured by standardized tests in a specified period of time, reflecting available disposal conditions”. Similarly, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) defined a biodegradable polymer as a “polymer susceptible to degradation by biological activity, with the degradation accompanied by a lowering of its molar mass” [184]. Essentially, during biodegradation, long macromolecular chains are broken down in vitro or in vivo by enzymes (and other biologically active entities) into shorter chains, which are further metabolized by microorganisms. Among all the available degradation processes, hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation are of special interest as they allow closed‐loop recycling processes which are seen as the preferred choice to face current plastic waste issues [187]. Indeed, hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation are the most important degradation mechanisms in polyesters thanks to the high susceptibility of the ester linkages to chemical hydrolysis and microbial/enzymatic chain cleavage reactions. Polyester hydrolytic degradation is defined as the scission of ester bond linkages in the backbone via H2O uptake to yield first oligomers, and then monomers [188]. Enzymatic degradation occurs when the action of living organisms such as enzymes cut down the macromolecules into lower molar mass chains, which are then bio-assimilated and mineralized by such living organism to yield H2O and CO2 or CH4 depending if the process is aerobic or anaerobic respectively [188], [189], [190]. In some cases, the degradation could also undergo through combined mechanisms of microbial, enzymatic and chemical hydrolysis.']
response: The primary environmental risk associated with the degradation of biodegradable polymers in anaerobic landfills is the **generation and release of methane (CH₄)**, a potent greenhouse gas. Under anaerobic conditions, biodegradation of organic materials, including biodegradable plastics, produces methane alongside CO₂. Methane has a global warming potential 25 times greater than CO₂ over a 100-year period. Landfills, especially those with uncontrolled management, often lack adequate biogas capture systems, allowing methane to escape into the atmosphere. In the U.S., methane capture rates in landfills were only ~20% as of 2017, exacerbating climate impacts. This uncontrolled methane emission from landfills represents a significant environmental hazard compared to controlled anaerobic digestion facilities, where methane is captured for energy use.
reference: In anaerobic landfill conditions, the microbial degradation of biodegradable polymers (like PLA or PHAs) generates methane (CH4) rather than just CO2. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential ~25-30 times higher than CO2, necessitating methane capture systems to mitigate climate impact.

retrieved_contexts: ['SEM studies confirmed that the degradation process mediated by glutathione takes place by bulk-degradation. The bioavailability of drugs systemically administered is usually very low, and plasma concentration may be below the effective levels. Advances in materials chemistry have improved the development of new biodegradable and biocompatible drug delivery systems to enhance the drug bioavailability, and are focused on a specific therapeutic target [1]. The development of advanced polymeric systems for drug delivery and release, capable of response under physiological stimuli, such as changes in pH, enzyme concentration, or redox gradients, has become a hot topic in the last few years [2], [3], [4] but biodegradability is a major objective to overcome side effects and avoid toxicity [5]. Today, cancer therapy demands more-efficient, non-toxic drug carriers, which specifically may reach the exact target site for delivery responding to endogenous stimuli such as the hypoxic microenvironment of tumor cells. Among different approaches, disulfide bond-containing polymers are the most common redox-responsive drug carriers because the disulfide bond is sensitive to thiol-type reductants, such as glutathione (GSH). A drug release mechanism based on thiol-disulfide exchange mediated by GSH in cells reduces the disulfide linkages in the polymer and the drug is subsequently released [5], [6]. It has been found that GSH is at a higher concentration in cytosol than in the extracellular fluids [7], [8], [9], and is greatly increased in tumor cells [10], [11], [12], [13], where higher GSH levels maintain the redox status and suppress apoptosis, which may explain certain drug resistance behaviors [6]. Another important observation deals with a direct correlation between the changes in the balance of the redox status with metastatic activity, which may benefit metastatic cancer treatment [14]. Moreover, a high degree of control over degradation is required for tunable release of encapsulated anticancer drugs, as well as bioconjugation for active tumor-targeting [15], [16].', "It is a critical issue to control the release of drugs in both temporal and spatial manners for maximum therapeutic benefits in cancer therapy. However, ordinary polyurethane nanocarriers fail due to the lack of a triggering mechanism, thus resulting in an insufficient drug concentration.19,20 To address the challenges, stimuli-responsive degradable polyurethanes have been extensively exploited by the programmable stimuli applied. In particular, the redox-responsive cleavage degradation has been recognized as an innovative and creative strategy for rapid degradation and enhanced site-specific drug release.21-25 These systems usually contain characteristic disulfide and diselenide bonds that demonstrate excellent stability during blood circulation but rapidly degrade and effectively trigger “on-demand” drug release in a reductive environment.26,27 Compared with disulfide bonds, the diselenide bonds have a preferable responsiveness due to the lower bond energy (Se-Se: 172 kJ mol−1; S-S: 240 kJ mol−1), which suggests that diselenide containing nanocarriers may improve the drug concentration at target sites to optimize the therapeutic efficacy.28-30 Thus, diselenide containing nanocarriers are considered more benign for clinical translation.31,32 Xu and Zhang's group has reported a series of diselenide-containing multi-cleavable polyurethanes via the polymerization of toluene diisocyanate (TDI) with di-(1-hydroxylundecyl) diselenide diols and finally terminated with poly(ethylene glycol) monomethylether. It is found that the micelles could almost entirely release the encapsulated drug in only 5 h under reductive conditions.31,33,34 Poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) is one of the most commonly used synthetic biodegradable polymers in various formulations for drug delivery due to its excellent biocompatibility and permeability for drugs.35,36 In our previous study, diselenide-centered copolymers methoxyl poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(ε-caprolactone)-b-methoxyl poly(ethylene glycol) were synthesized and employed for activated intracellular drug release.37 Nevertheless, only one diselenide bond was located on the backbone of the copolymers, which showed a slow release profile of the encapsulated drug. Only about 54% drug was released within 48 h in 30 mM GSH solution. It is well known that PCL is widely used as the soft segment to regulate the biocompatibility and biodegradability of polyurethane.38,39 However, few successful examples of redox-responsive polyurethane based on PCL have been reported. In this study, we report an enhanced bioreduction responsive system based on the amphiphilic diselenide-containing PCL-based poly(ester urethane) as a prominent controlled drug delivery platform. Multiple diselenide groups are positioned repeatedly on the backbone of hydrophobic blocks, resulting in an amplification of the reduction responsiveness. The self-assembly behavior of the copolymers and the redox responsiveness of the constructed micelles are further investigated in detail. Meanwhile, the glutathione (GSH)-mediated drug release and antitumor activity of DOX-loaded micelles are evaluated using a disulfide-containing analogue as the control. It should be noted that diselenide-containing polymers have an enhanced redox responsiveness in comparison with disulfide-containing analogues. Therefore, the smart nanocarriers, which unite an enhanced redox responsiveness and high biocompatibility, may represent an addition to the very small toolbox of systems for site-specific drug delivery to realize superior therapeutic efficacy.", 'Polymeric amphiphiles can form nanosized self-assemblies-spherical micelles-with an inner core of hydrophobic segments and an outer shell of hydrophilic segments in aqueous media, due to the intra- and/or intermolecular interactions of hydrophobic segments [1]. These polymeric micelles that form through the self-assembly of amphiphilic block copolymers exhibit many merits, such as nanoscale dimensions, core-shell structure, relatively high stability due to their low critical micelle concentration (CMC), and prolonged circulation because of their high water solubility [2]. In recent years, they have attracted wide scientific and technological interest due to their potential use as nanosized carriers of drugs that show poor solubility in water [3]. Controlled release of the loaded drug can be achieved through diffusion from the micelles or by the biodegradation of amphiphilic polymers. Many investigations [4-6] have reported that these self-assemblies, when used as drug-delivery systems, can reduce unwanted toxic side effects, increase the solubility of drugs that are poorly water soluble (by storing them within the hydrophobic core of the micelle), prolong the circulation time, reduce uptake by the reticuloendothelial system (RES), and enhance the therapeutic indices of drugs. Among the various polymeric amphiphiles that could potentially act as drug carriers, block copolymers of biodegradable poly-L-lactic acid (PLA) are the most attractive [7, 8]. Aliphatic polyesters such as PLA have high potential for use as biomaterials and environmentally friendly materials because of their hydrolytic and/or enzymatic degradation into products that are ultimately metabolized in most cases [9]. PLA is a biodegradable material with low toxicity and excellent biocompatibility; it has therefore been incorporated into the cores of micelles and used as a matrix for controlled drug release [1]. It has been reported that copolymers that include PLA can be synthesized through a combination of atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) and other polymerization methods such as chemical ring-opening polymerization (ROP) [10, 11]. In recent years, interest has grown in epoxy-based copolymers such as glycidyl methacrylate (GMA), which have been used in advanced biotechniques such as DNA separation, enzyme immobilization, and targeted drug delivery [12-14]. Controlled/“living” radical polymerization procedures can be used to prepare copolymers with predetermined molecular weights and narrow molecular weight distributions. Importantly, polymer chains prepared by atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) are highly end-functionalized and can therefore participate in various post-polymerization modifications and serve as macroinitiators in the synthesis of block copolymers [15, 16]. Amphiphilic acrylate- and lactone-based block copolymers find application in the fabrication of polymer systems for a variety of biomedical applications, ranging from controlled release systems used in drug delivery [17] to the fabrication of degradable surgical implants. The acrylate group allows the synthesis of systems that are nondegradable but readily tunable-in terms of hydrophilicity [18], pH- and temperature-induced phase behavior [19], and loading with therapeutic agents [20], for instance-through simple variation of the acrylate substituent. Further advantages of combining these blocks include the selective introduction of large numbers of functional groups via the polyacrylate block, the generation of amphiphilic block copolymers, and the creation of partially biodegradable structures. Nevertheless, only a few examples of the synthesis of polyester-block-polyacrylate copolymers via ROP of a lactone and ATRP of an acrylate have been described in the literature so far [10, 11, 17, 18, 21, 22]. Among the vast number of potential comonomer combinations, block copolymer systems based on lactide and glycidyl methacrylate (GMA) have not been reported so far, even though each of these polymers has been successfully and usefully employed in biomedical applications.', "Due to their biocompatibility, synthetic and naturally occurring polymers have been employed in the medical industry for various purposes, including enhanced medication delivery, 3-D printing, nanocarrier, etc. Since polymers can enhance the dosage of a specific effective component, they are thought to be more effective for pharmaceutical formulations. By permitting insertion into the sick tissue, they can also lessen the patient's adverse effects by increasing medication loading at the location while lowering systemic concentration [24]. It is well acknowledged that polymers can improve a formulation for ocular medication administration by their mucoadhesive characteristics. These increase the contact time of dosage form with the ocular layers and diminish the difficulty of quick elimination from the ocular segment, which is frequently encountered by topical ocular formulations [24, 25]. Biodegradable polymers are appealing as they can be broken down into monomers and produce a consistent rate of medicine release. In reaction to stimuli, bio-responsive polymers can change their form due to phase separation, shape changes, or permeability variations. This makes it possible for the medication to be discharged from the composition as per the requirement [26]. The improvements being made in the delivery of eye medications exemplify the benefits of biopolymers. For instance, numerous scholars have studied ocular implants for irritation reactions [27]. Although nanotechnology has been utilized to create many new formulations, polymers are likewise employed to improve or optimize more traditional medicaments. It has been demonstrated by including polymers with mucoadhesive belongings in an ophthalmic drop, the medicine will be maintained at the site longer and have a higher bioavailability [28]. These polymers are frequently engaged in biomedical studies due to their well-known biocompatibility and biodegradability [26]. The improvements in medicine delivery for the eyes show the benefits of bio-responsive polymers. For instance, numerous studies have examined implants to respond to the eye's inflammatory responses [29]. Various biopolymers used for ocular polymeric nanoparticles such as chitosan (CH), guar gum (GG), sodium hyaluronate (SH), collagen, locust bean gum (LBG), gelatin, gum cordia (GC), polydopamine (PD), and alginate are elaborated in the following.", 'Biodegradable polymers have increasingly gained attention in drug carriers, which can control the release rate of drugs to fit different requirements [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]. Some drugs need burst release within a short time to accelerate hemostasis and promote wound healing, whereas sustained release over a longer period is more widely used, which brings about stable drug absorption levels, fewer side effects, and better patient compliance [6], [7], [8], [9]. These different requirements of drug release can be regulated by the degradation rate of biodegradable polymers [10], [11], [12]. Therefore, controllable degradability plays an important role in biodegradable polymers used as drug delivery. Chitosan-graft-poly (lactic acid) (CS-g-PLA) is considered to be a promising candidate in drug delivery due to its nontoxicity, biodegradation, and excellent biocompatibility. CS-g-PLA exhibited better degradability than both chitosan and PLA, and its degradation rate can be controlled by regulating the molar substitution of PLA (MSPLA) [13]. CS-g-PLA with low MSPLA is easy hydrolyze in vivo, which is suited to the burst release of drugs in the early phases [14], [15]. There were much published studies on the CS-g-PLA with low MSPLA. For instance, it was earlier prepared in heterogeneous reaction media like dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) or N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF), where the DSPLA (the degree of substitution of PLA) was only 1.03 even though the copolymerization was carried out for 24 h, leading to a low MSPLA of 3.85 [13,16]. Compared to DMSO and DMF, ionic liquids are excellent homogeneous synthesis system for the glycan-graft-aliphatic polyester copolymers and are fewer harmful to human health [17], [18], [19]. Hence some research synthesized CS-g-PLA in the ionic liquid of chlorine such as 1-Allyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride (AmimCl) and 1-Butyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride (BmimCl) with a catalyst of Sn(Oct)2 [20], [21]. Although these ionic liquids of chlorine raised the DSPLA to 1.47, DPPLA was only 1.93 resulting in a low MSPLA as well. However, very few studies have focused on the efficient synthesis of CS-g-PLA with high MSPLA, even fewer on the controllable degradation of CS-g-PLA with high MSPLA. Therefore, we expect to synthesis a CS-g-PLA copolymer within a short time but with high MSPLA and controllable degradation rate, that the sustained release of drugs loaded in CS-g-PLA can be achieved by regulating the degradation rate. 1-ethy-3-methyimidazolium acetate (EmimAc), as an acetate ionic liquid, possessed not only better chitosan solubility but also smaller viscosity than chloride ionic liquid, so that its solution maintained good fluidity at a high feed ratio. Besides, 4-Dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP) was a more powerful catalyst for the ring-opening polymerization than Sn(Oct)2 [22]. Combining the advantages above two, in our study, chitosan-graft-poly(D, L-lactic acid) copolymers (CgPCs) with high MSPDLLA were synthesized fast through the eco-friendly system of EmimAc/DMAP. Then the biodegradability of these CgPCs was estimated in vitro by hydrolytic and enzymatic means. We selected PBS solution (pH 7.4), lysozyme, and porcine pancreas lipase as the medium to simulate in vivo environment. Meanwhile, hydrophobic curcumin was chosen as a model drug to investigate the drug release during the degradation of CgPCs (Scheme 1).', 'Over the last two decades, biodegradable polymers have been considered as one of the popular choices for oral drug delivery [1], [2], [3] and also for protein and peptide delivery in oral vaccination [4], [5], [6]. Natural and synthetic biodegradable polymers comprise of several advantages such as tissue compatibility, biodegradability, low toxicity, sustained release property with specific target-oriented delivery approaches [7], [8], [9]. The multifarious applications of biodegradable polymers cover an enormous area in novel drug delivery system and oral vaccination. If one considers various biomolecules like proteins and peptides to be used for vaccination through oral route, biodegradable polymer plays significant role either by protecting these substances from harsh acidic environment of stomach or by providing sustained release which may be useful in reducing dose (either booster or maintenance dose) frequency for oral vaccination [10], [11], [12]. Such kind of strategies have been employed in water borne diseases like cholera and auto immune diseases like atrophic rhinitis [13], [14]. Bioavailability is a major concern for various therapeutic molecules delivered through oral route [15]. Oral bioavailability problem of drugs arises due to their poor solubility and less permeability through biological membranes [16]. However, the pre-systemic metabolism also can significantly affect the bioavailability of therapeutic molecules along with these two parameters (solubility and permeability) [17]. Orally administered drugs (except drugs intended through buccal and sublingual route) generally have to pass through the intestinal wall and portal circulation of liver before they reach to systemic circulation [18], [19]. Intestinal and hepatic enzymes significantly metabolise drugs and may result in poor bioavailability due to inadequate plasma concentration required for the desired therapeutic response [20]. The importance and comparison of the role of hepatic and intestinal enzymes in the bioavailability of various therapeutic molecules are also studied. The reports suggest the predominant role of intestinal enzymes in pre-systemic metabolism over hepatic enzymes because there is relatively high blood supply in liver as compared to intestine. Thus, the residence time of therapeutic molecules in intestine is relatively high as compared to liver as a result drugs remain in contact with intestinal enzyme for more time and ultimately lead to higher metabolism and poor bioavailability [21], [22]. The biodegradable polymers have shown various promising applications in improving the bioavailability of such therapeutic molecules with poor bioavailability. Curcumin obtained from turmeric (Curcuma longa) possesses several medicinal properties but low aqueous solubility limits its therapeutic efficacy [23], [24]. Due to its hydrophobicity, curcumin is poorly bioavailable. Bioavailability of curcumin has been effectively modified by encapsulating it in biodegradable polymer preparations like PLGA-curcumin (poly lactic acid-co-glycolic acid curcumin) [25] and cyclodextrin encapsulated curcumin [26]. Several bioactive molecules effective in number of diseases have been successfully encapsulated using biodegradable polymers in order to obtain improved bioavailability, controlled release, targeted delivery and reduced side effects. Gomez-Gaete et al. encapsulated dexamethasone into biodegradable poly (D, L-lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) nanoparticles to avoid side effects arise in systemic administration of the drug alone into the vitreous cavity. The developed nanoparticulate delivery system provided improved drug retention in the vitreous cavity as well as improved targeting efficiency [27]. Oral bioavailability of daunorubicin (DAUN) was 10-fold improved when chitosan coated DAUN-PLGA nanoparticles were given to wister rats as compared to free DAUN [28]. Mady and Shaker enhanced oral bioavailability of ellagic acid (EA) (naturally occurring bioactive in cancer therapy), formulating ellagic acid-nanoparticles (EA-NPs) using poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) as the biodegradable polymer. In vivo study revealed 3.6-fold increase in area under the curve for EA-NPs as compared to EA alone [29]. When therapeutic molecules are incorporated into polymeric systems, some major criteria are taken into consideration such as encapsulation efficiency, retention time which ultimately lead to the improvement in bioavailability of therapeutic molecules [30]. It has also been observed that the drug conjugated with biodegradable polymer is much superior with respect to therapeutic impact and also in terms of controlled and targeted delivery [31], [32]. Further, improvement in therapeutic efficacy and targeted delivery may be influenced by particle size, hydrophobicity, surface charge and surface modification of conjugated system [33]. The size, shape and structure of nanoparticles control their physico-chemical properties which play very important role during their transportation across the biological membranes [34]. It is generally agreed that decrease in particles size increases absorption of particulate systems [35]. Surface charge is also important for absorption of therapeutic molecules across the biological barrier and generally it also determines the interaction of molecules with charged biological membranes [36], [37]. Lipophilicity is another important parameter to ascertain bioavailability of the drugs and in nutshell, smaller particle size with proper hydrophilic-lipophilic balance is always preferable to get desired therapeutic response. In this context, polymeric nanoparticles have done considerably better job to improve the bioavailability of numerous drugs. In some disease conditions like cancer, it is also desirable that drug concentration should be constant and continuous at the targeted site in single dose formulation [38], [39]. Sometimes chemotherapy with drug alone leads serious side effects due to higher concentration at a particular site and such condition may be completely avoided by incorporating the therapeutic molecule in conjugated system with biopolymers [40], [41]. In recent time, polymeric micro-/nano-particulate systems such as microspheres [42], [43], microparticles [44], [45], [46] and nanoparticles [47], [48], [49], [50] have gained much importance not only for the delivery of synthetic or natural drug molecules but also for the delivery of the therapeutic protein, peptide and oligonucleotides through oral route.', "Biodegradable polymers have vast applications in the areas of drug design, development and therapy [101]. To obtain steady drug release, the two prominent groups of polymeric materials, i.e., degradable polymeric and porous polymers, are used. These polymers are used to encapsulate the drug compounds [102]. The biodegradable hyper-branched polyglycerols consisting of oligo caprolactone segments in the backbone (hPGOCs) are used as intradermal drug delivery. This polymer penetrates the skin and transports the hydrophobic guest molecules through the stratum corneum into deeper skin layers [103]. These hPGOCs may degrade into lighter fragments in the presence of the enzymes' skin lysate [104]. Because of this property, there will be a facilitated release of drugs and less accumulation inside the tissues without causing any serious effect on the viable dermal layers [103]. The biodegradable silk fibroin (SF)/alginate blend films are used in the controlled release delivery system for water-soluble drugs. It is used in the controlled release of an antimicrobial model drug called tetracycline hydrochloride [105]. The biodegradable PLA thin-film composites which are developed by using polylactic acid and microspheres of hydrothermally converted coralline hydroxyapatite (cHAp) are used in drug delivery systems for regeneration [106]. In this system, PLA provides flexibility and biodegradability to the drug delivery system [107]. On the other hand, coralline hydroxyapatite supplies a sufficient amount of phosphate and calcium ions for bone regeneration [106]. Electrospun nanofibers have a high surface area-volume ratio and these fibers possess interconnected pores which enhance dissolution rate and therapeutics index because this property is more likely used in drug delivery [97]. Biodegradable thermoresponsive polymers like collagen, gelatin, cellulose, poly(N-vinyl caprolactam) is used for drug delivery system [98]. Silk fibroin-poly(sebacic acid) diacetoxy terminated (SF-PSADT) polymeric composite coatings are used in drug delivery. This polymer prevents drug denaturation and also enhances drug stability. Here, the SF matrix can be degraded by enzymes and get excretes without any side effects from the body [108].", 'To increase drug bioavailability, a new strategy is used, which consists to entrap the drug in appropriate delivery systems and aims to control drug release and prevent harmful side effects. Recently, the focus was mainly put on the application of biocompatible and biodegradable polymers to drug delivery systems that allow the transport of a specific drug in a small limited amount. Emulsion solvent evaporation is the most applicable method and has received much attention due to its ease of fabrication and the use of mild conditions (ambient temperature and pressure), without altering the drug activity.33 Moreover, this method gives good results when lipophilic drugs are encapsulated, such as valsartan.', 'Biodegradable polymers for drug delivery systems The development of biodegradable polymers for DDS exploits their ability to self-assemble into nanocarriers that encapsulate therapeutic agents with high specificity. Effective polymeric DDS must satisfy rigorous performance and safety standards: they should encapsulate the drug efficiently [103], exhibit prolonged residence at the target site, improve bioavailability for optimal therapeutic action, and support local tissue repair and regeneration [125]. Crucially, biodegradability alone is insufficient-biocompatibility is equally imperative. The polymers must be non-toxic in vivo and should not provoke adverse immune or inflammatory responses [126]. The efficacy of such nanocarriers is dictated by physicochemical factors including polymer composition, molecular weight, surface charge, nanoparticle size distribution, colloidal stability, hydrophobic-hydrophilic balance, and aggregation tendencies [78]. Many systems leverage the hydrophobic nature of drug molecules along with the amphiphilic architecture of polymeric carriers to achieve targeted and efficient delivery. PHA-based nanomedicine for targeted DDS', 'PEG-PCL co-polymeric nano formulations with various anticancer drugs as drug delivery platforms. Two essential criteria for an efficient drug delivery system include both the quantity and the duration of drug presence inside it. Drug delivery systems are mainly concerned with site-targeting within the body and pose various systemic challenges, e.g. minimizing drug degradation and loss, increasing drug bioavailability, averting unfavorable side-effects by delivering the drug at appropriate targeted area, developing broadened medicated conveyance frameworks, etc. Various medications focusing on frameworks which meet these requirements are currently under different levels of development. In a drug delivery system, the drugs/bioactives are carried inside the body in water soluble vehicles like polymers, microcapsules, lipoproteins, liposomes, micelles, vesicles or microparticles, etc. comprising of biodegradable synthetic polymers [1]. These carriers could be efficiently molded for slow degradation, stimuli-reactive responses and for their targeted delivery approach. The drug targeting is the ability of the drug-loaded system to act directly at the site of interest. The approach of site-directed drug release systems is differentiated by two major mechanisms: (i) passive and (ii) active targeting. The significant ways for the development of successful formulations are controlled drug release and successive biodegradation. The release mechanism depends upon (i) a surface-bound or adsorbed drugs that are released from or through a surface; (ii) diffusion of drug through the carrier matrix; (iii) in nanocapsules, diffusion turn up through the carrier wall; (iv) deterioration of carrier matrix; and (v) a combination of deterioration and diffusion process [2]. A wide variety of synthetic and natural polymers have attained significant attention in drug delivery processes, out of them the biodegradable aliphatic and aromatic polyesters have offered new perspectives in the field of anticancer drug delivery systems [[3], [4], [5], [6]]. In this category, the biodegradable polymers which have been well studied for the preparation of various types of nanoparticles for anticancer applications are poly (lactic-co-glycolic acid, PLGA) [7], polylactic acid (PLA) [8] and polycaprolactone (PCL) [9]. In drug delivery domain, poly (ethylene glycol) (PEG) has played a major fundamental role as both biocompatible and biodegradable carrier along with its other beneficial aspects. PEG is mostly used as a protective covering for anticancer drugs viz. as lysosome [10], nanoparticles [11] and also as covalently bonded conjugates to various proteins [12] and drug molecules [13]. PEG monomer unit comprises of both polar oxygen atom and a non-polar (CH2)2 unit. So, PEG is soluble in a wide assortment of both polar and nonpolar solvents [14] and has been commonly utilized as a bearer for hydrophobic drugs to improve their water solubility or disintegration attributes [[15], [16], [17]].', 'Biodegradable polymers offer a unique combination of properties that can be tailored to suit nearly any controlled drug delivery application. The most common biodegradable polymers used for biomedical applications are semicrystalline polyesters and polyethers which possess good mechanical properties and have been used in many controlled release applications. Drug release from these polymers may be controlled by several mechanisms and these include diffusion of drug through a matrix, dissolution of polymer matrix and degradation of the polymer. This study aims to investigate the degradation and drug release properties of polyglycolide (1.03 dL/g), in which, cis platin, an anticancer agent was used as the model drug. The degradation behaviour of the chosen polymer is thought to largely govern the release of the anticancer agent in vitro.', 'Controlling the release of pharmaceutical compounds to the specific site of action, with increased therapeutic bioavailability and minimized side effects or toxicity, has attracted much attention in recent years. Oral drug delivery is one of the most convenient and preferred routes of drug administration due to both ease of production and flexibility in the design of dosage form, but the barrier of the gastrointestinal tract remains the main obstacle.[1, 2] The incorporation of the drug into a polymeric matrix can enhance its protection against degradation in harsh physiological media, and it can prolong the biological activity by controlling the release.[3, 4] Recently, a wide range of biopolymers have been used as drug carriers that effectively protect the load from the highly acidic environment of the stomach and enhance the absorption of hydrophilic substances to the specific target.[5] Natural polymers are good candidates for drug carriers due to their excellent biocompatibility and biodegradability.[6-8] Chitosan is a natural linear polyaminosaccharide obtained by alkaline deacetylation of chitin, which is the second most abundant polysaccharide, next to cellulose.[9] Because of its biocompatibility, nontoxicity, and antibacterial properties, it is a very attractive biomaterial to be used as a drug carrier.[10-12] Sodium alginate is another readily available polysaccharide with nontoxic nature and also biocompatible.[13-15] Chitosan and sodium alginate can both form hydrogel beads when cross-linked with a suitable polyvalent cationic or an anionic cross-linking agent and, hence, they are potentially able to encapsulate a large number of therapeutic molecules in their structure.[16] Depending on the polarity of the polymer matrix, the release of the encapsulated drugs can follow different mechanisms. Based solely on the provided context, "smart biodegradable polymers" refer to polymers designed for drug delivery systems that exhibit biodegradability combined with responsiveness to specific physiological stimuli. Here are their key characteristics:

1.  **Stimuli-Responsiveness:** They degrade or change structure in response to specific biological triggers within the body ([1], [2], [4], [5]):
    *   **Redox Gradients:** Especially sensitive to glutathione (GSH) levels, utilizing disulfide or diselenide bonds that cleave in the high GSH environment of cytosol and tumor cells ([1], [2]).
    *   **pH Changes:** Degrade or release drug in response to pH variations in different body compartments ([1]).
    *   **Enzyme Concentration:** Designed to be cleaved by specific enzymes present at the target site ([1]).
    *   **Other Stimuli:** Context also mentions response to phase separation, shape changes, or permeability variations triggered by biological conditions ([4]).

2.  **Biodegradability:** They are designed to break down into non-toxic components within the body after fulfilling their drug delivery function, avoiding long-term accumulation and toxicity ([1], [2], [3], [5], [10], [14]).

3.  **Controlled/Targeted Drug Release:** The responsiveness allows for:
    *   **Site-Specific Release:** Degradation and drug release triggered primarily at the target site (e.g., tumor cells due to high GSH) ([1], [2]).
    *   **"On-Demand" Release:** Rapid release triggered by the specific physiological stimulus ([2]).
    *   **Tunable Release Rates:** Degradation rates can be controlled (e.g., by adjusting copolymer composition or substitution levels like MSPLA in CS-g-PLA) to achieve burst or sustained release profiles ([5]).

4.  **Enhanced Functionality:** Compared to ordinary biodegradable polymers, their "smart" nature provides:
    *   **Improved Therapeutic Efficacy:** Higher drug concentration at the target site ([1], [2]).
    *   **Reduced Side Effects:** Minimized systemic exposure and toxicity ([1], [4]).
    *   **Overcoming Drug Resistance:** Mechanisms like exploiting tumor redox status ([1]).

**Examples from Context:**
*   Disulfide bond-containing polymers responsive to GSH ([1]).
*   Diselenide-containing polyurethanes and PCL-based poly(ester urethane)s (with enhanced redox responsiveness compared to disulfide analogues) ([2]).
*   Bio-responsive polymers changing form in response to stimuli for ocular or other delivery ([4]).
*   Chitosan-graft-poly(lactic acid) (CS-g-PLA) copolymers with degradation rate controllable via MSPLA ([5]).

The rubbers included in this research were isoprene rubber (IR), acrylic rubber (AR), acrylic core-shell rubber (CSR), thermoplastic polyester (TPE) and thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). The performance of these rubber-toughened PLA will be discussed and compared.', 'Nowadays, the importance of bio-based polymers is emerging due to environmental issues.
