Notably, land-use change (LUC) emissions are frequently excluded from conventional LCA inventories, despite their critical influence. For example, reverting land to secondary forest can substantially decrease atmospheric CO₂ fluxes and deliver co-benefits for biodiversity and hydrological cycles. Conversely, diverting land for dedicated bioplastic feedstock cultivation can intensify ecosystem stress, reduce habitat complexity, and undermine soil carbon stocks. Under certain scenarios such as planting feedstocks on long-cultivated croplands increases in both soil and aboveground carbon stocks have been observed. However, these outcomes are highly system-specific and necessitate rigorous environmental and socio-economic analyses to validate their sustainability credentials [129]. Persisting industry gaps', 'The role of biodegradable plastics is in waste treatment due to aerobic degradation into CO2 and H2O or anaerobic degradation to CH4. Hence, they contribute at the back end. Our lessons learned while marketing PLA as biodegradable plastics are as follows. First, each after-use treatment has its own issues. For example, there are three main issues with composting: collection and sorting of biodegradable materials, quality of the final compost to meet public acceptance, and the number of facilities to accommodate the waste. (In the late 1990s, only 30 composting facilities existed in Japan.) Second, there is a concern that the word biodegradability may cause a moral hazard risk such as littering in the environment. Third, the balance between stability during use and storage and the degradability after use needs to be adjusted in each application. Although appropriate physical properties, including stability, are required during storage and use, biodegradable products need to degrade after use. For example, applications for fishing nets and lines were anticipated as a solution to marine pollution in the early 1990s, but the physical properties of such products did not meet the requirements. Expectations for biodegradable plastics can be summarized in the following messages. Only providing biodegradable materials is not a viable solution. A business model, social “Closed System,” and materials for waste treatment such as composting for each use must be taken into consideration. Second, education, cultural, and behavioral changes are important to promote sorting and prevent moral hazards such as littering. In addition, if bio-based resources are used, they contribute to GHG emission reduction. Technology and market developments of biodegradable plastics have continued after the completion of social implementation projects using biodegradable plastics such as the ones shown in Section 4. Such initiatives include changes in raw materials and production process development31 to further reduce the environmental burden as well as a biodegradability study32, 33 from the viewpoint of sustainability. Additionally, business activities to demonstrate a “closed loop” system have been implemented in a fast food restaurant chain34 in which all cups, forks, knives, and packaging are compostable. These materials, along with leftover foods, are gathered, transported to a municipal composting facility, and composted. We believe that large-scale and successful businesses will not be realized without accumulating this type of niche business model.', 'The role of biodegradable plastics is in waste treatment due to aerobic degradation into CO2 and H2O or anaerobic degradation to CH4. We believe that large-scale and successful businesses will not be realized without accumulating this type of niche business model.', 'The recycling of bioplastics: advantages and Obstacles The sustainability of plastics, regardless of their origin or compostability, heavily depends on their inclusion in recycling systems. While non-biodegradable plastics are commonly viewed as recyclable, biodegradable bioplastics are often considered suitable only for biodegradation [84]. However, bioplastics like PLA and PHA degrade slowly under natural conditions, limiting their environmental benefits as they might not break down fast enough to reduce pollution [128]. This process transforms waste bioplastics into new monomers and compounds, conserving renewable resources and reducing the reliance on virgin materials [121]. There are some claims of oxo-degradable LDPE plastic packaging and UV-degradable plastics, however they only physically degrade, and do not produce CO2.39 These types of packaging can't be deemed biodegradable in such cases as they physically degrade into microplastics, and biodegradation is not achieved, which is of significant concern for the potential harm chemicals and polymers can cause on the wildlife both physically and chemically when ingested122 and of particular concern is the extremely small particles that can find their way into water systems and cause severe harm to ocean-life. One major limitation of these withdrawn standards is the static test conditions, whereas the natural environment is more susceptible to changes in conditions from climate, weather etc.", 'Biodegradability of different biopolymers, reproduced with permission [555] A comparative study on different degradation of biodegradable plastics shows that the average degradation rates are in the descending order from industrial composting, anaerobic digestion, degradation in marine, soil, to aerobic aqueous environments [53]. Biodegradation of PLA, bio-PA, PCL, and PBAT has a doubtful impact either as PLA and certain bio-PA are not easily degradable to CO2 and water. On the other hand, PBAT, PCL may end up releasing harmful chemicals. CO2 entrapment or sequestration in renewable-based polymers helps; however, after biodegradation, it releases this CO2 back, and during the process, it already gives rise to a carbon footprint. So reducing environmental impact during polymer processing, along with CO2 sequestration, would remain a challenge toward the carbon neutrality goal.', '• Assimilation and mineralisation: microorganisms can take up small molecules released from the previous stage and utilise them as substrate for metabolism and biomass growth.38 In this phase, polymer carbon is converted into CO2 and biomass under aerobic conditions (or to CO2 and CH4 under anaerobic conditions), typically via the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA).33,49,51 Generally, these end products resulting from complete biodegradation do not pose an ecological toxicity risk. Microorganisms in this stage may differ from those involved in depolymerisation.37 Clearly, disintegration of a polymer is only the beginning of this process and therefore not a good definition for biodegradability. Thus, we recommend the published scientific opinion of the European Union, where biodegradation of plastics is considered as “the microbial conversion of all its organic constituents to carbon dioxide (CO2) (or carbon dioxide and methane in conditions where oxygen is not present), new microbial biomass and mineral salts, within a timescale short enough not to lead to lasting harm or accumulation in the open environment”.52 This emphasises that the ‘results’ from biodegradation of (biodegradable) plastics should have relatively less environmental impact on nature. The “timescale short enough not to lead to lasting harm or accumulation” is powerful, as this will be very different for each material and for all local circumstances. “Lasting harm and accumulation” are criteria that can be objectively assessed. Consumers expect that the so-called biodegradable plastics can biodegrade fast in nature without resulting in any negative impact on the environment.53 However, some of those commercial plastics claimed to be biodegradable were tested under industrial composting conditions, as described in standard methods ISO 14855,54 ASTM D6400,55 EN 13432.56 The fact that industrial composting provides more favourable conditions (i.e. higher temperature, higher total concentration of microorganisms, a higher moisture content for soil) can easily explain that polylactic acid (PLA), a well-known bio-based biodegradable polyester, completely degrades within several months under these conditions, yet only very slow degradation has been observed at ambient temperature.57-60 Particularly, the temperature of industrial composting (55-60 °C) could be equal to or above the Tg of poly(lactic acid) (PLA) (55-62 °C), which leads to the glassy and crystalline polymer becoming softer. This change of state is believed to accelerate the biodegradation rate.57 Overall, testing biodegradation at ambient temperature instead of under industrial composting conditions is more representative to evaluate fate-in-nature for biodegradable plastics.', "First published on 5th March 2024 To reduce global CO2 emissions in line with EU targets, it is essential that we replace fossil-derived plastics with renewable alternatives. This provides an opportunity to develop novel plastics with improved design features, such as better reusability, recyclability, and environmental biodegradability. Although recycling and reuse of plastics is favoured, this relies heavily on the infrastructure of waste management, which is not consistently advanced on a worldwide scale. Furthermore, today's bulk polyolefin plastics are inherently unsuitable for closed-loop recycling, but the introduction of plastics with enhanced biodegradability could help to combat issues with plastic accumulation, especially for packaging applications. It is also important to recognise that plastics enter the environment through littering, even where the best waste-collection infrastructure is in place. This causes endless environmental accumulation when the plastics are non-(bio)degradable. Biodegradability depends heavily on circumstances; some biodegradable polymers degrade rapidly under tropical conditions in soil, but they may not also degrade at the bottom of the sea. Biodegradable polyesters are theoretically recyclable, and even if mechanical recycling is difficult, they can be broken down to their monomers by hydrolysis for subsequent purification and re-polymerisation. Additionally, both the physical properties and the biodegradability of polyesters are tuneable by varying their building blocks. In addition to the impact of plastic manufacturing on climate change, plastic waste is also a severe problem. As conventional plastics are resistant to (bio)degradation, they remain in the environment, and eventually disintegrate into micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs). Prarat and Hongsawat found that microplastics in samples collected from the shore areas in Thailand are mostly polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP) and polystyrene (PS).11 Additionally, MNPs interact with (hydrophobic) contaminants (as carrier). This raises additional concerns about MNPs as they could contribute to the migration and accumulation of pollutants in the food chain worldwide.12-17 For example, in a simple artificial food chain experiment, zebrafish were fed with Artemia nauplii (crustaceans) in which very small (1-20 μm) nanoplastics were accumulated with and without benzo[a]pyrene as a persistent organic model pollutant (POP).18 Microplastics passed the intestinal tracts of zebrafish without significant accumulation and without signs of severe disease even after chronic dietary exposure. The potential of microplastics to act as a vector for POPs was tracked and uptake and distribution within intestinal tracts of zebrafish in histological cryosections was shown. Although problems caused by MNPs in the human body have not been reported yet, the observation of microplastics in the human body raises serious public concern. Recently, plastic particles, including PS, PE and poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET), were detected and quantified in human blood by Leslie et al.19 To avoid risks to human health and ecosystems, it is necessary to change our attitude towards plastics and their use and waste-management, and to improve relevant infrastructure.", 'Public awareness of the environmental impact of plastic waste has led to initiatives aimed at reducing its negative effects on natural resources and CO2 emissions [26, 27]. Due to insufficient disposal capacity and environmental concerns, the focus is now on recycling waste goods [28, 29]. Recycling plastic materials presents challenges such as diverse polymer composition, desirable features, and advanced technology requirements, making the process complex and time-consuming [30]. Traditional plastic composite [31] recycling releases particulate matter and toxic gases (CO2, NOx, and SOx) into the atmosphere [26]. Bioplastic misconceptions persist, as the final product may not naturally biodegrade due to bio-related feedstock [32]. Recyclable and bio-based plastics are eco-friendly polymers, albeit they sometimes have different basic notions. Biodegradable and bio-based plastics are examples of eco-friendly polymers [33]. In contrast with conventional plastics produced from fossil resources, bio-based materials are derived from renewable resources. They include some fully biodegradable ones and others to some degree [30]. Bio-based materials are entirely or partially biodegradable, unlike conventional plastics derived from fossil fuels and non-renewable natural resources [30]. Bioplastics are made from bio-based polymers from renewable resources, including corn, sugarcane, and cassava. The name "bio-based" describes the technique of making these materials, even if not all bio-based polymers are biodegradable [34]. Figure 1b categorizes biopolymers based on their source or biodegradability. The demand for biodegradable plastic Materials is rising due to environmental laws, bag bans, and global warming. Bioplastics, a broad term used to describe bio-based or biodegradable plastics, have become significant because they possess a lower environmental impact. Bioplastics, which account for 0.5 percent of the world’s plastic production Yearly, can Help with disposal and advance sustainable development. Global plastic production is expected to rise sharply from 2.18 Million tons in 2023 to 7.43 Million tons in 2028, as shown in Fig. 1c [35, 36]. Over the next 5 years, the manufacturing capacity for bioplastic substitutes such as PLA, PHAs, Polyamides (PA), and Polypropylene (PP) is expected to rise, accounting for 43% of the global bioplastics Market in 2023. Despite variations in polymer compositions and properties, the industry operates at nearly full capacity, with an average utilization rate of 82% [37]. The literature indicates biodegradable plastics such as starches and lignocellulosic products decompose naturally in composting facilities [38]. They are used in packaging, salt containers, fiber, and plastic components. The starch plastics will degrade completely under wet and composting environments, but retain adequate tensile strength for temporary applications such as packaging [39].', 'After the creation of simple and convenient plastic products, large amounts of non-biodegradable plastics have caused serious and irreversible pollution to the environment. More than 320 million tonnes of plastics are produced each year. Plastics made from petroleum still dominate the packaging industry and reducing the impact of plastics on the environment is a global issue [1]. A good strategy to solve the pollution of plastics is to manufacture and use biodegradable plastics [2]. With the continuous development of modern industry, non-degradable plastics have caused serious environmental pollution. The use of bio-based and biodegradable polymers can help solve environmental problems. Some biodegradable plastics have emerged, such as poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) [3,4,5], poly(lactic acid) (PLA) [6, 7], poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) [8, 9], and poly(glycolic acid) (PGA) [10], and so on. Some of these polymers occupy a very large proportion of the green packaging industry due to their excellent degradation properties. Biodegradable PLA, derived from renewable resources, is the most successful "green polymer". PLA is a polymer with high Young\'s modulus (~ 3 GPa) and tensile strength (50-70 MPa) [11]. Lactic acid can be extracted from renewable resources (glucose and maltose from corn or potatoes) through fermentation. The products of complete degradation are CO2 and H2O. PLA is used for industrial packaging as well as biocompatible medical products [11]. The tensile strength of PLA is comparable to that of the thermoplastic polyester poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) [12]. However, the drawbacks of PLA should not be ignored. Because PLA has low elongation at break (~ 4%) and impact strength (2.5 kJ/m2), it cannot be used for applications requiring significant deformation [11, 13]. In recent years, to achieve the enhancement of the mechanical and biological properties of PLA, a number of studies about blending [14, 15], copolymerization [16], and nucleating agents [17, 18] have appeared. The improvement of mechanical properties is an important research direction. There have been several studies focusing on the blending of PLA with other polymers [19,20,21], which is currently considered to be the most cost-effective means. For example, Burzic [22] investigated the use of bio-based polyhydroxyalkanoate (a-PHA) copolymers for the toughening modification of PLA without compromising the bio-based carbon content and the compostability of PLA. Meanwhile, the effect of two different amorphous copolymers PHAs on PLA was evaluated. These results demonstrated that the addition of PHA with higher molecular weight can effectively improve the crystallinity of PLA and form a more stable crystal. In addition, the highest elongation at break (> 30%) was achieved for the PLA/PHA blend with an 80/20 blending ratio. Su [23] used different techniques to prepare PBAT/PLA blends to study their miscibility and mechanical properties. The results of tensile experiments showed that the elongation at break increased with the increase of the PBAT content, and the limited miscibility between PBAT and PLA was demonstrated by DSC analysis and Fox equation calculations.', 'Many strategies have been used to mitigate the environmental impact caused by plastics pollution, including recycling,7-9 incineration,7,10,11 landfilling;12,13 application in construction of roads and pavements,14-16 use in the composition of fuels17,18 and the development of biodegradable polymers with interesting and applicable mechanical properties.19-21 Among these strategies, the biodegradation of biodegradable polymers is the most eco-friendly.22,23 According to Alshehrei, biodegradation is any chemical or physical process caused by biological activity, which impacts in terms of weight loss, loss of mechanical properties or visual changes.24 The biodegradability is related to the ability of a material to decompose after the interaction with specific biological elements such as microorganisms. The molecular structure of the polymer is the main contributing factor for its biodegradability.25,26 Non-biodegradable plastics (based on fossil resources) may be degraded in more than 1000 years,27 while bioplastics and biodegradable plastics may be degraded within 6 to 13 months.28 According to the European Bioplastic, in 2018 bioplastics represented roughly one percent of the 335 million tons of plastic produced annually, implicating in just 935 thousand tons of biodegradable consumed plastics.29 The long-period-degradation of non-biodegradable plastics, as polyolefins, is due to the fact that most of the microorganisms failed to adhere to the polymer surface hindering the production of enzymes necessary to degrade the polymer carbon backbone with its high molecular weight long chains.30 The environmental conditions also play an important role in the degradation kinetics of polymers.30,31 On the other hand, bioplastics, mainly the biodegradable ones, have showed a great degradation potential,32 in terms of percentage of biodegradability: polylactide (PLA) range 60-100%,33-36 polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA) range 64.3-100%,37-39 and polybutylene succinate (PBS) 90%.40 Furthermore, vegetal fillers can be incorporated to non-degradable plastics to improve the properties of the polymer matrix and potentially accelerates degradation compared to the pure non-biodegradable fossil based plastics. The polyethylene manufactured from ethanol was the fourth most produced bio-based plastic in the world. In 2019, it represented 11.8% of the global production capacity of bio-based plastics.31 Therefore, polymers composed by biopolyethylene with vegetable fillers are very promising. Degradation of polymers through the use of microorganisms is extensively studied.41-43 Sangale et al., for instance, demonstrated that Aspergillus sydowii was able to partially degrade polyethylene and they described the highest reduction in tensile strength so far.23 In another study performed by Ojha et al., it was isolated from soil samples two species of fungi (Penicillium oxalicum and Penicillium chrysogenum) that exhibited good abilities to degrade plastics such as low density polyethylene (LDPE) and high density polyethylene (HDPE).44 However, there are no data available concerning the metabolites produced by these microorganisms in the biodegradation process or the biodegradation products.', 'Switching from traditional plastics to bioplastics-those made from biological sources and/or designed to be biodegradable-does not inherently solve the problems of resource depletion and the buildup of plastic waste. Creating a fully sustainable plastics value chain requires that the increasing production of bioplastics be accompanied by effective strategies for managing the ultimate disposal and breakdown of bioplastic waste, irrespective of whether these bioplastics are biodegradable. There is broad agreement on the importance of recycling bio-based non-biodegradable bioplastics, such as bio-polyethylene terephthalate (bio-PET), polytrimethylene Terephthalate (bio-PTT), Polylactic Acid (PLA), bio-polyethylene (bio-PE), and bio-polypropylene (bio-PP). However, the approach is less straightforward for biodegradable bioplastics, where biodegradation is frequently considered the only viable end-of-life option. In contrast, recycling processes specifically target the recovery of plastic materials or monomers for reuse in the production cycle; biodegradation generally does not serve this purpose. These recycling processes, both mechanical and chemical, not only manage waste but also help preserve fundamental resources. As the production of bioplastics continues to expand, and these materials are expected to coexist with traditional plastics for a significant time, it is essential to identify the most appropriate end-of-life pathways for each type of commonly used bioplastic.', 'The big question is whether the biodegradation of biodegradable polymer blends and composites raises concerns regarding the degradation of by-products and their potential environmental impact. While biodegradation offers the advantage of reducing the accumulation of plastic waste in landfills and oceans, concerns have been raised about the potential of releasing harmful substances. Under controlled industrial or laboratory conditions, assessing biodegradation based on standard procedures is simpler than in real-life contexts including soils and oceans, which have varying microbial populations.301 According to Ali et al.,302 because biodegradation involves a mixture of identified and unidentified substances that may be hazardous to animals and soil health, it can both pose challenges and offer advantages in complex ecosystems. Unknown substances with roughly 32% cytotoxicity, 23% anti-androgenicity, 42% oxidative stress, and 67% baseline toxicity in bioassays have been shown to be present in bioplastics according to some studies. These compounds have the potential to negatively impact soil and animal health. Ecotoxicity assessments play a crucial role in evaluating the environmental implications of biodegradable polymer blends and composites. These assessments involve evaluating the potential toxicity resulting from the degradation of various organisms in aquatic and terrestrial environments. Such testing includes a focus on endpoints such as reproductive effects, acute and chronic toxicity, and bioaccumulation potential. To be deemed environmentally benign, these polymers, their blends, and composites must pass toxicity testing and break down into fragments within a given amount of time. However, one of the major setbacks in assessing the ecotoxicity of biodegradable polymers is the lack of standardized testing procedures and regulatory frameworks, unlike the biodegradation and compostability of plastics that have standardized and established testing procedures with clearly outlined regulatory requirements.303 Unlike biodegradation and controlled composting, there seems to be no specific standard for assessing the ecotoxicity of these materials in different environments. In fact, two ASTM standards, i.e., ASTM D5152-91; practice for water extraction of residual solids from degraded plastics for toxicity testing304 and ASTM D5951-96(2002); standard practice for preparing residual solids obtained after biodegradability standard methods for plastics in solid waste for toxicity and compost quality testing305 were withdrawn in 1998 and 2011, respectively, with no replacements. Hence the assessment of the ecotoxicity of biodegradable materials presents unique complexities as a result of their various compositions and degradation pathways. The multifaceted complexities in the assessment of the ecotoxicity of polymer blends and composites require ecotoxicity testing procedures suited for biodegradable polymers for understanding the possible environmental problems that may be associated with them. A study by Palsikowski et al.306 on ecotoxicological assessment of PLA, PBAT, and their compatibilized blend in soil found that the biodegradable materials and their blends did not exhibit phytotoxic (adverse effects on plant growth, physiology, or metabolism), cytotoxic (quality of being toxic to cells), genotoxic (damaging to DNA or genetic material), or mutagenic (causing genetic mutations) effects on the meristematic cells of Allium cepa, except for a chromosomal aberration index observed in one experiment with the blend 25/75. Sforzini et al.307 used biotests to evaluate the ecotoxicity impact of Mater-Bi, a biodegradable plastic, on soil organisms. The ecotoxicity tests on Mater-Bi biodegradable plastic showed no harmful effects on soil organisms, including autotrophic organisms, Daphnia magna, and Eisenia andrei. In their discussion of the environmental fate and ecotoxicity assessment of biodegradable polymers, Farachi et al.308 emphasized the importance of assessing the possible ecological dangers that may be connected to biodegradable materials. Carteny et al.309 hypothesized that in marine environments, biodegradable microplastics may accumulate more contaminants than conventional microplastics, despite emitting fewer additives. Life cycle analyses (LCAs) are the most complete tools to evaluate the entire lifecycle of recyclable polymers, blends and their composites, starting from the raw material stage to the final disposal stage or end of life. Through LCAs, factors such as greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, and ecotoxicity potential are evaluated. These analyses help identify challenges and opportunities to enhance the sustainability of biodegradable materials.', 'Biological waste treatments tailored for biodegradable plastics represent sophisticated end-of-life management strategies. These treatments can be implemented under aerobic conditions (with oxygen, such as composting) or anaerobic conditions (without oxygen, such as anaerobic digestion). Composting, which utilizes a diverse microbial community including fungi, bacteria, and actinomycetes, can occur at psychrophilic temperatures (below 35 °C for home composting) or thermophilic temperatures (50-60 °C for industrial composting) [11]. For example, kitchen scraps and garden waste are commonly composted in home settings, while large-scale operations might process municipal organic waste. This process reduces waste and produces valuable compost, rich in nutrients and beneficial for soil health. It can also be used in agriculture and landscaping. Similarly, anaerobic digestion, exclusively facilitated by bacteria, can be performed under mesophilic (below 35 °C) or thermophilic (50-60 °C) conditions. This method is often applied in wastewater treatment plants and livestock farms, where organic materials such as food waste, manure, and sewage sludge are digested [108]. The primary factor determining a bioplastic’s suitability for specific waste Management methods is its duration for complete degradation. International standards for biodegradability, such as those set by ISO and ASTM, define a Material as biodegradable if it fully decomposes within 56 days in aquatic environments or within two years in soil. However, these standards often rely on elevated temperatures that surpass typical conditions found in unmanaged natural environments, leading to a disparity between laboratory results and actual biodegradation in the real world. This highlights the importance of aligning biodegradation standards with actual environmental conditions when developing policies for managing plastic waste. Additionally, the design of plastic products must account for potential end-of-life scenarios, ensuring they align with the degradation timelines and processes of intended waste management systems. A cohesive strategy integrating policy, standards, and design is key to crafting practical and reliable solutions for bioplastic waste [101]. The study of biodegradation kinetics and carbon fate of bioplastics under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions offers valuable insights, but it also highlights critical limitations in their practical applications. While PHB and PHBV exhibit versatility by biodegrading under both conditions, PCL’s reliance on aerobic environments restricts its utility in anaerobic waste systems [99]. Integrating carbon balance analysis adds depth by tracking carbon sinks, such as gases, biomass, and soluble compounds; however, its complexity and resource demands may hinder scalability in industrial contexts. Additionally, the observed enhancement of mineralization rates with smaller particle sizes, though beneficial for assay duration, is impractical for real-world waste management, where uniform particle reduction is challenging and costly. Combining carbon balance with kinetic analysis provides a promising framework for testing and improving biodegradable materials, but the feasibility of implementing such rigorous methods at scale remains questionable. Addressing these challenges by focusing on scalable, realistic conditions and simplifying analytical methodologies will be critical to translating these findings into effective waste management solutions [99].']

This persistence contributes to pollution like ghost fishing [1] and allows microplastics to act as vectors for pollutants [2].
3.  **Moral Hazard:** The "biodegradable" label can create a **moral hazard**, misleading the public into thinking littering is acceptable because the plastic will disappear quickly, which is often not the case [3, 4]. This potentially increases littering.

The melt processing of poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) without plasticizers is challenging due to its **narrow thermal processing window** and **intrinsic material properties**, as highlighted in the provided contexts:

1. **Narrow Processing Window**:  
   PHB's melting temperature (~180°C) is close to its thermal degradation onset temperature, leaving a limited processing range (160–190°C) [1,2,5]. Above this range, chain scission occurs, reducing molecular weight and compromising mechanical properties [1,3]. This proximity necessitates precise temperature control during processing, which is industrially difficult.

2. **High Crystallinity and Brittleness**:  
   PHB’s crystallinity (>55%) contributes to rigidity and brittleness, limiting ductility and elongation at break [1,2]. High crystallinity also accelerates secondary crystallization (physical aging), further embrittling the material over time [2,14], complicating melt processing without additives to disrupt crystalline domains.

3. **Thermal Degradation**:  
   At processing temperatures, PHB undergoes thermal degradation via chain scission, leading to reduced melt viscosity and molecular weight [1,3,12]. This degradation narrows the processing window and produces inconsistent material properties [3,5,14]. Plasticizers lower the required processing temperature, mitigating thermal damage [1,8].

4. **Melt Strength and Viscosity Issues**:  
   Unplasticized PHB exhibits poor melt strength and viscosity, making it unsuitable for processes like film blowing or extrusion, which require stable melt flow [8,11]. Plasticizers reduce melt viscosity and enhance processability by improving chain mobility [8,11].

In summary, without plasticizers, PHB’s thermal instability, high crystallinity, and narrow processing window lead to degradation, brittleness, and processing inefficiencies. Plasticizers address these issues by lowering \( T_g \), reducing crystallinity, and enabling lower-temperature processing, thereby expanding the practical utility of PHB [1,2,8].

The typical elongation at break for **pure PLA** is less than **10%**, often around **5%** or lower, as noted across multiple contexts ([1], [6], [9], [10], [12]). For **PLA/PBAT (70/30) blends**, the elongation varies significantly depending on compatibilizers or processing methods:  

- **Without compatibilizers**:  
  - Some studies report minimal improvement (~4.7% elongation) due to poor interfacial adhesion ([2]).  
  - Others, like Farselti et al. ([4]), observed elongation increases to **45%** with 20% PBAT, suggesting higher PBAT content (30%) could yield further improvements, though not explicitly quantified here.  

- **With compatibilizers** (e.g., PLA-g-GMA, ADR):  
  - Significant enhancements are achieved, such as **over 200%** elongation ([1], Lyu et al.) and **96.6%** with crosslinkers like TAIC ([13]).  

In summary, PLA/PBAT (70/30) blends demonstrate a wide range of elongation values, from **~5%** (unmodified) to **over 200%** (compatibilized), highlighting the critical role of interfacial modification in maximizing ductility.

Reactive extrusion utilizing peroxides like **dicumyl peroxide (DCP)** improves PLA/PBAT blends through the following mechanisms:  

1. **Formation of Copolymers via Radical Coupling**:  
   - Peroxides generate free radicals on PLA and PBAT chains (e.g., via hydrogen abstraction). These radicals (**PBAT·**, **PLA·**, or peroxy radicals like **PBAT-O-O·**) couple to form **PLA-PBAT graft/branch copolymers** at the interface [[1]–[2], [8], [12]]. These copolymers act as compatibilizers, reducing interfacial tension and enhancing adhesion between the immiscible phases.  

2. **Reduced Phase Domain Size**:  
   - The in-situ-formed copolymers refine the blend morphology by reducing the size of dispersed PBAT domains (e.g., from ~10 μm to ~0.6 μm [[6], [12]]). Smaller phase domains improve stress transfer, leading to higher elongation at break (e.g., up to **96%** [[4], [12]]) and impact toughness.  

3. **Crosslinking and Branching**:  
   - DCP promotes partial crosslinking/branching (especially with co-agents like **TAIC**), increasing melt viscosity and melt strength [[1], [4], [5]]. This enhances processability (e.g., bubble stability in blown films [[5], [7]]) while maintaining stiffness (e.g., Young’s modulus of **2.4 GPa** [[4]]).  

4. **Atmosphere Dependency**:  
   - Reactions under **oxygen** favor radical coupling and copolymer formation over chain scission, improving mechanical properties compared to nitrogen atmospheres [[1]–[2]].  

5. **Synergy with Co-agents**:  
   - Multi-functional agents (e.g., **TAIC**) react with radicals to form crosslinks or branched structures, optimizing phase morphology and preventing over-crosslinking at optimal concentrations (e.g., **0.3 phr TAIC** with 0.02 phr peroxide [[4], [12]]).  

**Result**: Enhanced interfacial compatibility, balanced stiffness-toughness, and improved processability, enabling applications like high-strength, biodegradable films [[4], [7], [12]].

retrieved_contexts: ['Buy this article in print Chronic wounds are a global health problem, and their treatments are difficult and long lasting. The development of medical devices through tissue engineering has been conducted to heal this type of wound. In this study, it was demonstrated that the combination of natural and synthetic polymers, such as poly (D-L lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) and gelatin (Ge), were useful for constructing scaffolds for wound healing. The aim of this study was to evaluate the influence of different PLGA/gelatin ratios (9:1, 7:3 and 5:5 (v/v)) on the physical, chemical and biological properties of electrospun scaffolds for wound dressings. These PLGA/Ge scaffolds had randomly oriented fibers with smooth surfaces and exhibited distances between fibers of less than 10 μm. The 7:3 and 5:5 PLGA/Ge scaffolds showed higher swelling, hydrophilicity and degradation rates than pure PLGA and 9:1 (v/v) PLGA/Ge scaffolds. Young’s moduli of the scaffolds were 72 ± 10, 48 ± 6, 58 ± 6 and 6 ± 1 MPa for the pure PLGA scaffold and the 9:1, 7:3 and 5:5 (v/v) PLGA/Ge scaffolds, respectively. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) seeded on all the PLGA/Ge scaffolds were viable, and the cells were attached to the fibers at the different analyzed timepoints. The most significant proliferation rate was observed for cells on the 7:3 PLGA/Ge scaffolds. Biocompatibility analysis showed that all the scaffolds produced inflammation at the first week postimplantation; however, the 7:3 and 5:5 (v/v) PLGA/Ge scaffolds were degraded completely, and there was no inflammatory reaction observed at the fourth week after implantation. In contrast, the 9:1 PLGA/Ge scaffolds persisted in the tissue for more than four weeks; however, at the eighth week, no traces of the scaffolds were found. In conclusion, the scaffolds with the 7:3 PLGA/Ge ratio showed suitable physical, chemical and biological properties for applications in chronic wound treatments. The contact angle is a critical parameter in assessing biodegradable polymer films as it determines their hydrophilicity or hydrophobicity, which directly influences their interaction with water and suitability for specific applications. Key points include:

1. **Hydrophilicity vs. Hydrophobicity**:  
   - A contact angle **<90°** indicates **hydrophilic** surfaces, promoting water interaction, swelling, and biodegradation by enhancing microbial adhesion.  
   - A contact angle **>90°** denotes **hydrophobic** surfaces, which resist water penetration and may be preferred for moisture-sensitive applications (e.g., food packaging) [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12].  

2. **Biodegradation Facilitation**:  
   - Lower contact angles (increased hydrophilicity) improve wettability, enabling microbial colonization and accelerating biodegradation by facilitating water absorption and polymer chain scission [5, 6, 7, 15].  
   - Additives like cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) or ionic liquids (e.g., [Cho]Ac) can reduce contact angles, enhancing hydrophilicity and biodegradability [3, 6, 10].  

3. **Mechanical and Functional Properties**:  
   - Contact angle measurements correlate with hydrogen bonding and interfacial interactions within the polymer matrix, affecting tensile strength, elongation at break, and elasticity. For example, [Cho]Ac improves mechanical properties by enhancing hydrogen bonding [3, 6, 9].  
   - Hydrophobic modifications (e.g., PLA with lactic acid-modified fibers) increase contact angles, making materials suitable for applications requiring water resistance (e.g., disposable utensils) [9].  

4. **Surface Morphology and Additive Effects**:  
   - Surface roughness, porosity, and additive dispersion (e.g., CNC, PVA) influence contact angles. Smaller fiber diameters and uniform additive distribution lower contact angles, improving hydrophilicity [8, 10].  
   - Oxidative degradation reduces contact angles over time, increasing hydrophilicity and biodegradation rates [5, 7].  

5. **Application-Specific Design**:  
   - Tailoring contact angles through material composition (e.g., PVA content, plasticizers) allows optimization for drug delivery (controlled swelling) or packaging (moisture resistance) [3, 9, 10].  

In summary, the contact angle is pivotal in evaluating how biodegradable films interact with water, guiding material design for targeted performance in biodegradation, mechanical strength, and application-specific requirements.
reference: The contact angle measures the wettability of a surface. For biodegradable polymers, a lower contact angle (<90°) indicates hydrophilicity, which generally correlates with faster hydrolytic degradation onset and better cell adhesion. High contact angles (>90°) indicate hydrophobicity, often requiring surface modification for biomedical use.

The top layer contained the antibiotic drug gentamicin for controlled release to the wound site. It is of very high importance to use an appropriate sterilization process for this special new wound dressing, which will not have a deleterious effect on its function. Our investigation therefore focused on the effects of gamma-irradiation sterilization (10, 25, 35 and 50 kGy) on the structure properties of this wound dressing. The physical and mechanical properties were of the wound dressings were affected by the gamma irradiation because of a combination of chain scission and crosslinking of the collagen layer mainly. The weight loss and water vapor transmission rate were increased, while the water uptake was decreased with the increase in the irradiation dose. The changes were small when doses of 10 or 25 kGy were applied at room temperature. The gamma-irradiation resulted in stronger but more brittle wound dressings. Use of an irradiation dose lower than the standard 25 kGy is of special interest in sterilization of medical devices, because of the damaging effect that this dose might have on physical-mechanical properties. During gamma irradiation at room temperature, the product temperature is elevated as a result of gamma ray absorption. For the sterilization of bioresorbable polymers, temperatures must be kept below the temperature at which changes occur in the polymer's molecular weight, in order to prevent degradation. For this reason, cooling the product to 0°C or less during irradiation is advised. This requires the use of cooling agents in the irradiation container to prevent heating to the critical temperature where molecular weight is affected. Various combinations of doses and temperatures can be employed to achieve product sterility without adversely affecting the product. The balance between the selected gamma radiation doses and the process temperatures allowing minimal damage is referred to as optimum sterilization.19 In the current study, the effects of gamma radiation on the physical and mechanical properties of our new biodegradable drug-eluting wound dressing were investigated. It is important to note that our new hybrid wound dressing, which contains the synthetic polymer PDLGA with the natural polymer collagen, combines the desired properties of both materials and therefore it is superior compared to other types of wound dressings. However, in the absence of further surface modification, the lack of functional moieties on the PCL chain results in non-ideal surface properties of such scaffolds, especially in terms of the inability to tailor the presentation of functional ligands for directed cell adhesion and growth. The current study investigates gamma irradiation-induced grafting as a means of improving the biofunctionality of the PCL surface. Plasma treatment has limited penetration depth,11 as well as imparting undesired chemical functional groups onto the surface. In contrast, gamma irradiation has high penetration depth into a polymer matrix and allows for a variety of monomers to be grafted, with good control over the chemical moieties introduced.7,9', "Our study shows that irradiation doses of 10 and 25 kGy, which are commonly used for sterilization of medical devices, practically do not change the structural features of the hybrid wound dressing's layers. Unfortunately, while terminal sterilization of the GelMA is a critical step for translational tissue engineering applications, it can potentially cause thermal or chemical modifications of GelMA. Overall, this study provides further insight into GelMA-based material design with consideration of the effect of terminal sterilization. 1.  **Gamma irradiation causes chain scission and crosslinking:** The sterilization process primarily affects the polymer structure through chain scission and crosslinking reactions, particularly in natural polymers like collagen within hybrid systems containing PLGA ([1], [5], [11]).
2.  **Dose-dependent changes in physical properties:**
    *   **Weight loss increases** with higher irradiation dose ([1], [5], [11]).
    *   **Water vapor transmission rate (WVTR) increases** with higher irradiation dose ([1], [5], [11]).
    *   **Water uptake decreases** with higher irradiation dose ([1], [5], [11]).
3.  **Dose-dependent changes in mechanical properties:**
    *   **Tensile strength and Young's modulus increase** with higher irradiation dose (up to 35 kGy at room temperature), mainly due to crosslinking, leading to stronger but **more brittle** materials ([1], [5], [11], [14]).
    *   **Maximal strain (elongation at break) decreases** with higher irradiation dose, indicating increased brittleness ([1], [5], [11], [14]).
    *   At very high doses (e.g., 50 kGy), **massive chain scission occurs**, causing a dramatic **decrease in tensile strength, modulus, and strain**, and a collapse of the microstructure, leading to very low WVTR and strength ([5], [11], [14]).
4.  **Temperature dependence:** The changes in properties (both physical and mechanical) are **significantly smaller when sterilization is performed in liquid nitrogen** (cryogenic conditions) compared to room temperature irradiation, due to reduced degradation and chain scission ([1], [5], [11]).
5.  **Feasibility at standard dose:** Irradiation at the standard medical device sterilization dose of **25 kGy causes changes that are not dramatic for most properties** and allows function similar to non-sterilized samples. Some changes (increased WVTR, stress, modulus) might even be beneficial, provided the dressing doesn't become too brittle ([5], [11]).

The typical processing window temperature for Thermoplastic Starch (TPS) is **120–160°C**, based on the following evidence from the context:  

1. **Optimal gelatinization conditions** were identified at **120°C** (Context [1]), with lower temperatures failing to achieve complete gelatinization. Higher temperatures (above 120°C) risk thermal degradation unless carefully controlled.  
2. **Extrusion processes** for TPS blends (e.g., with LDPE) used temperatures up to **140–160°C** in specific zones to balance starch gelatinization/devolatilization and polymer melting while minimizing degradation (Context [2]).  
3. **Thermal degradation** of TPS begins at temperatures above ~230°C (Context [9]), but excessive mechanical energy (e.g., high screw speed) or prolonged residence time at elevated temperatures (e.g., >160°C) can accelerate degradation (Context [1, 3]).  
4. **Melting transitions** of plasticized TPS films occur between **155–178°C** (Context [4, 5]), but processing must avoid exceeding degradation thresholds.  

Thus, the processing window for TPS typically ranges from **120°C** (minimal for gelatinization) to **160°C** (upper limit to prevent degradation), with adjustments based on plasticizer content, shear conditions, and compatibility with other polymers.

The mechanism of chain scission in ester bond hydrolysis involves the **cleavage of ester linkages** via hydrolytic degradation, influenced by environmental conditions and polymer structure. Key aspects include:  

1. **Base-Catalyzed Hydrolysis**:  
   Under basic conditions (e.g., in LPEEC polymers), **carbonate ester groups** are attacked by nucleophiles like alcoholate anions ([1]). This triggers chain scission, breaking the polymer backbone into smaller fragments (e.g., Eo and Ec subunits). The kinetic model **d(Ec)p/dP = k (Ec)p/P – 1** reflects the proportionality between the split component (Ec)p and molecular weight (P/Mn), supported by a linear correlation between Mp,Ec and Mn ([1]).  

2. **Role of pH and Catalysts**:  
   - **Base catalysis** accelerates ester hydrolysis more effectively than acid due to hydroxide ions attacking ester bonds directly ([5], [7]).  
   - Acidic conditions hydrolyze esters into carboxylic acids, which may re-form ester bonds with hydroxyl groups under specific conditions (e.g., transesterification in hemp-pectin composites; [2], [3]).  

3. **Polymer Structure Effects**:  
   - **Crystallinity**: Lower crystallinity enhances water penetration, promoting hydrolysis (e.g., branched polyesters in [6]).  
   - **Ester Bond Density**: Higher ester bond density increases hydrolysis susceptibility, though steric hindrance (e.g., azide groups in energetic polyurethanes; [7], [8]) or reduced bond accessibility (e.g., crosslinking; [9]) can slow degradation.  

4. **Environmental Factors**:  
   - Water content and temperature drive hydrolysis. Heating shifts equilibrium toward ester bond formation by removing water ([2], [3]).  
   - Enzymatic degradation (e.g., lipase cleaving ester bonds in CWBPEs; [9]) further modulates chain scission.  

5. **Material Property Changes**:  
   Hydrolysis reduces molecular weight (Mn), alters crystallinity ([6], [9]), and generates carboxylic acid groups (FTIR evidence; [7], [8]), leading to mechanical property degradation (e.g., tensile strength loss in LPEEC; [1]).  

In summary, chain scission in ester hydrolysis is a nucleophilic process accelerated by basic conditions, influenced by polymer crystallinity, steric effects, and environmental factors like pH and water availability.
reference: Hydrolytic chain scission involves the cleavage of the ester linkage by a water molecule. The water oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon, leading to the formation of a carboxylic acid end group and a hydroxyl end group. The reaction is often acid-catalyzed, meaning the generated carboxylic acid can accelerate further degradation (autocatalysis).

retrieved_contexts: ['Nowadays, the study of innovative degradable biomaterials is one of the most interesting research topics in biomaterials. Degradable biomaterials have been proposed from polymers, ceramics, and metals. Metals are more mechanically interesting compared to polymers for load-bearing implants, such as internal bone fixation screws/pins and plates and for coronary stents, which require high strength to bulk ratio [7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 17,18,19,20,21]. The most promising candidates for designing biodegradable metallic implants are magnesium, zinc, and iron alloys. Among these, Mg-based alloys and Fe-based alloys are the most widely explored [3, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 19, 22]. Magnesium and its alloys have already been successfully tested in vivo and in clinical studies (Fig. 1) [15, 23, 24]. Most of the studies on Mg-based implants reported a rapid degradation rate in physiological environments accompanied by the evolution of considerable amounts of hydrogen [14, 15, 25]. Excessive rate of degradation can lead to undesired loss of mechanical integrity of the implant; therefore, various methods have been used to control it [26]. An alloying with other elements (Al, Zn, Ca, Ag, Ce, Th) and the preparation of composites were used to improve mechanical properties of Mg-based biomaterials [27]. The main challenge for both Mg and Fe materials is the successful implementation of long-term in vivo experiments. A look at the status of Mg-based metals shows that it is very complicated to develop the material that would be load-bearing, biodegradable, and biocompatible. Reprinted from [24] with permission from Elsevier', "Biomedical metallic materials that are currently used can be harmful to the human body in the long term due to metallic particles that are released and accumulated by means of degradation and corrosion of the material. Therefore, metallic materials for temporary implants must have excellent biocompatibility and bifunctionality, adequate load capacity, high wear resistance, low density, and a gradual and controlled biodegradation rate that allows once the bone is healed; then, reabsorption of the biodegradable material is completed [60]. Appropriate selection of biodegradable materials reduces the health risks associated with the use of implants and a second surgery to remove the implant after the tissue has healed [97]. Zinc-based metal alloys have good biocompatibility, high bioabsorbability (up to 15 mg/day [98]), ideal corrosion rate in vitro (approximately 0.022 mm/year [99]) and relatively low Young's modulus (80-90 GPa, see Fig. 2). Zinc is essential for the normal operation of human body; for instance, it is indispensable for heart functioning and protects endothelial cells [100]. Zinc alloys do not produce harmful gases during biodegradation, and the corrosion products are biocompatible and harmless [100]. The low melting temperature of these alloys and the low reactivity during melting allow successfully casting components [98, 100]. All these advantages justify the successful use of the zinc alloys as biodegradable implant material. However, zinc alloys implants are limited in size, because they are brittle, have low mechanical properties and show poor ductility under compression loading. In addition, production costs are relatively high for these alloys due to the high purity elements that are required in the fabrication process of the zinc alloys [98, 101].", "Biodegradable metals with good mechanical properties, excellent degradability and biocompatibility have recently been suggested as a class of promising metallic biomedical materials for orthopedic implants, attracting a great amount of interest.4-11 Magnesium and its alloys have attracted much attention as biodegradable metals for implants owing to their similar mechanical properties to those of the body's natural bone and the biocompatibility of magnesium ions.4-7 Nevertheless, one of the most significant risks of Mg-based biodegradable devices is that they are corroded so rapidly. It has generally been acknowledged that Mg-based biodegradable metals with a very low corrosion potential (−2.36 VSCE), which exhibit a rapid corrosion rate in physiological environments, cannot offer effective support and their mechanical integrity is compromised prior to recovery after implantation in the body.4,7,10 Compared with Mg-based alloys, Zn and its alloys might be considered to be interesting candidates owing to their higher electrode potential and similar mechanical properties.12 Furthermore, Zn element is generally considered to be an essential element for humans, playing an important role in the metabolic processes of the human body.13 After these factors were considered, Zn and its alloys were suggested as new members of the family of biodegradable materials. However, preliminary studies have demonstrated that pure Zn had poor mechanical properties and hardness (the tensile strength of as-cast pure Zn was only 20 MPa, its elongation was 0.3% and its hardness was approximately 25 HV9,14), which might not offer sufficient support for implanted devices. Therefore, as an indispensable strengthening process, alloying has been adopted to improve their mechanical performance. Many novel types of zinc alloys have been designed and developed, with the main concentration on Zn-Mg,9,14-19 Zn-Ca,19 Zn-Sr,19 Zn-Mg-Ca,20,21 Zn-Mg-Sr,20-22 Zn-Ca-Sr20 and Zn-Mg-Mn alloys.23 As an effective alloying element in zinc alloys, Mg was found to prominently improve their mechanical performance, and the addition of 0.93 wt% or 1.55 wt% Mg to pure Zn provided superior tensile strength and hardness.9,14 Nevertheless, the maximum elongation of Zn-Mg alloys was approximately 1.5%, which might be suggested as indicating poor ductility for implanted devices. However, advanced processing technology such as extrusion,16,18-20 rolling19,20,22,23 and high-pressure torsion (HPT)24 could be employed to greatly improve the mechanical properties of Zn-based biodegradable metals, which were significantly superior to those of the well-known Mg-based biodegradable metals that have been developed.23,25 In the present work, Zn-1.2Mg alloy has been designed and, in consideration of its effective composition between Zn-1Mg alloy and Zn-1.5Mg alloy, its development as a biodegradable metal and its feasibility for implants were evaluated, in particular after hot extrusion. Its microstructure, mechanical properties, in vitro degradation behavior, in vitro hemocompatibility and cytotoxicity were tested to investigate its feasibility as a new biodegradable material.", 'Biodegradable metal implants are gaining attention over traditional bio-inert/bio-stable implants owing to the fact that most of the clinical problems need only short-term support while healing. These implants deteriorate by releasing metallic components that the body metabolizes and are finally replaced by bone tissue [1,2,3]. Performing a secondary surgery to remove the implant is unnecessary because biodegradable implants are designed to provide initial mechanical support and gradually dissolve in the body without causing any harm. The temporary implant experiences a gradual decrease in mechanical strength and integrity due to deterioration. This process also allows for a gradual transfer of load from implant to bone, hence reducing the stress shielding effect [4, 5]. Zinc, iron and magnesium are the biodegradable metals that have been studied the most. Notably iron has been identified as suitable material with high strength, formability and slow corrosion rate. However, degradation rate can be improved by fabrication of porous scaffolds [6, 7]. Zinc enhances the functioning of the immune system and is a constituent of numerous dietary supplements, thereby making it regarded as a non-toxic element. The optimal daily dosage of zinc is approximately 40 mg; however, temporary amounts of up to 100 mg do not result in any health issues. Zinc is reported to have good biocompatibility, making it a potential biodegradable implant material [8, 9]. Zinc has an optimal corrosion rate; yet, its inadequate mechanical qualities have consistently been a significant concern among researchers. Zn could be combined with Fe to produce a composite biomaterial to overcome the demerits of both the metals and harness the beneficial properties resulting to the development of a more suitable biomaterial. Bioceramics can be added in low concentrations to facilitate bone ingrowth and ensure an effective bond between bone and implant material. This is because it possesses remarkable biocompatibility and closely resembles the mineral composition of human bones, which primarily consist of calcium and phosphorous [12,13,14,15,16]. HAp is reported to enhance the bioactivity of titanium dental and orthopaedic implants; magnesium and iron biodegradable implants in various studies [17,18,19,20,21].', 'In recent years, the market of implant biomaterials is rapidly expanding due to the increasing bone trauma and cardiovascular disease cases.
