The high extrusion speed promotes the creation and accumulation of large concentrations of crystal lattice defects, leading to grain refinement and an improvement in mechanical properties [14].', 'Electrochemical inhomogeneities of steel in steel/copper alloy couple during galvanic corrosion in static and flowing seawater Biodegradable medical implants for orthopedic applications such as bone screws and pins, or vascular stents are now firmly established in the clinical field.[1-3] In contrast to their non-degrading counterparts, implants made of biodegradable polymers or metals degrade progressively after providing temporary support during the healing process of diseased tissue. These implants benefit patients by eliminating the need for revision surgery, reducing the risk of chronic inflammation, and being especially beneficial for pediatric patients.[4-8] Ongoing research is focused on the development of materials with tailored mechanical, chemical and biological properties to create implants with sufficient strength and suitable degradation times, as well as appropriate biological response.[9] The three main systems considered for biodegradable metal implants are Mg-based, Zn-based, and Fe-based alloys.[9] While initial reports focused on pure iron, their shortcomings regarding too slow degradation and low mechanical strength, compared to the clinically applied benchmark AISI 316L stainless steel,[10] stirred research toward increasingly complex material systems. Recently, a metal-polymer composite technique has been suggested to enhance degradation rate which led to a new generation of biodegradable Fe-based coronary stent that have already passed a clinical trial.[11, 12] Meanwhile, alloys based on FeMn[13, 14] have been recently considered for biodegradable implant applications due to their desirable mechanical strength (ultimate tensile strength of about 0.4-0.9 GPa[15-17]), degradation times, and better processability with, e.g., modern manufacturing techniques such as laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF).[18-20] Furthermore, the combination of materials with drastically different electrochemical potentials has opened alternative pathways to control degradation behavior.[21] The intentional formation of galvanic couples can both enhance the degradation of implants, e.g. through the addition of Pd or Pt to FeMn-based alloys,[21, 22] applying a conducting polymer coating as cathode[23] or hinder corrosion by applying less noble metals as sacrificial anode coatings.[24, 25] While considerably extending the versatility of such systems, these additions can only passively control degradation over the whole time of their presence. Despite considerable progress, these passive strategies cannot address the following three challenges. First, it is immensely challenging to achieve a desired combination of degradation time and mechanical strength solely through alloy engineering.[26] Second, individual variations of the recovery time of patients cannot be taken into account after implantation. And finally, revision surgery is still required when an implant induces an acutely dangerous situation for the patient, e.g. due to aseptic loosening of the implant, periprosthetic fractures, osteolysis or immunological response toward bacteria or toxic material compounds.[27, 28] With these challenges in mind, an intelligent implant that is stable until an operator triggers its degradation on demand appears highly desirable. Such a functionality can be achieved through the integration of electronic components that receive and process an external signal to initiate implant degradation at desired rates.', 'Recently, biodegradable metals have attracted considerable attention as implant materials, like magnesium alloy, zinc alloy, and ferroalloy. Among these metals, Mg and its alloys are considered a potential candidate for biodegradable applications because of their inherent biosafety, good mechanical properties, and ease of biodegradation [1,2,3]. Magnesium can be completely degraded in physiological environments to produce only hydrogen gas and release magnesium ions [4]. Existing research has shown that Mg2+ enhances human biological enzymatic activity, supports metabolism, and promotes the growth and specialization of bone cells, which aids in developing new bone tissue and healing around the implant [5,6,7]. Further, Mg ions can stimulate M2 polarization in macrophages, leading to an anti-inflammatory response [8, 9]. However, the uncontrollable and rapid degradation of Mg in physiological environments limits its application in implant materials [10]. The rapid degradation of Mg can result in the premature mechanical failure of implants, the formation of hydrogen voids, and a sharp increase in the local pH, adversely affecting surrounding tissues [11,12,13]. Consequently, regulating the rate of magnesium corrosion is crucial for its clinical biodegradability. Coating is the simplest and most feasible method for controlling the corrosion rate of Mg compared to other methods such as microalloying and heat treatment [14,15,16,17]. Thus far, many studies have focused on methods for preparing magnesium coatings, including microarc oxidation [18,19,20], sol-gel process [21], ion implantation [22], organic/polymer coating [23, 24], and composite coating [25]. Among these methods, organic coatings bind to substrates via chemical bonding, making them strong, tough, and less prone to detachment. Such a barrier can function to shield the Mg substrate from its surroundings [26].', 'To date, magnesium, iron, zinc and their alloys have been extensively researched as potential biodegradable metals for hard tissue applications.3, 7-9, 11-13, 15, 16, 18-20 Biodegradable implants based on Mg are particularly interesting because of their exceptional biocompatibility, ability to promote bone cell activation, and bone-mimicking elastic modulus significantly eliminating the stress-shielding effect. However, Mg and its alloys exhibit a rapid corrosion rate under the physiological conditions associated with hydrogen gas evolution, resulting in pH increase and an early loss of mechanical integrity.9, 11-13, 16, 19-21 Bioabsorbable Fe-based materials are attractive for orthopedic implants mainly due to their good biocompatibility, outstanding mechanical properties and excellent formability. Iron is also a vital nutrient and an essential trace element in the human body.3, 8, 15, 19 However, Fe and Fe-based alloys degrade very slowly, and these materials, as well as their corrosion products, are retained in tissues for long periods, producing complications analogous to those found with permanent implants.7, 11-13, 16, 22', 'To date, magnesium, iron, zinc and their alloys have been extensively researched as potential biodegradable metals for hard tissue applications.3, 7-9, 11-13, 15, 16, 18-20 Biodegradable implants based on Mg are particularly interesting because of their exceptional biocompatibility, ability to promote bone cell activation, and bone-mimicking elastic modulus significantly eliminating the stress-shielding effect. However, Mg and its alloys exhibit a rapid corrosion rate under the physiological conditions associated with hydrogen gas evolution, resulting in pH increase and an early loss of mechanical integrity.9, 11-13, 16, 19-21 Bioabsorbable Fe-based materials are attractive for orthopedic implants mainly due to their good biocompatibility, outstanding mechanical properties and excellent formability. Iron is also a vital nutrient and an essential trace element in the human body.3, 8, 15, 19 However, Fe and Fe-based alloys degrade very slowly, and these materials, as well as their corrosion products, are retained in tissues for long periods, producing complications analogous to those found with permanent implants.7, 11-13, 16, 22', 'Historically, corrosion has been thought to be a critical issue that should be controlled to a level as minimal as possible for structural materials. In recent years, there has been a paradigm shift in thinking in the biomaterial community in terms of corrosion. There is now increasing interest in intentionally using a corrodible alloy in some medical device applications such as intravascular stents and orthopedic implants [1] because the use of biodegradable materials can avoid a second surgery. In this case, the human body must be able to deal with the corrosion products and their effects. There are three major groups of biodegradable metallic biomaterials: (1) iron and its alloys (Fe-Mn) [2-4], (2) magnesium (Mg) and its alloys [5-8], and (3) tungsten (W) [9]. Magnesium has attracted a great deal of interest due to its exceptional mechanical and physiological features. Physiologically, Mg2+ ions are a cofactor in many enzymatic reactions and essential for normal neurological and muscular functions. Also, the presence of magnesium benefits the mineralization process of bony tissue and is important to bone’s strength and health [10]. An adult human body contains approximately 30 g of magnesium in muscle and bone [11] and also need to take in 420 mg/day. From the perspective of physical and mechanical features, magnesium has good compatibility with human bone. For example, its density of 1.74 g/cm3 and Young’s modulus of 41-45 GPa are close to natural bone (1.8-2.1 g/cm3 and ~30 GPa, respectively). Advantageous over inorganic and polymeric biomaterials, Mg has much higher fracture toughness and yield strength. Even more important and attractive is its biodegradability. Current surgical orthopedics requires a secondary surgical procedure to remove the orthopedic plate, screw, or pin after the tissue has healed sufficiently. But if these orthopedic tools are made of magnesium, instead of stainless steel or titanium, then they can naturally degrade in, and be excreted from, the human body and therefore the secondary surgery can be avoided. The potential application of magnesium in orthopedics was realized in the early twentieth century. The first surgical attempt was reported by Lambotte in 1907 [12], but it was not successful because the pure magnesium metal corroded too rapidly in vivo, losing its mechanical integrity only 8 days after surgery and leaving hydrogen gas pockets beneath the skin. As such, the use of magnesium in orthopedic devices was quickly abandoned. Attempts at using magnesium were spurred again in the 1940s [12] and subsequently boosted in the early 2000s, in line with the advancement and development of magnesium technologies. The past few years have seen a big leap in the development of magnesium biomaterials [1, 13]. Magnesium metal stents (e.g. AMS, Biotronik GmbH) have moved to the clinical arena [4, 14, 15]. With the success of the clinical experiments, it is envisaged that biodegradable Mg will attract more academic investigations and capital investment.', 'Engineers and scientists have constantly been improving the mechanical and degradation characteristics of these biodegradable metallic implants. Pure iron (Fe), pure magnesium (Mg), pure zinc (Zn) and their alloys are widely studied to evaluate their implantation potentials [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16]. Numerous animal experiments and clinical trials show that these biodegradable metals are safe and feasible as implants [17], [18]. They have good biocompatibility despite their differences in degradation rate. The degradation rate of pure Fe is very slow [19], while the degradation rate for Mg is very rapid [20]. Pure Zn exhibits an intermediate degradation rate [21]. The advantage of using ferroalloys (Fe-based alloys) is that they have a higher tensile strength compared to Mg and Zn alloys. For example, Fe alloys can achieve a tensile strength of up to 433 MPa, whereas Mg alloys are limited to around 186 MPa [22]. While having a similar modulus of elasticity to human bone and could promote bone growth, Mg alloys suffer from mechanical integrity issues due to their rapid corrosion rate. Zn alloys show tunable mechanical properties with an intermediate corrosion rate but generally have lower strength than Fe alloys [21]. Despite several benefits of Fe and Mg in medical applications, the swift degradation of Mg and the low degradation of Fe restrict their uses as medical implants [17], [20], [23]. To control the degradation rates of Fe, Mg as well as their alloys, many attempts have been performed such as surface coating [24], [25], [26], [27], [28], surface modification [29], [30], [31], and alloying [32], [33], [34]. Alloying elements including Ga, Mn, Sr, Si, C, Sn, Pd, B, W, Al, S and rare-earths (REs) have widely been utilized to control the degradation rates of various Mg and Fe-based implant products [35], [36], [37], [38]. However, the biocompatibility of these elements is still uncertain and some of them are toxic and unsafe for human use, particularly in the concentrated form [35], [39], [40], [41], [42]. There are limited studies on Fe-Mg alloys [43], [44], in particular for biomedical applications due to their low solubility and huge dissimilarity in their melting temperatures, making them hard to prepare by conventional methods. Due to the large difference in melting temperature of Mg and Zn as well as difference in atomic radius that lead to very low solubility of Mg in Fe (i.e., maximum solid solubility of Mg in Fe at the eutectic temperature (approximately 460°C) is reported to be around 0.03 wt.%) [45], the alloying of Mg with Fe via traditional casting is almost impossible and greatly difficult. Thus, alternative alloying approaches and processing routes to produce metallic biodegradable materials that meet the requirements to be used as implants are needed and inevitable. One of the potential way to alloy Fe with Mg is by mechanical alloying (MA) method. The mechanical alloying can produce one-phase alloys besides its convenience of operation and greater control over composition to produce the alloys. The mechanical alloying is a non-equilibrium process where the alloying in the MA process is occurring at a solid state and no melting is involved. In the aspect of Fe-Mg alloys, the high-energy impacts and the resultanty atomic diffusion and during milling is expected to enhance the solid solubility of Mg in the Fe matrix.', 'Using biocompatible metals with good corrosion resistance like Ti6Al4V can cause several complications such as long-term irritation, chronic local inflammatory reactions possibly leading to secondary surgery. Biodegradable metals corrode gradually in vivo without causing an immune response while triggering tissue healing [1], [2], [3], [4]. They are mainly used as medical implants that are temporarily required until complete tissue healing, e.g., bone implants. Scaffolds provide space for bone tissue to grow with little resistance to body fluid flow thus improving osteoconduction and -integration [5]. Biodegradable materials must withstand compressive stresses and show a stiffness similar to that of bone to avoid stress shielding effects [6]. Mg and Fe have been studied as biodegradable metals. For Mg, the biodegradation rate is too fast for natural tissue recovery [5], [6], [7]. The biodegradation rate of Fe is slow compared to natural tissue growth and the biodegradation products remain in the human body for a longer period than expected [7], [8]. Although technical approaches such as adding alloying elements and surface modification can improve the aforementioned problems of Mg and Fe [9], [10], Zn is considered to be a promising alternative. Zn is an abundant trace elements and ranks sixth among all the life metal elements in the human body [12], [13], [14]. The degradation rate of Zn is between that of Mg and Fe, while corroding, no gases are generated, and the degradation products are biocompatible.', 'Recently, magnesium (Mg) alloys have shown their potential in the field of biodegradable materials attracting considerable attentions [1, 2]. The density of Mg alloys (1.74-1.9 g cm−3) is close to human bone (1.75-2.0 g cm−3) [3]. Compared with traditional non-degradable metals, such as stainless steels and titanium alloys, the modulus of elasticity of Mg (about 45 GPa) is much lower than the other medical metal materials and close to the bone elastic modulus (20-40 GPa). Thus, Mg alloys can effectively avoid stress shielding effect in the repairing bone [4]. As an essential element, Mg participates in metabolic reactions and stimulates the healing of tissues [5]. Moreover, the degradability of Mg alloys could avert secondary surgery that exposes patients to additional risks. However, the negative electrode potential of Mg (− 2.372 V) results in a fast degradation rate in the physiological environment. The rapid degradation rate accompanied by a large amount of hydrogen gas results in severe alkalization, which may easily lead to the loss of the integrity of mechanical properties before the healing of damaged tissues [6]. To improve the properties, element alloying has been widely used [7, 8]. Zn is found in human body as one of the nutritionally elements [9]. Zn is usually added into Mg to improve mechanical properties with a solid solubility of 6.2 wt% [10]. In addition, a small amount of Zr benefits in the corrosion prevention diffusion [11]. Rare earth elements can form intermetallic compounds with impurities in Mg and thus reduce the impact of impurities [12]. The volume fraction of other intermetallic compounds is reduced, and the microgalvanic corrosion is inhibited by the formation of low-cathode-rich rare earth phases in Mg alloys. Furthermore, rare earth elements facilitate the grain refinement of Mg alloys to make the microstructure more uniform [13, 14]. Feyerabend et al. [15] and Witte et al. [5] suggested that rare earth elements (Dy, Gd, Y and Nd) were suitable for biomedical materials. A group of new biodegradable materials by complexation of Gd ions with cationic poly(urethane amide) was developed represented a new platform for use in tumor theranostics [16]. According to the results of Yao et al. [17], the addition of Gd element could effectively improve the mechanical properties and corrosion resistance of Mg-Zn-Zr alloy. Mg-2.0Zn-0.5Zr-3.0Gd exhibited better mechanical properties and lower corrosion rate (0.845 ± 0.035 mm y−1). However, coarse second phase with higher rare earth elements content in the alloy was prone to local corrosion near grain boundaries. Grillo et al. [18] stated that slightly cytotoxic effects of rare earth elements (La and Gd) may be found in vivo close to the local rapid corrosion area releasing a large number of metal ions. The as-extruded Mg-2.5Zn-0.7Zr-11.3Gd and Mg-3.3Y-0.6Zr-10.2Gd alloys had low corrosion rate of 0.17 mm y−1 and 0.55 mm y−1 with mild cytotoxicity to L-929 cells [19]. Thus, Gd can effectively improve the corrosion resistance of Mg alloys, but the concentration should be lower in the local area of the implanted region. Wang et al. [20] summarized that the addition of Y could promote the formation of Mg- and Ca-containing phosphates, predicting good biocompatibility of Y. In Mg-1.5Y-1.2Zn-0.44Zr alloy, no significant cytotoxicity toward L-929 cells was found and the immersion extracts of this alloy could enhance the cell proliferation with time in the cytotoxicity evaluation [21]. In addition, it is reported that Y forms an Y2O3 passivation layer effectively retarding the corrosion rate [13, 22,23,24].', "Bioabsorbable materials for orthopedic applications Bioabsorbable or biodegradable materials have been the focus of the recent investigation on implant materials due to their potential use in temporary implants and fixation elements. Using these types of materials for orthopedic implants, it is possible to avoid the need for a second surgical intervention to remove the implant, because the body itself can reabsorb the biodegradable material. Therefore, risks associated with the patient's surgery are reduced, time required for postoperative physical rehabilitation process is diminished, and the cost inherent to the clinical procedures is also lowered. The biodegradable materials in Fig. 2 are alloys and composites of Mg and Zn. Currently, these are the most investigated biomaterials, and the use of these materials in orthopedic applications is expected to increase in the coming years. The alloys and composites of Mg in Fig. 2 have mechanical properties closer to the bone, and they are also suitable for using as fixation and load bearing elements. Therefore, these materials do not damage the bone due to stress shielding. The first developed and the most used biodegradable materials for commercial implants are polymeric, which are obtained from polyglycolic acids (PGA), polylactic (PLA) and polylactic glycolic acid (PLGA). Biodegradable polymers have been successfully utilized for several biomedical applications including suture threads, drug delivery devices and in the orthopedic industry as pins and screws [57, 60, 92]. Polymers are manufactured through a wide range of methods, such as additive manufacturing, which allows to create custom-made parts economically and with controlled porosity [93, 94]. However, polymeric materials still have some challenges regarding the mechanical properties that must be addressed, which limit the use in orthopedic applications."]

retrieved_contexts: ["Plasticizers increase flexibility and reduce the glass transition temperature. In PLA, common plasticizers include citrate esters like acetyl tributyl citrate (ATBC) and triethyl citrate (TEC), glycerides, polyethylene glycol (PEG), and lactic acid esters. While these plasticizers enhance flexibility, they present several disadvantages. They can migrate from the polymer to the surface or environment, reducing their effectiveness [11]. Certain plasticizers may have toxic or allergic effects on humans and animals, especially in medical or food packaging applications [12]. Additionally, not all plasticizers are fully compatible with PLA, possibly resulting in non-uniform distribution and adverse mechanical and optical properties [13]. Research focuses on bio-based plasticizers for PLA to find alternatives that offer better performance without the associated disadvantages of traditional plasticizers [14], [15]. Alternatively, blending PLA with other polymers like polycaprolactone (PCL) and polybutylene succinate (PBS) can enhance flexibility and processability but presents challenges. Incompatibility can cause phase separation, negatively affecting mechanical properties and appearance. Optimizing processing conditions for each polymer combination increases costs and manufacturing complexity. Adding certain polymers may also affect PLA's biodegradation rate and mode, undesirable for ecological applications [16], [17]. Phenethyl esters are compounds of great interest due to their unique chemical properties formed by esterification of carboxylic acids with different chain length with phenol [18]. Both products involved can be obtained from natural resources, a sustainable route for the obtention of biobased material with low impact for the environment [19]. The ideal plasticizer is proposed to possess a combination of structural features, including aliphatic chains that act as spacers to increase the free volume and consequently lower the glass transition temperature, ester groups that contribute to molecular cohesion, and aromatic rings that enhance compatibility with the polymer matrix, thereby promoting miscibility [20]. In this context, phenethyl esters represent a promising alternative, as they incorporate all the aforementioned functional groups, facilitating the development of an effective plasticizer. As part of the ongoing search for high-performance plasticizers, the use of naturally derived compounds containing ester functionalities has previously been explored [21]. Importantly, these phenethyl esters have not been previously used as plasticizers for PLA, confirming the novel opportunity to explore their potential in enhancing the mechanical and processing properties of the polymer. Phenethyl esters have diverse applications, due to their chemical and sensory properties [22]. Phenethyl propionate serves as an intermediate in the synthesis of pharmaceuticals, including steroid hormones used in hormonal therapies [23]. As described, these esters generally have a favorable safety profile, making them suitable for use in products with direct skin, food, or medical contact.", 'Numerous techniques have been explored to enhance the ductility of PLA without compromising its environmentally friendly potential. One such approache is blending PLA with other more ductile polymers, such as poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) [8], poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) [9], or thermoplastic starch (TPS) [10]. Despite the appeal this approach offers, in some instances the poor miscibility between PLA and the other polymers reduces its viability. Thus, another more frequent strategy to improve the ductility of PLA involves the use of plasticizers, low molecular weight compounds that are incorporated into the PLA polymeric chains and mitigate the intensity of the polymer-polymer chain interactions, thus enhancing the processability and flexibility of the polymer [11]. Plasticization is very simple and cost-effective as it involves de addition of the plasticizer during the processing. However, the plasticizer must be compatible with PLA. Some environmentally friendly plasticizers that have been extensively studied include citrates [12], modified vegetable oils [13], esters of cinnamic acid [14], esters of geraniol [15] and esters of linalool [16], among others. All these plasticizers allow PLA to boost its elongation at break from a very low value (5 %) to values between 200 and 500 %. More recently, attention is being given to tartaric acid (TA) derivatives as potential plasticizers for PLA. Plasticizers derived from TA are sourced from natural origins and are biodegradable, so they preserve the biodegradability of PLA. Tartaric acid can be obtained from grapes [17] or tamarind [18]. These derivatives, which include several tartrates, show high compatible with PLA, as most widely used citrates [19]. Previous studies have shown that diethyl-l-tartrate (DET) is a highly effective plasticizer for PLA, delivering elongation at break exceeding 550 % for a DET content of 20 wt% and a reduction of the glass transition temperature of PLA from 60 down to 23 °C for a 50 wt% DET content. Zawada et al. [20] have shown the potential of 13 different tartrate compounds as “double green” biobased plasticizers for PLA. Despite they reported exceptional plasticization properties of various synthesized tartrates, most of them are not commercially available which can limit their industrial use. Although they observed good plasticization properties of diethyl tartrate (DET), they concluded the exact composition of the mixture needs further optimization to improve the overall performance, as well as the use of processing conditions similar to industrial processes. On the other hand, Gomez-Caturla et al. [19], demonstrated that a plasticizer content of 20 wt% DET, gives optimum balanced mechanical and thermal properties on plasticized PLA. Therefore, the potential of other commercially available tartrates as biobased plasticizers for PLA could be of interest. Another promising group of plasticizers yet to be explored are α-tocopherol based plasticizers. α-tocopherol is considered one of the most biologically active compounds in the phenol family. It exhibits significant antioxidant potential and has been used in several studies to enhance the food preservation capacity of polymeric materials, such as chitosan/zein mixtures [21], polyolefins [22] or polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) films [23]. Esters derived from α-tocopherol have also been used in medical applications, such as the treatment of acne [24], or the production of bi-layer membranes of α-tocopherol acetate for wound healing and skin regeneration [25]. These esters offer significant potential as plasticizers for PLA, which could additionally give this polymer antioxidant properties and other features. An additional huge advantage of α-tocopherol and its derivatives is their natural origin and environmentally friendly nature, as they are non-toxic organic, biodegradable and biocompatible compounds. Esters of α-tocopherol offer a unique chemical structure which could provide multifunctional properties to PLA since it has been demonstrated to provide melt stabilization during polyolefin processing [26], as well as antioxidant properties to PLA [27]. On the other hand, the plasticization properties of α-tocopherol, has been described by Kangarlou et al. [28], in ethyl cellulose films, therefore corroborating the potential of α-tocopherol as biobased plasticizer in polymer formulations.', 'Citrate esters triethyl citrate, tributyl citrate, and acetyl tributyl citrate were used as plasticizers for amorphous poly(D,L-lactide) (PDLLA). The resultant compositions were analyzed by means of differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), dynamic mechanical thermal analysis, and tensile testing to investigate the properties of the blends. Glass transition temperatures (Tgs) obtained by DSC were also compared to theoretically calculated Tgs. Increasing plasticizer content decreased the resultant Tg of the blend with plasticizer efficiency enhanced as the molecular weight of the citrate ester increased. However, in blends with high plasticizer content, a lack of miscibility also occurred with increased molecular weight. Theoretical results were comparable with those obtained experimentally at compositions, which were miscible. Increasing plasticizer content increased the ductility and decreased the strength of the polymer. The addition of 10 wt % plasticizer to PDLLA decreased tensile strength by over 50% with the deterioration larger at higher concentrations of plasticizer. © 2012 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. J. Appl. Polym. Sci., 2013 Of the many polymeric materials that are biodegradable, the α-hydroxy acid polylactide (PLA) is among the most extensively investigated. This is due to its proven biocompatibility and good material properties. PLA can exist in three stereochemical forms: poly(L-lactide) (PLLA), poly(D-lactide) (PDLA), and poly(DL-lactide) (PDLLA). Because of the stereo regular chain microstructure, PLLA and PDLA are semicrystalline. The polymerization of a racemic mixture of L- and D-lactides (a 50 : 50 mixture of L and D isomers) leads to the synthesis of PDLLA, which is amorphous1 and is the type of material used in the work reported here. PLA possesses good mechanical properties and generally has an elastic modulus and tensile strength in the ranges of 3.2-3.7 GPa and 55-60 MPa, respectively.2 In the unplasticized form, it has a glass transition temperature (Tg) greater then 37°C, causing PLA devices to possess brittle characteristics in physiological conditions.', 'One approach to enhance the crystallization of PLA is through the addition of plasticizers.4 Plasticizers promote the growth rate of crystallites5 and act as processing aids6; they also enhance the flexibility and ductility of polymer materials.4 Triethyl citrate (TEC) is a biodegradable, nontoxic, and efficient plasticizer for PLA.7 However, TEC also has some drawbacks is that it degrade the thermal,8 optical,9 and mechanical properties10 of PLA. Another approach is to use nanosized additives and reinforcements; because of their large surface area, they can act as effective nucleating agents and promote the crystallization of polymers.11 Several inorganic additives/reinforcements such as clays (e.g., montmorillonite,12 silica,13 and halloysite nanotubes14) and carbon-based materials (e.g., carbon nanotubes2 and graphene15) have been widely used in nanocomposites. However, the poor biodegradability and toxicity of some of these materials restrict their use in food packaging applications. Therefore, the use of polysaccharide-based reinforcements would be more beneficial not only because of their biodegradable nature, low toxicity, low cost, and easy availability16 but also because of their role as better nucleating agents. The most commonly used nanosized additives are nanocelluloses17 and starch nanoparticles.18 For example, Mathew et al.17 studied the crystallization of PLA in the presence of three different types of cellulose reinforcements: microcrystalline cellulose, cellulose fibers, and wood flour. They found that the crystallization temperature influences both the number and size of the spherulites. Gray19 investigated the crystallization of polypropylene (PP) on the surface of cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs); in the study, he employed CNC that acted as a nucleating agent and a transcrystalline layer (TCL) of PP was formed around the CNC film. The CNCs were found to increase the crystallization of PP. Pei et al.11 studied the crystallization of PLA in the presence of CNCs. The CNCs were functionalized with silane to improve their dispersion in the PLA matrix, and their role as nucleating agents was explained. The results showed that the crystallization rate was improved by the addition of 1 wt % silane-functionalized CNCs (SCNCs); this improvement was attributed to their stronger nucleating ability compared to that of nonmodified CNCs. The degree of crystallinity improved from 14% (PLA) to 30% (PLA-SCNCs). Sullivan et al.20 investigated the crystallization of PLA films prepared by melt compounding with different CNC contents (1, 2, and 3 wt %). They found that the crystallinity of the PLA film improved from 11 to 30% by the addition of 3 wt % CNCs. Trifol et al.21 studied acetylated cellulose nanofibers (CNFs), CNCs, and clay (C30B) as additives for PLA nanocomposites. They observed that the addition of just 1 wt % CNFs and 1 wt % CNCs significantly improved the crystallization kinetics of PLA without affecting its transparency. They explained that the improved crystallinity could be a result of better nucleation abilities of the CNFs and CNCs than that of the nanoclay. Furthermore, the added CNCs provided better crystallinity than the added CNFs. A recent study [35] has demonstrated that the introduction of 10 wt% of biodegradable poly(ε-caprolactone)-based random copolyesters leads to a significant improvement of PLA toughness. More surprisingly, the benefits of plasticization disappear when increasing test speeds. In addition, plasticization is accompanied by a drastic drop in material stiffness that is out of line with automotive applications. Consequently, a ternary composition made of PLA, impact modifier and plasticizer is then tested. Here the key objective is to take advantage of plasticization to increase material ductility while preserving valuable stiffness and toughness via the addition of an impact modifier. 1.  **Increase Flexibility:** Plasticizers like citrate esters (e.g., acetyl tributyl citrate (ATBC) and triethyl citrate (TEC)) enhance the flexibility of PLA [[1], [6], [8], [14], [15]]. This is achieved by reducing the intensity of polymer-polymer chain interactions [[2]] and embedding themselves between the chains, spacing them apart [[14]].
2.  **Reduce Glass Transition Temperature (Tg):** Citrate esters lower the glass transition temperature (Tg) of PLA [[1], [2], [3], [14]]. A lower Tg makes the polymer softer and more flexible at lower temperatures [[1], [14]]. The plasticizer efficiency increases with the molecular weight of the citrate ester, but higher molecular weights can lead to miscibility issues at high concentrations [[3]].
3.  **Improve Processability:** Plasticization is a simple and cost-effective method to enhance the processability of PLA [[2]].
4.  **Increase Ductility / Elongation at Break:** The addition of citrate esters significantly boosts the ductility and elongation at break of PLA, transforming it from brittle (e.g., ~5% elongation) to much more ductile (e.g., 200-500% elongation) [[1], [2], [6], [8], [15]].

This migration is due to their low molecular weight and lack of chemical bonding to the polymer chains [[8]].
    *   Potential **toxicity or allergic effects** are a concern, especially in medical or food packaging, though citrate esters are generally considered safer alternatives to phthalates [[1], [9], [10], [11]].

retrieved_contexts: ['Biomass-derived lignocellulose is the most abundant natural product on earth and has many potential applications as an additive for biodegradable plastics. On the other hand, lignin, a secondary component of lignocellulose, has recently been actively attempted to be used in the material industry based on its UV-blocking properties, antioxidant properties, and high organic carbon content [8]. However, when lignin is added to biodegradable plastics, it exhibits various disadvantages, such as self-aggregation of lignin occurring during the polymer melt process, low miscibility with the matrix polymer, and subsequent deterioration of the mechanical properties of the composite material strongly hindering its use [[9], [10], [11], [12]]. To overcome this problem, lignin fractionation, homogenization, and chemical modification have been proposed to increase the miscibility between lignin and a biodegradable polymer matrix [13]. A typical method for the chemical modification of lignin is acetylation, which has been reported to increase its hydrophobicity and compatibility with biodegradable polymers [14]. However, in the case of most biocomposites to which chemically modified lignin is added, the focus is on supplementing mechanical strength by enhancing the compatibility of the existing biodegradable matrix and demonstrating the UV-blocking effect of lignin [[15], [16], [17], [18]]. In particular, there are only a few studies reporting the effect of lignin addition on the biodegradation properties of manufactured biocomposites. Understanding the biodegradability and degradation mechanisms of bioplastics is important from an industrial and scientific point of view to predict their useful life and establish utilization plans. Therefore, it is essential to investigate the biodegradability of composite materials according to the addition of natural polymer fillers in biocomposite materials [[19], [20], [21], [22], [23]]. In fact, since general biopolymer fillers are hydrophilic, many studies have reported that most of them increase accessibility to the hydrolysis environment and accelerate biodegradation accordingly [24]. It has been also been reported that the addition of cellulose accelerated the biodegradation of PLA-based composites by 34 % and that the addition of microalgae-based biomass increases the degradation rate of PLA-based composites [[25], [26], [27]]. However, only a few additives have been designed to inhibit the degradation of these biodegradable plastics references [28]. The main purpose of this study is to prepare chemically modified lignin, improve compatibility with PLA, and use it as a functional additive to control the biodegradation behavior of PLA-based biocomposites. Firstly, AL was prepared through chemical modification to improve the low compatibility and dispersibility with PLA, which are the shortcomings of commercial technical lignin KL, and incorporated as an additive in PLA biocomposites. Changes in the physicochemical properties of lignin due to acetylation were investigated through Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR), gel permeation chromatography (GPC), phosphorus-31 nuclear magnetic resonance (31P NMR), proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR), and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). In addition, improved compatibility between PLA and AL was confirmed by observing the hygroscopic properties of AL, the dissolution and dispersion properties of AL in organic solvents, and the fracture surface morphology of the AL/PLA biocomposite. Ultimately, to investigate the effect of adding chemically modified lignin on the biodegradation characteristics of the lignin/PLA composite, a biodegradation experiment was performed for 45 days in a thermophilic composting environment above the glass transition temperature of PLA. Changes in physicochemical properties of lignin/PLA biocomposite according to biodegradation behavior were analyzed through GPC, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), TGA, and X-ray diffraction (XRD).', "Several studies have focused on chemical [7,18,19,29] or physical [25,30,31] modifications of lignin, as well as the use of compatibilizers [18,32], to achieve enhanced compatibility and performance of lignin/biodegradable polymer compounds. However, this is usually accompanied by additional costs and is not always required to substitute fossil-based and/or non-biodegradable existing products [3]. The incorporation of unmodified Kraft lignin into PBS resulted in elastic modulus and ductility maintenance, in addition to providing antioxidant and antimicrobial properties [8]. Biodegradable polyesters are considered good candidates for use as matrices for lignin, since there can be specific intermolecular interactions between them due to the numerous functional groups in the structure of lignin [33]. These interactions, such as hydrogen bonds, can enhance phase compatibility and even allow complete or partial miscibility, as reported in previous works [[34], [35], [36], [37], [38]]. When incorporated into thermoplastic polymers, lignin can behave as a macromolecular substance if the compound is processed at temperatures above lignin's glass transition temperature (Tg) or as a particulate filler, otherwise. In the first case, the resulting material is usually called a blend or a composite in the latter [40]. In all circumstances, investigations of the miscibility or compatibility, phase distribution and interactions of lignin/polymer systems are fundamental to understanding structure-properties-applications relationships [41]. The miscibility or compatibility of lignin/polymer compounds have been investigated by analyzing their glass transition and thermal behavior, phase morphology and intermolecular interactions. Advanced AFM techniques, such as nanomechanical mapping, can provide significant additional data to investigate miscibility, compatibility and interphase characteristics of polymer blends and nanocomposites [[44], [45], [46], [47], [48]]. Nevertheless, this technique has not been explored for lignin-based thermoplastic compounds yet.", 'Despite the potential benefits of incorporating lignin into traditional polymers to mitigate the shortcomings of composite materials, the utilization of lignin-based bioplastics is limited due to their inferior processability and mechanical properties [17]. The problem caused by poor processability of some types of lignin, such as Alkali lignin, can be solved by neutralization or acidification of lignin [18]. Moreover, it can only be blended in small amounts due to its immiscibility in the majority of polyesters. It was discovered that the organosolv lignin and its butyrate derivative were highly miscible with some polymers, such as PHB, and that lignin inhibits and delays the crystallization of PHB [19, 20]. In particular, there are only a few studies reporting the effect of lignin addition on the biodegradation properties of manufactured biocomposites.', 'Research in polymer nanocomposites has been motivated by the opportunities to enhance or augment the physical properties of polymeric materials. Biomass-derived fillers, including cellulose nanofibers or lignin, have attracted particular interest in the context of ‘sustainable materials engineering’ as a means towards more benign (and low-energy) polymer materials. However, although the concept of reducing the environmental footprint of synthetic polymers by dilution with bio-sourced fillers appears to be straightforward, the loss of desirable physical properties, such as mechanical strength or optical clarity, that is often observed in biomass-based polymer composites limits the impact of the ‘nanocomposite approach’ for sustainable material engineering. The effect of filler addition on the physical properties of polymers sensitively depends on the morphology of the composite material and filler-matrix interactions. Aggregation of dispersed particle fillers is generally considered to be detrimental to physical properties of nanocomposites due to embrittlement of the material as well as the loss of optical clarity [1], [2], [3], [4]. This presents a particular challenge for biobased fillers - such as lignin - due their inherent chemical incompatibility with most engineering plastics [5], [6]. For example, blends of hydroxypropyl lignin in PMMA were found to exhibit a strain-to-fracture of less than 2% (about half of the value typically observed for pristine PMMA at moderate strain rates) - the embrittlement was attributed to weak polymer-filler interactions and the formation of micron-scale lignin aggregates [7]. A large number of studies involving both bio-sourced as well as inorganic particle fillers have corroborated the particular relevance of filler-matrix interactions as governing parameter that determines the physical properties of polymer nanocomposite materials [8]. retrieved_contexts: ["Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting is an emerging tissue engineering approach that aims to develop cell or biomolecule-laden, complex polymeric scaffolds with high precision, using hydrogel-based “bioinks”. Hydrogels are water-swollen, highly crosslinked polymer networks that are soft, quasi-solid, and can support and protect biological materials. However, traditional hydrogels have weak mechanical properties and cannot retain complex structures. They must be reinforced with physical and chemical manipulations to produce a mechanically resilient bioink. Over the past few years, we have witnessed an increased use of nanoparticles and biological moiety-functionalized nanoparticles to fabricate new bioinks. Nanoparticles of varied size, shape, and surface chemistries can provide a unique solution to this problem primarily because of three reasons: (a) nanoparticles can mechanically reinforce hydrogels through physical and chemical interactions. This can favorably influence the bioink's 3D printability and structural integrity by modulating its rheological, biomechanical, and biochemical properties, allowing greater flexibility to print a wide range of structures; (b) nanoparticles can introduce new bio-functionalities to the hydrogels, which is a key metric of a bioink's performance, influencing both cell-material and cell-cell interactions within the hydrogel; (c) nanoparticles can impart “smart” features to the bioink, making the tissue constructs responsive to external stimuli. Responsiveness of the hydrogel to magnetic field, electric field, pH changes, and near-infrared light can be made possible by the incorporation of nanoparticles. Additionally, bioink polymeric networks with nanoparticles can undergo advanced chemical crosslinking, allowing greater flexibility to print structures with varied biomechanical properties. Taken together, the unique properties of various nanoparticles can help bioprint intricate constructs, bringing the process one step closer to complex tissue structure and organ printing. In this review, we explore the design principles and multifunctional properties of various nanomaterials and nanocomposite hydrogels for potential, primarily extrusion-based bioprinting applications. We illustrate the significance of biocompatibility of the designed nanocomposite hydrogel-based bioink for clinical translation and discuss the different parameters that affect cell fate after cell-nanomaterial interaction. Finally, we critically assess the current challenges of nanoengineering bioinks and provide insight into the future directions of potential hydrogel bioinks in the rapidly evolving field of bioprinting. Among the different types of materials, hydrogels have been suitably used as bioinks for extrusion-based tissue printing applications.11-13 Hydrogels are water-retaining, crosslinked, polymeric chains that closely resemble macromolecular-based structures in the body.14-16 Hydrogels are excellent candidates for biomedical applications, including 3D bioprinting, because of their bio-friendly material properties.17 Biopolymers, such as polysaccharides and polypeptides, derived from plant and animal sources are crosslinked either physically or chemically to form natural hydrogels.18 Natural hydrogels are easily degradable and form desirable scaffolds for cell encapsulation and adhesion. Because of these favorable biological properties, natural polymer-based hydrogels are often selected for 3D bioprinting.19 However, hydrogels made from purely natural polymers find limited applications.20 Hydrogels originating from natural sources like gelatin, sodium alginate and chitosan exhibit inferior mechanical properties. This is particularly problematic for in vivo tissue engineering applications. Premature wearing-out of hydrogels can lead to the early degradation of the scaffold and unnecessary formation of cracks at the site of application. Degraded scaffolds can even fall prey to harmful opportunistic microorganisms.21 Different strategies to modify the polymer chemistry and enhance the applicability of such materials have been investigated over the past decade. Some of the examples include the use of double-network hydrogels,22 multi-network hydrogels,23 click chemistry-based hydrogels,24 and supramolecular hydrogels.25 However, they are currently limited by one or more of the following parameters - mechanical resilience, printability, shape fidelity, proper mechanical energy dissipation mechanism, biocompatibility, cell-instructive, or biofunctional properties. Introducing nanoparticles into the polymeric network of hydrogels (also known as nanocomposite hydrogels) has the potential to address the current drawbacks of conventional bioinks.26,27 In fact, reinforcing hydrogels with nanoparticles can offer unique advantages over earlier discussed strategies.28Fig. 1 summarizes some of the crucial functionalities that can be imparted by the appropriate use of nanoparticles. The figure also highlights some possible areas of application of these bioinks. Unique properties, such as photo-responsiveness,29 magnetic field-responsiveness,30 and so on, can be integrated by functionalizing the hydrogels with nanoparticles. Different types of nanomaterials are being considered for the functionalization process. For example, carbon-based nanomaterials, such as carbon nanotubes and carbon dots, can make hydrogels electroconductive, thermally conductive, optically active, and mechanically strong.31,32 Bioactive inorganic nanoparticles have also been studied for designing nanocomposite hydrogels. Inorganic materials like silicon, calcium, magnesium, and many more, are essential to the proper functioning of the body.33 Nanoparticles synthesized with these minerals can impart properties unique to such nanomaterials. For instance, nanosilicates, also known as nanoclay/LAPONITE®® silicate nanoplatelets, can be added to hydrogels to introduce osteogenic properties.34 Nanosilicates can also enhance the mechanical properties of hydrogels and help in modulating the release of drugs.35,36 Metal and metal oxide nanoparticles are also commonly used for fabricating nanocomposite hydrogels.37 Silver-based nanoparticles show antimicrobial properties that are often used to design nanocomposite hydrogels to counter antibiotic-resistant bacteria.38 Gold nanospheres can introduce photothermal-responsiveness in hydrogels.39 These unique nanocomposite hydrogels are being implemented as drug delivery devices, biosensors, bioactuators, tissue engineering scaffolds and so on. An emerging application of these materials is in the field of 3D bioprinting where they serve as the bioinks.26,40,41Fig. 2A-D display injectable nanocomposite hydrogels that have the potential to become bioinks.36,42-44 However, it should be noted that there are strict process requirements for 3D bioprinting, which will be discussed in section 2. The examples presented in Fig. 2 can become biomaterial inks only when such rigorous process standards are met. In this review, we will focus primarily on the material properties of different nanocomposite hydrogels that are essential to generate the next generation of biomaterial inks and/or bioinks for diverse biomedical applications. Additionally, the review will also provide an insight into the future of these newly formulated bioinks and nanocomposite hydrogels.", 'Natural hydrogels are widely used for 3D-bioprinting because of their qualities for tissue engineering. Thus, material modification and a method to incorporate cell attachment motifs are required in order to create a stable hydrogel with appropriate cell-material interactions.', 'Three-dimensional (3D) printing is an additive manufacturing process that is now widely accepted for the bottom-up fabrication of components from different materials, including metals [1, 2], ceramics [3, 4], and polymers [5-7]. Based exclusively on the provided context, 3D bioprinting utilizes biodegradable hydrogels in the following ways:

1.  **As Primary Bioink Materials:** Hydrogels, particularly those derived from natural biopolymers like alginate, gelatin, chitosan, hyaluronic acid, and collagen, are widely used as bioinks due to their biocompatibility and biodegradability (Context 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15). Their biodegradability is essential for eventual replacement by native tissue.
2.  **Mimicking the Extracellular Matrix (ECM):** Hydrogels closely resemble the natural macromolecular-based structures and water-rich environment of the body's ECM (Context 1, 4, 7, 8, 11, 14, 15). This resemblance is crucial for cell encapsulation, adhesion, growth, and differentiation within the bioprinted constructs.
3.  **Cell Encapsulation and Support:** Hydrogels provide a supportive, hydrated 3D environment that protects encapsulated cells during the bioprinting process and supports their viability and function afterward (Context 1, 11, 14, 15).
4.  **Structural Scaffolding:** Bioprinted hydrogel constructs act as temporary scaffolds. Their biodegradability allows them to gradually degrade as newly formed tissue replaces them (Context 1, 4, 6, 14, 15).
5.  **Functionalization for Enhanced Performance:** Biodegradable hydrogels serve as a base material that can be modified or combined with other components (nanoparticles, other polymers, bioactive molecules) to enhance their properties while retaining biodegradability:
    *   **Mechanical Reinforcement:** Nanoparticles (e.g., nanosilicates, carbon-based materials) or other strategies (e.g., double networks, phenolated complexes) are incorporated into biodegradable hydrogels to improve their often weak mechanical properties and printability/shape fidelity without sacrificing biocompatibility/degradability (Context 1, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14, 15).
    *   **Adding Biofunctionality:** Nanoparticles or biological moieties (e.g., bioactive glass, platelet lysate) are added to biodegradable hydrogels to impart specific biological functions like osteogenesis, mineralization, angiogenic properties, or controlled drug/growth factor release (Context 1, 2, 4, 6).
    *   **Imparting Responsiveness:** Nanoparticles can make biodegradable hydrogels responsive to external stimuli (e.g., magnetic field, pH, temperature, light) enabling "smart" constructs (Context 1, 9).
    *   **Improving Printability/Shape Fidelity:** Strategies like nanocomposite formation (Context 1), blending polysaccharides (Context 7, 13), enzymatic crosslinking (Context 10), shear-thinning designs (Context 4, 11), or using dual-crosslinkable systems (e.g., GelMA/SFMA) (Context 15) are applied to biodegradable hydrogels to achieve the necessary rheological properties (e.g., shear-thinning, viscosity) for successful extrusion-based printing and maintaining the printed structure.
6.  **Drug Delivery Vehicles:** Biodegradable hydrogels are used to bioprint constructs designed for controlled drug release. Their degradation rate influences the release profile of incorporated therapeutic agents (Context 3, 9). Stimuli-responsiveness (e.g., pH, temperature) can further control release (Context 9).

In summary, biodegradable hydrogels are the fundamental material in 3D bioprinting, primarily serving as cell-laden bioinks that mimic the ECM, provide structural support, protect cells, and are designed to degrade controllably. They are continually engineered (e.g., as nanocomposites, blends, or modified polymers) to overcome limitations like poor mechanical strength or printability while enhancing biofunctionality for specific tissue engineering applications.

The effect of moisture content on the processing of PHBV is primarily mediated through hydrolysis reactions and interactions with hydrophilic components, as evidenced by the contexts:  

1. **Hydrolysis of PHBV during Processing**:  
   Residual moisture in natural fibers (e.g., wheat straw) used in PHBV composites induces hydrolysis of ester bonds in PHBV, reducing its molecular weight and increasing crystallinity. This occurs due to residual water molecules facilitating chain scission, even if fiber/matrix adhesion remains visually unaffected (Contexts 3, 4, 7).  

2. **Impact of Hydrophilic Additives**:  
   Incorporating hydrophilic agents like PEG or cellulose derivatives (e.g., MCC) increases the wettability and water absorption of PHBV blends. While this enhances interfacial adhesion with hydrophilic fibers, it also accelerates hydrolytic degradation during processing or long-term use, necessitating moisture control to prevent premature degradation (Contexts 9, 10).  

3. **Thermal Degradation**:  
   Moisture present during thermal processing (e.g., melt blending) can hydrolyze carboxylic acid groups in PHBV, lowering thermal stability. For example, in PHBV/PCL blends, moisture released from PHBV degradation accelerates PCL degradation, though nanoparticles like TiO₂ mitigate this by retarding volatilization (Context 5).  

4. **Fiber Pre-Treatment**:  
   Chemical treatments (alkaline, acid, or solvent extraction) reduce fiber moisture content by removing hydrophilic non-cellulosic components (hemicellulose, lignin), thereby minimizing hydrolysis risks during PHBV composite processing (Context 7).  

5. **Environmental Humidity**:  
   High relative humidity during storage or processing can plasticize PHBV composites, altering mechanical properties. However, PHBV’s inherent hydrophobicity and crystallinity slow water diffusion, making it less moisture-sensitive unless modified with hydrophilic additives (Contexts 8, 9).  

In summary, moisture content during PHBV processing must be carefully managed to avoid hydrolysis-induced molecular weight reduction and thermal degradation. Pre-drying fibers, optimizing hydrophilic additive levels, and controlling environmental humidity are critical for maintaining PHBV’s structural and mechanical integrity.

Biodegradable shape memory polymers (SMP) have attracted a great deal of attention as a novel class of biomaterials able to fulfill growing clinical requirements [1,2]. SMPs undergo significant macroscopic deformation upon the application of an external stimulus (e.g., heat, electricity, light, magnetism, moisture and even a change in pH value) [3]. The SMPs can be fabricated in a specific permanent shape, deformed and fixed in a second, temporary shape. They are able to return to their original, permanent shape when exposed to a suitable external stimulus. On the molecular/morphological level SMPs consist of at least two components: switching domains and permanent netpoints [4]. The switching domains act as molecular switch with a well-defined melting temperature (Tm) or a glass transition temperature (Tg) and enable the fixation of the temporary shape. The permanent netpoints are physical netpoints (hard domain) associated with a high thermal transition temperature (Tm or Tg) or covalent netpoints (covalently crosslinked polymer network). Among thermo-responsive SMPs physically and covalently crosslinked polyurethanes (PU) have been extensively investigated for their shape memory effects. Macromolecules of polyurethane consist of alternating sequences of hard and soft segments, which due to thermodynamical dissimilarity separate into hard and soft domain microstructure. Hard segments, that are produced by the reaction between the diisocyanate and the chain extender, act as physical crosslinks due to polar interaction, hydrogen bonding, and/or crystallization, and are therefore responsible for the “permanent” shape. Whereas polyether, polyester, or polycarbonate diol comprises the soft segments that act as the thermally reversible phase and the vitrification or crystallization of these soft segments is able to fix the temporary shape. By varying the molecular weight of polyol and the composition of the different segments, mechanical properties and transition temperature of PUR can be tuned up for required application [[5], [6], [7]]. In order to describe the thermomechanical properties of thermo-responsive SMPs the viscoelastic models could be especially useful. The specific feature of thermo-responsive SMPs is that their mechanical properties vary greatly in the transition region and the creep recovery is quite different above and below the transition temperature [8]. In the work [8] the authors proposed four-element viscoelastic model having slip mechanism due to internal friction. The proposed idea was further developed by Ref. [9]. In the mentioned paper, a thermomechanical viscoelastic constitutive model describing typical thermomechanical cycle was presented. The shape memory effect was explained by interaction of two distinct phases: the active phase and the frozen phase. In-depth understanding of the thermodynamics of the thermo-responsive SMPUs at different length scales requires using of many sophisticated material characterization techniques. Most of the conventional materials characterization techniques used in the polymer science are not enable for carrying investigation of the mechanical properties of the shape memory effect in nanoscale. The most suitable technique, which enable for this is the atomic force microscopy (AFM). The above mentioned technique gives investigators exceptional opportunity of characterization of the surface morphology as well as for mechanical characterization of a given material, both in nanoscale. In the work of [10] the thermomechanical formation and recovery of the SMP was investigated in nano-scale using the heated AFM tip as well as atomic force microscope hot-stage. Based **ONLY** on the provided context, the 'Shape Memory Effect' in biodegradable polyurethanes is defined as follows:

1.  **Molecular Mechanism:** Biodegradable shape memory polyurethanes (SMPUs) consist of two distinct phases:
    *   **Reversible Phase:** Typically the soft segments (e.g., poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), poly(lactic acid) (PLA), lactone copolymers) [1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 13]. This phase has a thermal transition (melting temperature, Tm, or glass transition temperature, Tg).
    *   **Frozen Phase/Permanent Netpoints:** Typically the hard segments [1, 3]. This phase acts as physical netpoints (due to polar interactions, hydrogen bonding, crystallization) or covalent netpoints (crosslinks), defining the permanent shape and providing the restoring force. It has a high thermal transition temperature [1].

2.  **The Effect:**
    *   The polymer is fabricated in its **permanent (original) shape** [1, 10].
    *   It is **deformed** above the transition temperature (Tm or Tg) of the reversible phase (soft segments) [1, 3, 10].
    *   The deformed shape is **fixed as the temporary shape** by cooling the material below the transition temperature of the reversible phase. This cooling causes vitrification or crystallization of the reversible phase (soft segments), locking the temporary deformation [1, 3, 6].
    *   Upon exposure to a suitable **external stimulus** (most commonly heat above the Tm or Tg of the reversible phase) [1, 3, 6, 10], the reversible phase softens (melts or transitions from glassy to rubbery state).
    *   The stored elastic energy within the frozen phase/permanent netpoints (hard segments) drives the material to **recover its original, permanent shape** [1, 3, 8, 10].

**Key Aspects from Context:**
*   The effect relies on the entropy elasticity of the polymer network driven by the permanent netpoints [8].
*   High crystallinity of the soft segment regions is often crucial for effective shape fixation [3].
*   The transition temperature (Ttrans) for recovery is dictated by the Tm or Tg of the reversible phase (soft segments) and can be tuned near body temperature for biomedical applications [5, 6, 7, 10].
*   This effect enables applications like minimally invasive surgery (e.g., self-expanding stents, sutures, tissue engineering scaffolds) [1, 7, 10, 11, 12].
reference: The Shape Memory Effect allows the polymer to be deformed and fixed in a temporary shape and then recover its original permanent shape upon heating above a transition temperature (Ttrans, usually Tg or Tm). In biodegradable polyurethanes, this is driven by the phase separation between hard segments (permanent shape fixation) and soft segments (switching transition).

The role of 'stratification' (interpreted as **phase-separated morphology** in the provided context) in the degradation of PCL/PLA blends is critical due to the immiscibility of these polymers. When blended, PLA and PCL undergo **phase separation**, creating distinct PCL-rich and PLA-rich domains within the material matrix. This stratified structure enhances degradation through the following mechanisms:  

1. **Enhanced Accessibility to Degradation Agents**: Phase separation creates interfacial boundaries and localized PCL-rich regions. These domains allow easier penetration of water and enzymes (e.g., lipases, esterases) into the material, accelerating hydrolysis and enzymatic attack. PCL's aliphatic ester bonds are particularly susceptible to enzymatic degradation compared to PLA's ester bonds [25, 44].  

2. **Crystallinity Modulation**: PCL is inherently more crystalline than PLA, but blending disrupts polymer chain packing. Higher PCL content reduces overall crystallinity in the blend, increasing amorphous regions. Amorphous phases are more accessible to hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation than crystalline ones, further accelerating mass loss [51, 52].  

3. **Dynamic Degradation Kinetics**: The interplay between crystalline and amorphous regions in stratified blends creates a dynamic degradation profile. Amorphous regions degrade rapidly due to water/enzyme penetration, while residual crystalline regions provide temporary structural stability, extending degradation over time [53, 54].  

4. **Autocatalytic Effects**: In stratified blends, degraded low-molecular-weight fragments (e.g., from PCL-rich regions) can induce autocatalytic hydrolysis, accelerating PLA chain scission even in less accessible regions [46, 47].  

Thus, stratification (phase separation) in PCL/PLA blends optimizes the balance between structural integrity and degradability by tailoring polymer accessibility, crystallinity, and enzymatic susceptibility.

Based on the provided contexts, the oxygen barrier properties of PLA compared to PET are discussed indirectly through their structural characteristics. While explicit numerical values for PET's oxygen permeability are not provided, the contexts highlight that PET's crystalline structure increases tortuosity, which reduces gas permeability. In contrast, PLA exhibits a decoupling between its crystalline and amorphous phases, attributed to the high flexibility of its molecular chains, which limits the formation of a tortuous path for oxygen molecules. This structural difference implies that **PET has superior oxygen barrier properties (lower oxygen permeability) compared to PLA**. 

Key points from the contexts:  
1. PET's crystalline phase creates a more tortuous path for oxygen diffusion, enhancing its barrier properties ([12]).  
2. PLA's amorphous phase allows greater molecular mobility, leading to higher oxygen permeability ([11], [12]).  

Thus, PLA's oxygen barrier is inferior to PET's due to differences in polymer morphology affecting gas diffusion pathways.

In this study, we developed a biodegradable and temperature-sensitive injectable hydrogel system based on heparin-bearing poly(ε-caprolactone-co-lactide)-b-poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(ε-caprolactone-co-lactide) (Hep-PCLA) as the carrier system for lysozyme. The 'sol-gel' transition in injectable biodegradable hydrogels refers to a **temperature-responsive phase change** where a polymer solution (sol) transforms into a gel network upon exposure to physiological conditions (e.g., body temperature). This process is driven by **physical crosslinking** mechanisms, such as hydrophobic interactions or micelle aggregation, without requiring toxic chemical cross-linkers. Key features include:

1. **Mechanism**: 
   - **Amphiphilic copolymers** (e.g., PEG-polyester block copolymers) exhibit a delicate **hydrophobic/hydrophilic balance**. At lower temperatures (e.g., room temperature), the solution remains in a free-flowing sol state. Upon heating to body temperature, hydrophobic segments (e.g., PLA, PLGA, PCL) aggregate, forming micelles that entangle into a three-dimensional gel network. 

2. **Thermoresponsive Behavior**: 
   - The transition is reversible and relies on temperature-dependent dehydration of hydrophilic components (e.g., PEG) and hydrophobic interactions. Rheological studies (e.g., storage modulus \( G' \) exceeding loss modulus \( G'' \)) confirm the gelation.

3. **Applications**:
   - Enables **minimally invasive delivery** via syringe injection, forming depots for **sustained drug release** or **cell scaffolds** in tissue engineering. 
   - Adjustable gelation properties (e.g., via copolymer architecture, blending ratios) allow customization of mechanical strength and degradation rates.

4. **Advantages Over Chemical Gels**:
   - Avoids **toxicity** from cross-linkers, UV irradiation, or organic solvents.
   - Preserves protein/cell viability and supports biocompatibility.

5. **Challenges**:
   - Physical gels may revert to sol under high hydration, limiting duration. Solutions include combining with covalent bonds (e.g., stereocomplexation) or using slow-degrading polyesters (e.g., PCL).

In summary, the sol-gel transition is a critical property enabling injectable hydrogels to serve as versatile, biocompatible platforms for biomedical applications, leveraging temperature-sensitive self-assembly of amphiphilic polymers.

This allows for minimally invasive injection of the material, which then solidifies in situ to form a depot or scaffold.

Based solely on the provided context:

1.  **Stereocomplexation reduces degradation rate:** Stereocomplexes formed between PLLA and PDLA (or d-LA oligomers) exhibit **increased resistance toward hydrolytic degradation** ([1], [5]) and **enhanced hydrolysis resistance** ([2], [7]) compared to pure PLLA homocrystals. This slower degradation is attributed to the **stronger intermolecular interactions** (van der Waals forces like CH3⋯CO and hydrogen bonding) and **higher degree of crystallinity** in the stereocomplex structure ([1], [2], [7], [14]).

2.  **Degradation Products:** Stereocomplexes with specific architectures (star-shaped with four alcoholic end-groups) undergo **slow hydrolytic degradation with low release of degradation products**. Materials with linear d-LA oligomers exhibit similar mass loss but release **higher concentrations of shorter acidic degradation products** ([1]). Stereocomplexes with d-LA oligomers having carboxylic chain-ends show **increased release of degradation products** alongside faster mass loss ([1]).

3.  **Influence of End-Groups and Architecture:** Slower mass loss occurs with d-LA oligomers having **alcoholic end-groups** (especially four) due to a **higher degree of stereocomplexation**. Faster mass loss occurs with d-LA oligomers having **carboxylic end-groups** due to **lower stereocomplexation**. Increasing the number of alcoholic chain-ends from four to six **decreases stereocomplexation and increases mass loss**. Linear structures *can* also promote slower mass loss if they facilitate stereocomplexation ([1]).

4.  **Optical Purity:** Decreasing the optical purity (increasing the "wrong" isomer content within a chain) below critical levels (e.g., <76%) eliminates crystallizability, leading to amorphous materials ([7], [5]). **Amorphous PLA (like D,L-PLA) generally degrades faster than semicrystalline PLA** ([5]), implying that lower stereochemical purity within a chain accelerates degradation by hindering crystallization.

5.  **Crystallinity Link:** The degradation rate depends on the surface area and crystallinity ([8], [12]). Stereocomplexation enhances crystallinity ([1], [2]), which contributes to its slower degradation. Conversely, materials with lower stereocomplexation degrees (e.g., due to carboxylic end-groups, higher molecular weight) or lower optical purity (leading to amorphous) degrade faster ([1], [7]).

Therefore, the stereochemistry (L vs. D isomers) dramatically impacts PLA degradation primarily through its influence on crystallinity and intermolecular interactions. The formation of stereocomplex crystallites (L and D polymers) dramatically slows down degradation rates compared to pure homocrystals or amorphous material. End-group chemistry and architecture further modulate this effect through their impact on stereocomplexation and crystallinity.

Based solely on the provided context, glycerol serves the following roles in TPS production:

1.  **Primary Plasticizer:** Glycerol is a widely studied and used polyol plasticizer for converting native starch into TPS. It interacts with starch molecules, primarily amylose, by forming hydrogen bonds ([1], [2], [5], [6]).
2.  **Lowers Glass Transition Temperature (Tg):** Glycerol effectively reduces the Tg of starch, transforming it from a brittle material into a flexible, processable thermoplastic. For example, with 15% moisture and 30% glycerol, Tg decreases from ~87°C to 25°C ([1], [2], [6], [13]).
3.  **Improves Processability:** By disrupting intermolecular hydrogen bonds between starch chains via its high hydrophilicity, glycerol facilitates the gelatinization process under heat and shear, enabling melt processing techniques like extrusion and injection molding ([1], [6]).
4.  **Cost-Effective:** Glycerol is highlighted as a low-cost plasticizer, especially advantageous for mass production of TPS due to its abundance as a by-product of biodiesel production ([1], [3]).
5.  **Non-Toxic Option:** Glycerol is FDA-approved as a food additive, making it suitable for food and biomedical applications of TPS ([1], [2], [5]).

**Limitations noted in the context:**
*   Glycerol is known to leach out during aging and humidity exposure ([1]).
*   It exhibits higher volatility and lower thermal stability compared to sorbitol, especially above 200°C ([2], [4]).
*   Glycerol-plasticized TPS generally has higher moisture sensitivity and lower water resistance than sorbitol-plasticized TPS ([2], [4], [6], [10]).
*   The interaction between glycerol and starch is sometimes insufficient to fully prevent retrogradation ([5]).

The 'lag phase' in the biodegradation of plastics in compost refers to the initial period during which microbial and physicochemical processes prepare the material for active degradation but no significant biodegradation is yet observed. This phase is characterized by:  
1. **Time for Environmental Penetration**: Water and microorganisms infiltrate the polymer matrix.  
2. **Enzyme Activation**: Microbes secrete extracellular enzymes to initiate cleavage of polymer chains (depolymerization).  
3. **Biofilm Formation**: Microbial colonization and establishment of biofilms on the material surface.  

For example, in cellulose (a reference material), the lag phase lasts ~10 days, while composites like pineapple leaf fiber-PP require ~30 days ([1], [2], [3]). The duration depends on factors such as material composition, crystallinity, and environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, microbial consortia). This phase precedes the active degradation phase, where rapid breakdown of oligomers/monomers occurs, leading to mineralization ([3], [9]).
reference: The lag phase is the initial period where no significant mineralization (CO2 evolution) occurs. During this time, microorganisms colonize the surface and secrete extracellular enzymes to begin fragmenting the polymer chain. Only after the molecular weight drops sufficiently to produce water-soluble intermediates does rapid assimilation and mineralization begin.

PHBV (polyhydroxybutyrate-co-valerate) is preferred over pure PHB due to several critical improvements in material properties and processability:  

1. **Reduced Brittleness**: PHBV has **lower crystallinity** compared to PHB (which often exceeds 50% crystallinity). The incorporation of 3-hydroxyvalerate (HV) units disrupts PHB’s rigid crystalline structure, enhancing flexibility and reducing brittleness, making PHBV less prone to cracking [[1], [4], [5]].  

2. **Improved Processing Window**: PHB’s melting temperature (~172°C) is dangerously close to its thermal decomposition temperature (~200°C), complicating melt processing. PHBV’s melting point decreases with increasing HV content (e.g., to ~108°C at 95 mol% HV), widening the processing window and reducing degradation risks during manufacturing [[1], [7]].  

3. **Enhanced Toughness and Ductility**: Higher HV content in PHBV (>20 mol%) improves impact resistance and elongation at break, addressing PHB’s mechanical fragility. Even commercial PHBV with low HV content (e.g., 3 mol%) exhibits better flexibility than PHB [[1], [2], [14]].  

4. **Controlled Crystallization**: PHBV’s slower crystallization rate compared to PHB reduces the formation of large, crack-prone spherulites, mitigating brittleness. This also improves dimensional stability during cooling [[2], [13]].  

5. **Biodegradability**: PHBV degrades faster than PHB under composting conditions, with biodegradability increasing with HV content. This aligns with environmental goals for sustainable materials [[8]].  

6. **Blending Compatibility**: PHBV blends more effectively with other polymers (e.g., PBS, PLA) via in situ compatibilization, enhancing interfacial adhesion and mechanical properties. Such blends are challenging with PHB due to poor affinity [[2], [10], [11]].  

7. **Broad Applications**: PHBV’s balanced properties enable use in biomedical (tissue engineering, drug delivery), packaging, and agricultural applications, where PHB’s rigidity and processing limitations are prohibitive [[4], [5], [9]].  

In summary, PHBV’s tunable HV content optimizes crystallinity, thermal stability, and mechanical performance, overcoming PHB’s key drawbacks while retaining biodegradability and biocompatibility.
