retrieved_contexts: ['Poly(ortho esters) (POEs) are a group of biodegradable polyesters that were firstly synthesized in the 1970s by the ALZA Corporation in order to develop materials that may potentially undergo surface erosion degradation process, which is not commonly found in biodegradable polyesters [138], [139]. The high hydrophobicity provided by the orthoesther linkages ensures that the degradation proceeds faster than the H2O diffusion into the material. POEs are synthesized by using diols having different chain flexibility. Till the date, four types of these surface eroding materials have been reported [140], [141]. 1st generation POEs (or POE I) are obtained upon transesterification of a diol together with diethoxytetrahydrofuran. POE II (2nd generation) were developed to avoid the release of acidic by-products during its degradation (as occurring in POE I). Such materials are obtained by reacting diols with diketene acetal 3,9-bis(ethylidene 2,4,8,10-tetraoxaspiro[5,5]undecane). POE III (3rd generation) could be obtained upon direct polymerization of a triol together with an orthoester, yielding a highly mechanically flexible gel-like material. Finally, 4th generation POEs (POE IV, Fig. 2) were developed to solve the up-scaling difficulties of POE III and, similarly to POE II, they can be obtained by incorporating soft segments based on LA and GA into the chain backbone. Although generally speaking POE IV show weak mechanical properties, their good biodegradability has boosted their use in tissue engineering and drug delivery applications [142]. This last group of POE presents a scalable synthetic procedure and has the highest versatility as their properties could be tuned by properly selecting the nature of diols and the amount of LA or GA in the main chain [141], [143], [144]. Thus, depending on the flexibility of the diol chain, a wide variety of thermo-mechanical properties can be achieved; from hard, glassy materials showing a high glass transition temperature to semi-solid polymers showing low glass transition temperature. As polyesters usually display rather brittle mechanical behaviour which is not adequate for some biomedical applications, novel elastomeric biodegradable polyesters such as poly(diol citrates) and poly(glycerol sebacate) (PGS) have been synthesized for soft tissue engineering applications (Fig. 2) [145], [146]. Poly(diol citrates) can be synthesized via polycondensation reactions using non-toxic and inexpensive monomers, such as citric acid. Besides, considering the availability of various diols with different chain flexibility, biodegradable elastomers with tuneable mechanical properties can be obtained through relatively simple synthesis procedures. In this sense, a series of poly(diol citrates) were synthesized by reacting citric acid with various diols: poly(1,6-hexanediol-co-citrate) (PHC), poly(1,8-octanediol-co-citrate) (POC), poly(1,10-decanediol-co-citrate) (PDC) and poly(1,12-dodecanediol-co-citrate) (PDDC) [147]. All the synthesized polymers were totally amorphous and displayed low Tg ranging from −5 to 10 °C. Regarding the mechanical properties, which are summarized in Table 5, all the poly(diol citrates) displayed an elastomeric behaviour with no permanent deformation. Moreover, these mechanical properties were finely adjusted, not only by the selected diol, but also through cross-link density, by adjusting the post-polymerization temperature and time [148]. Similar to the poly(alkylene dicarboxylate)s based on dicarboxylic acids and dihydroxy compounds analysed in the previous section, polymers based on glycerol can also be synthesized, being PGS the most studied one within this category. The first polymerization of PGS was reported in 2002 through polycondensation reaction of equimolar ratios of glycerol and sebacic acid reacted at 120 °C in the absence of a catalyst under inert conditions [145]. Owing to its physico-mechanical properties and easy of synthesis, these non-toxic polyesters show a huge potential for developing inexpensive and biodegradable elastomeric materials for tissue engineering applications [146]. The thermo-mechanical properties of PGS, which have been recently reviewed by Rai et al. [149], can be adjusted by varying the glycerol to sebacic acid ratio, curing temperature and time. In general, this thermoset polymer shows a Tg at around −37 °C. It has an unsaturated linear structure and could be obtained via a transesterification reaction of fumaric diester [150]. Thanks to the presence of fumarate double groups in its main backbone, PPF shows a unique property to form crosslinked structures [151], resulting in higher mechanical strength material that can be employed as an injectable material as bone cement [152]. Overall, the physico-mechanical properties of PPF are mainly dependant on the molecular weight and crosslinking. 1.  **Crosslinking Mechanism:** Citric acid acts as a cross-linking agent primarily by forming stable covalent intermolecular ester bonds between its carboxylic groups and the hydroxyl groups of starch molecules under the action of heat or catalyst [[7], [10]]. This connects multiple starch molecules, acting as a "chemical bridge" [[7], [10]].
2.  **Chemical Changes:** This process reduces hydrophilic groups (hydroxyls) and introduces hydrophobic ester bonds [[7], [10]].
3.  **Functional Effects:** Cross-linking:
    *   Reduces the mobility of starch molecules [[5]].
    *   Decreases the number of hydrogen bonds between hydroxyl groups of thermoplastic starch [[5]].
    *   Limits starch dissolution/fragmentation leading to more homogeneous but potentially more brittle matrices [[13]].
    *   Reduces water sensitivity, improves water resistance [[7], [10]].
    *   Can lead to the generation of regions of micropores [[5]].
    *   Makes starch less biodegradable [[1]].
4.  **Concentration-Dependent Effects:**
    *   At lower concentrations (e.g., 1-3 wt%), it primarily crosslinks, improving stiffness (Young's modulus) and tensile strength [[11]].
    *   At higher concentrations (e.g., 7-15 wt%), a plasticizing effect dominates, reducing stiffness and tensile strength while increasing elongation; hydrolysis reactions may also break starch chains, reducing molar mass and increasing fluidity [[11]].
    *   An optimum concentration (e.g., 5% w/w) exists for improving physical and mechanical properties like tensile strength, elongation, swelling, solubility, and biodegradability [[4], [11]].
5.  **Mechanism Detail:** When heated, citric acid initially forms a five-membered cyclic anhydride intermediate. This reacts with starch to form a monoester. A second cyclic anhydride forms and reacts with another starch hydroxyl group, promoting cross-linking [[2], [3]].

The mechanical strength of PLA parts produced via fused filament fabrication (FFF) is significantly influenced by build orientation due to the anisotropic nature of the process. Key findings from the contexts include:  

1. **Optimal Orientation (0°):**  
   - Specimens printed with a **0° build orientation** (aligned with the deposition direction) exhibit the **highest ultimate tensile strength (UTS)** and stiffness. For example, pure PLA parts printed at 0° showed up to **64% higher UTS** compared to raw PLA material ([9], [10]). This is attributed to better alignment of deposited strands with the loading direction, minimizing interlayer shear stress and promoting uniform load transfer.  

2. **Non-Optimal Orientations (45°, 90°):**  
   - **45° and 90° orientations** result in **lower tensile strength** due to weaker interlayer bonding and increased susceptibility to crack propagation along layer boundaries ([1], [6]). For instance, PLA samples printed at 90° experienced failure via layer separation, while 0° samples failed through layer fracture ([6]). Thermal post-processing (e.g., low-temperature conditioning) can improve UTS by up to **28%** for non-optimal orientations by enhancing interlayer bonding ([1]).  

3. **Anisotropy and Fracture Behavior:**  
   - FFF-printed PLA exhibits **pronounced anisotropy**, with mechanical properties varying significantly across orientations. Fracture analysis reveals **brittle failure** in untreated samples, with cracks propagating along layer interfaces in non-0° orientations ([1], [6]). Thermal treatments reduce anisotropy by promoting polymer diffusion across layers, leading to more isotropic fracture behavior ([1], [13]).  

4. **Raster Angle Effects:**  
   - Raster angles also influence strength. **0° raster angles** (parallel to loading) maximize tensile strength and stiffness, while **90° angles** (perpendicular) yield the lowest values ([6], [12]). For composites (e.g., carbon fiber-reinforced PLA), optimal raster angles may differ due to fiber alignment interactions ([12], [14]).  

5. **Fatigue and Dynamic Loading:**  
   - Under cyclic loading, **45° orientations** show improved fatigue life compared to X/Y orientations, despite lower static strength ([9], [10]). This suggests trade-offs between static strength and dynamic performance based on orientation.  

**Conclusion:** Build orientation is a critical determinant of mechanical strength in FFF-printed PLA parts. A **0° orientation** maximizes tensile strength and stiffness, while non-optimal orientations (45°, 90°) introduce anisotropy and weaker interlayer adhesion. Thermal post-processing can mitigate anisotropy but does not fully eliminate orientation-dependent effects.

In addition, the different processing strategies to produce the microcapsules lead to different pore structures, which play a critical role in determining the ultimate properties of the microcapsules.', 'The use of polymers in biomedical applications is continuously increasing [1], [2], [3]. Moreover, the incorporated degradable linkages can generate some side products upon degradation, conditioning the application and the effectiveness of the polymer.', "Of the polymers that can be incorporated into chitosan-crosslinked networks to yield semi-IPNs, poly(ethylene) glycol (PEG) (Figure 1) attracted our attention. 2.  **Low Interaction with Blood Components:** PEG's properties, including its hydrophilicity, contribute to low interaction with blood components, enhancing blood compatibility ([2], [11]).
3.  **Low Antigenicity and Low Immunogenicity:** PEG exhibits low antigenicity and low immunogenicity ([5]). This reduces the likelihood of triggering immune responses.
4.  **Evasion of Cellular Uptake:** PEG coatings create "stealth" particles that evade uptake by cells, particularly macrophages, leading to prolonged circulation times ([1]). This is a direct consequence of resisting protein adsorption and cellular recognition.
5.  **Biological Inertness:** PEG is considered biologically inert and biocompatible ([3]).

**In summary, the biocompatibility mechanism of PEG coatings, as described in the context, primarily revolves around its ability to resist protein adsorption and cellular recognition, leading to reduced immune response and biofouling.**

In order to alleviate those undesired effects, in our study, these nanotubes were further coated by PLGA films through a simple spin-coating process.', 'First published on 16th April 2020 As a new type of intestinal stent, the MAO/PLLA/paclitaxel/Mg-Zn-Y-Nd alloy stent has shown good degradability, although its biocompatibility in vitro and in vivo has not been investigated in detail. Therefore, paclitaxel is selected as a sustained-release drug of the stent to explore the compatibility of the drug-eluting stent in intestinal environment in this study. However, few studies to date have reported on the biocompatible and biodegradable properties of magnesium alloy in the intestine.', 'The introduction of permanent metallic stents was a major advance over balloon angioplasty in the treatment of arterial diseases, being highly effective in preventing acute vessel closure due to balloon-induced dissection, and in reducing the rate of restenosis [1]. However, it has been suggested that the role of the stent is temporary and limited to the intervention and shortly thereafter, until healing and re-endothelialization of the vessel wall is achieved [2].     *   **Increased Surface Area & Medium Interaction:** Higher porosity provides a larger surface area exposed to the degrading medium (e.g., water, PBS, lysozyme solution) ([3], [4], [5], [8]). This facilitates greater interaction between the scaffold material and the degrading medium.
    *   **Enhanced Water Penetration:** Porosity allows easier penetration of water into the scaffold structure ([8], [9]). This is crucial for hydrolytic degradation, the dominant mechanism for many polymers ([3], [9]).
    *   **Efficient Removal of Degradation Products:** In highly porous scaffolds, acidic degradation products (monomers/oligomers) can diffuse out more easily, preventing autocatalytic acceleration *within* the scaffold and allowing degradation to proceed ([3]). Dynamic flow conditions further enhance this removal in porous scaffolds ([3]).

3.  **Reduced Porosity Slows Degradation:** Conversely, scaffolds with lower porosity or smaller pores exhibit slower degradation rates.
    *   The phosphorous-containing collagen/P-PCL scaffold had "lower swelling ratio" and "smaller pore size" compared to collagen/PCL, resulting in "lower" weight loss during degradation ([9]).
    *   Chitosan degrades more slowly than pectin partly due to factors like molecular weight and hydrophobicity, but the context also shows that cryogels with lower pectin (and thus different porosity) degraded slower ([1]).

**In summary, the context consistently shows that higher porosity in ceramic/polymer composite scaffolds increases the degradation rate by enhancing water penetration, increasing the surface area exposed to the degrading medium, and facilitating the removal of degradation products.** Lower porosity slows degradation.

1.  **Piezoelectric Property Origin:**
    *   PLLA's piezoelectricity arises from its **semi-crystalline structure** and **natural chiral conformation**.
    *   The key mechanism is the alignment of **electric dipoles** associated with the **C=O bonds** within the polymer chain structure. These dipoles are "branched out of the polymer backbone" and require alignment.
    *   Specifically, the **rotation of C=O dipoles** under shear stress is responsible for the observed piezoelectric effect (shear mode).

2.  **Key Piezoelectric Characteristics:**
    *   PLLA exhibits primarily **shear mode piezoelectricity**.
    *   The piezoelectric coefficient is denoted as **d₁₄** (parallel to the z-axis).
    *   The value of **d₁₄** typically ranges from **7-12 pC N⁻¹**, though post-treatment can potentially enhance it up to **~20 pC N⁻¹**.
    *   Its piezoelectric properties **depend critically on crystallinity and molecular orientation**. Techniques like **stretching/drawing** and **electrospinning** are essential to align the chains and enhance crystallinity/alignment, thereby improving piezoelectricity. Optimal drawing ratios are around **2.5 to 4.5**.
    *   Electrospinning can align nanofibers, resulting in "macro piezoelectricity". **Supercritical CO₂ treatment** on electrospun fibers can further enhance crystallinity and piezoelectricity.
    *   PLLA **does not require electric poling** to impart piezoelectricity because the shear mode originates intrinsically from its chemical structure.
    *   The piezoelectric response also depends on **optical purity (low D-isomer content)** and **high molecular weight**.

3.  **Biomedical Relevance:**
    *   **Biocompatibility and Biodegradability:** PLLA is biocompatible, biodegradable, bioabsorbable, and non-toxic. This makes it suitable for implantable and transient medical devices that degrade after fulfilling their function, reducing electronic waste and long-term biocompatibility issues.
    *   **Physiological Sensing:** Used to fabricate **force/pressure sensors** for measuring physiological pressures (e.g., diaphragmatic contraction pressure in mice, arterial pulse, pressure ranges of 0-18 kPa).
    *   **Ultrasonic Transducers:** Used in **biodegradable ultrasonic transducers** for applications like physiological monitoring, drug delivery assistance, blood-brain barrier opening, and underwater structural health monitoring. These devices are sensitive in detecting imperfections in air and liquid.
    *   **Self-Powered Devices:** Functions in **nanogenerators** converting mechanical energy (like body movement, vibration) into electrical signals, enabling self-powered sensors for vital sign monitoring (e.g., blood pulse sensors generating pA currents, muscle movement detection, joint motion).
    *   **Wearable Health Monitoring:** Basis for **flexible piezoelectric bio e-skin (PBio-e-skin)** for non-invasive monitoring of physiological signals (muscle movement, joint motion, arterial pressure, voice recognition), offering mechanosensitivity and operational stability.
    *   **Implantable Devices:** Suitable for **acute and short-term implantable biomedical applications** (e.g., wound healing, bone regeneration, transient monitoring) due to its controlled biodegradation timeline (e.g., complete degradation demonstrated over ~56 days at elevated temperature).
    *   **Tissue Engineering Scaffolds:** Its piezoelectricity is relevant in scaffolds for applications like bone healing and tissue regeneration, where electrical stimulation can promote healing.

The relative viscosity of the formulation #4 is presumably affected by thermal degradation during compounding extrusion at high temperature. Degradation can reduce significantly the mean molecular weight of the PLA in it and, thus, cause the concurrent decrease in the relative viscosity of the formulation. The formulations #1, #2, and #3 that involve talc behave in the same fashion. The formulation #2 that involves talc and maleic anhydride (MAH) grafted PLA (PLA-MA) has the greatest relative viscosity after extrusion compounding. This result can be attributed to the effect of the expected interactions of the PLA-MA chain extender with the talc and Poly(Lactic Acid) (PLA). In fact, the chain extender is designed to lead to an increase in the molecular weight and/or promote branching of the polymeric chains.8 This can, in turn, determine an increase in the mean hydrodynamic volume of the PLA macromolecules in the solution and, therefore, the increase in the relative viscosity. This result can be ascribed to effectiveness of the PLA-GMA chain extender, which is probably less active to combine with both talc and PLA. reference: A reduction in melt viscosity (or increase in Melt Flow Index, MFI) indicates a reduction in molecular weight due to thermal or hydrolytic degradation. retrieved_contexts: ['A common phenomenon during the drug-release process is called “burst release”, (18,19) which means more than 50% of drug is released at initial or in very short time. (36) Noteworthy, there is no existing research using VB2 in drug delivery.', 'From obtained data of kinetic parameters in Table 3 the mechanism and the best fitting with model was evaluated. Therefore, nanoindentation measurements were performed on compressed nanofiber mat samples and compared with non-compressed ones.', 'Precise delivery of drugs is essential for improving medical treatment outcomes and minimizing side effects. However, this approach could facilitate synergistic effects and reduce the dosing frequency. (15,16) These diseased tissues often undergo substantial alterations in their physiochemical properties under pathological conditions (like an increase in temperature or acidity), which can also be used to develop SDDS that respond to disease symptom-associated triggers. (17)', 'The release of drugs was investigated by removing the supernatant and the subsequent addition of specific media to the drug-loaded microgels. The low presence of drug at the surface of the microparticles also explains the reduced burst release in this case.", 'Drug delivery systems (DDS) basing on macromolecule polymers have been widely researched and have been shown to improve the stability and release-control of drugs [24, 25]. Microspheres, as multiple-unit DDS for oral drugs, have been reported to provide more uniform distribution, good absorption, and steady release-control of the drug [26, 27]. reference: Burst release is the uncontrolled, rapid release of a significant portion of the loaded drug (often 20-50%) immediately upon administration. Wan et al. reported the same behavior for compression-molded PBS samples drawn at a lower rate under 50 mm min−1 and also at a rate of 10 mm min−1 under different temperatures [42]. Their study presents a clear explanation for the occurrence of these self-stress necking oscillations on the tensile curves, which can be attributed to the local increase in temperature at the neck front of the samples, the crystallization induced by the orientation of the polymer chains or to the formation of cracks and micro-cavities which were observed on their drawn samples [42]. These cracks and micro-cavities were noticed in our PBS and PBS/PBAT nanocomposite drawn samples. The tensile tests curves in water conditions (Figure 4b) of neat polymers and their blends show almost the same behavior as in air with some changes in the second yield for the PBS/PBAT and PBS/PBAT/NFC\uf8ffEster1% blends, which appear in the same strain as PBS, while the second yield of PBS/PBAT/ChNCs\uf8ffLac1% has shifted to 120% compared to PBS which remains at 80% strain. The presence of water in PBAT also led to a similar Young's modulus but an increased elongation at break by 24%-that is, 250% versus 310%, before and after immersion, respectively. It is obvious that the PBS/PBAT blend also increases both Young's modulus (+6%) and elongation at break (+11%) in water conditions. These results relate to those found in the literature, which demonstrate an improvement of the mechanical properties of PBS/PBAT monofilaments, notably in elongation at break, when used for the first time in water [17, 43]. In the case of PBS/PBAT/NFC\uf8ffEster1%, considering the standard deviation of the measurements, both Young's modulus and elongation at break remain constant in water conditions. Thus, the PBS/PBAT/ChNCs\uf8ffLac1% shows a slight decrease in Young's modulus (−10%) from 402 in air conditions to 364 MPa in water and a significant increase in elongation at break value (+52%) from 200% in air conditions to 304% in water. In fact, many factors can affect the mechanical behavior of these nanocomposites. The presence of water generally acts as a plasticizer for many polymers, including PBS and PBAT, which reduces Young's modulus values, indicating a decrease in the stiffness of the materials. It also leads to an increase in elongation at break values that indicate an enhanced ductility that was shown in particular for PBS/PBAT, PBS/PBAT/ChNCs\uf8ffLac1%, and PBS/PBAT/NFC\uf8ffEster1%."]

retrieved_contexts: ["As conventional plastics for packaging, i.e., polypropylene, polyethylene, and other petro-sourced thermoplastics, full-biocomposites can be manufactured using industrial techniques such as compounding, mixing, extrusion, injection molding, compression molding, and resin transfer molding (RTM).9 Though depending on the studied matrix and the aimed application, and often for research purposes, samples are prepared by solvent casting in several studies.54-57 Among the disadvantages associated with classical thermal treatments, there is a risk of degrading both the bioplastic used as matrix and the lignocellulosic fibers. Indeed, most biopolymers are especially sensitive to temperature, their melting temperature being close to their degradation temperature (e.g., PHBV58). In the case of proteins, wheat gluten's degradation temperature is even below its melting temperature; therefore, such material has to be plasticized, generally with water and/or glycerol.59 Fibers are also sensitive to thermal treatments as degradation can occur that weakens the fibers. Furthermore, heat-treated biomass is known to globally become darker and brittle, due to the loss of its tenacious and fibrous nature resulting from the decomposition of hemicelluloses and partial depolymerization of lignin and cellulose. Natural polymeric materials tend to be highly susceptible to enzymatic and oxidative degradation, and as a consequence of varying enzymatic and macrophage levels from patient-to-patient, uniform degradation profiles may be unachievable. Conversely, the uniformity of degradation and thermo-mechanical properties achieved with synthetic biodegradable biomaterials, which generally undergo hydrolytic degradation, makes these approaches more attractive.16-18 Although exhibiting high charge values (0.45-0.72), amide, carbonate, carbamate, urea and aromatic ester-based polymers exhibit lower rates of hydrolysis owing to stable conjugate structures (Scheme 2) which reduce the susceptibility of hydrolytic attack at the carbonyl site through delocalisation of the positive charge. Furthermore, steric effects exhibited by substituted reactants can drastically reduce the rate of hydrolysis as a consequence of bond inaccessibility. An excellent example of steric effects can be seen in the reduced rate of hydrolysis of polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), where the two methyl substituents significantly protect the silicon atoms from hydrolysis irrespective of its high charge value (0.62). Importantly, it has been shown that the hydrolytic degradation of polymers, both in solution and in bulk, proceed by random scission of hydrolysable bonds e.g. all chemically identical hydrolysable bonds in a polymer are equally reactive irrespective of chain position (i.e. chain end vs. mid-block).20', 'Acceleration of the biodegradation process of biodegradable polymers has been reported by using different approaches, in terms of abiotic and biotic methods utilized during the processing step or after the consumer-use stage (before or during the biodegradation process itself). From an abiotic aspect, incorporation of additives, copolymerization and blending were identified as the most common methods to accelerate the biodegradation of biodegradable polymers such as aliphatic and aliphatic/aromatic polyesters. In general, these methods are less expensive and offer easy accessibility in terms of components in comparison to other abiotic methods that require longer times and can be energy-intensive such as plasma, UV, electron beam irradiation, or catalysis of chemical hydrolysis. Catalysis of chemical hydrolysis remains an expensive and highly advanced technology and hard to obtain at lower temperatures such as in a compost environment. The main outcome of abiotic methods was identified as the deterioration of the chemical and physical structure, reflected in an improved mechanical and hydrolytic degradation with faster Mw reduction. Reduction of size to increase the surface-to-volume ratio offers the advantage of being an economical and feasible method that can improve the efficiency of abiotic degradation and biotic degradation due to greater exposure of the polymer surface to the microbial population. On the other hand, several works show that biotic methods, such as biostimulation and bioaugmentation, are now being considered more frequently to accelerate the biodegradation of polymers since it does not require the modification of the initial polymer. Although agriculture biomaterials are in abundance, their thermo-mechanical properties are a disadvantage for use as substitutes for synthetic polymers. The drawbacks include hydrophilicity, poor binding, and high viscosity. Conversely, polyesters such as PLA or polycaprolactone (PCL) are expensive ($3-5/lb) relative to polystyrene and polyolefin.1 Polymer blends with at least one biodegradable polymer are called bio-blends. Materials blended with biodegradable polymers for economical product development include: natural polymers, other biodegradable polymers, nonbiodegradable synthetic polymers, compatibilizers,2 plasticizers,3-5 and salts.6 Some of the natural polymers that have been blended with biodegradable polymers for new products include starch,7, 8 lignin,9 gluten,10 and nonstarch polysaccharides.8, 11, 12', 'As electronic devices become more multifunctional, miniaturized, and integrated, there is a greater demand for efficient thermal dissipation, which necessitates the use of thermally conductive materials. (1,2) Among the materials used for electronic packaging and thermal management, polymer-based composites have gained popularity due to their light weight, ease of processing, good insulation properties, and corrosion resistance. However, the rapid development of electronic devices in recent years has led to an increase in plastic waste resulting from disposal, which can seriously affect the environment. (6−11) However, most biodegradable polymers possess very low intrinsic thermal conductivity (typically between 0.1 and 0.5 W m-1 K-1), requiring further improvement. One effective approach to enhancing the thermal conductivity of biodegradable polymers is incorporating high thermal/conductive fillers through melt blending. (12) Commonly used thermal fillers include silicon carbide (SiC), (13,14) aluminum oxide (Al2O3), (15) aluminum nitride (AlN), (16) and boron nitride (BN). (17−19) Nevertheless, high filler loadings can negatively impact mechanical properties and impose processing difficulties. (23,24) With a total filler content of 21 vol %, the composites exhibited a thermal conductivity of 2.69 W m-1 K-1 and good electrical insulation properties (4.13 × 10-9 S/m). (25,26) To the best of our knowledge, there has been no research conducted on preparing biodegradable polymer composites with the combination of balanced mechanical performance, high thermal conductivity, and good electrical insulation properties by using the specific structure described above.', 'macromolecules inside cells or in tissues, such as cell membrane disruption and succedent necrosis/non-apoptotic cell death [[34], [35], [36]]. To explore this potential, incorporation of pesticides into degradable baroplastics and release of the agrochemical incorporated in liquid medium and in soil using granule-type formulations were studied. The long-term efficacy of these pesticide granules was also examined.", "A widely used method to tailor materials properties making use of what is commercially available is melt blending, and several studies have been devoted to the issue of obtaining properly dispersed blends using diverse combinations of polymers [2]. Under the bombardment of accelerated electron beam, a more cost effective hydrogels were formed and characterized.', 'In recent years, stimuli-responsive polymers have attracted more attention for their potential applications in the field of biomedical area [[1], [2], [3], [4], [5]]. Therefore, the enhancement of overall performance through composite modification and microstructure engineering, while retaining the inherent characteristics of biomass materials, presents a significant challenge in current research efforts.', 'Concept of electroactive paper actuator: (a) cellulose microfibril has ordered crystalline regions and disordered regions; (b) EAPap is made from cellulose paper on which gold electrodes are deposited on both sides; (c) water molecules are bonded with hydroxyl groups on the cellulose surface (bound water) or clustered in free (free water). It also must minimize any process that may negatively influence the electrochemical energy efficiency of the batteries. The separator helps ion conductivity when soaked in an electrolytic solution. This phenomenon is due to the fact that the porous structure of these separators facilitates ion transportation.1 For the separators used in lithium-ion batteries, it is important to have characteristics such as high thermal, mechanical, and electrochemical resistance with no dimensional changes.2', 'A suitable membrane offers a variety of structural and functional characteristics, including a combination of excellent species selectivity, long service life, low fouling rate, and sufficient thermal, chemical, and mechanical resistances under operating conditions [22, 23], and considering the degradation of the environment, the focus on using biopolymers instead of synthetic polymers is increasing day by day. Biopolymers are the ones that are derived from nature and can be decomposed without affecting the environment significantly [24,25,26,27]. It is being researched on how to improve ion transport in secondary batteries using biopolymers such as cellulose-based biopolymers, including cellulose itself [28] with its mechanical strength and thermal durability, cellulose acetate with its capacity to form films, and micro fibrillated cellulose (MFC), which has a porous nanostructure [29, 30]. There is potential for chitosan-based variations, such as modified chitosan for better ion conductivity and chitosan-polyelectrolyte blends for better transport characteristics. Alginate is being investigated for flexible battery components because of its biocompatibility and ability to produce hydrogels [31]. After chemical modification, compounds based on starch show potential as battery separators, different modifications are made to starch-based compounds to provide the best possible battery separator performance. While surface changes fine-tune interactions with electrolytes and electrodes, nanotechnology integration refines attributes like conductivity and strength. With these specific modifications, starch-based materials are optimized to provide them with improved ion conductivity, mechanical durability, and chemical stability which are essential for effective battery separators [6, 32]. One of the most prevalent biopolymers in use today is chitin, which can be deacetylated with an alkaline chemical like sodium hydroxide to produce chitosan, an amino polysaccharide (Fig. 1). The use of chitosan to improve membranes is one of the key developments in membrane technology [35]. Chitosan is very intriguing because of its biocompatibility, which permits safe interactions with biological systems, and its inherent film-forming qualities, which simplify processing [36,37,38,39]. Its biodegradability reduces its environmental impact while its inherent antibacterial properties increase its value in wound care. It can also be used in drug delivery systems and may enhance ion conductivity in battery separators because of its positive charge, which allows interactions with ions [38, 40]. Chitosan-based secondary batteries can be effectively utilized as electrode scaffolds to stabilize cathodes, and anodes concerning the highly porous framework, enhanced electronic conductivity, and substantial mechanical characteristics. They also find applications as active substances to be incorporated into the battery electrodes without the necessity of carbonization stages, and can also serve as additives (conductive materials, or binding agents) for secondary battery electrodes. Moreover, the chitosan biopolymeric system can also be used as electrolytes and separators in secondary batteries [41]. It is anticipated that novel synthesis methodologies, like holographic lithography, direct dispensing, and 3D printing, could assist in developing biocompatible secondary batteries encompassing three-dimensional architectures [42].', "First published on 18th February 2019 Lithium (Li) metal batteries have shown great promise for next-generation electrical energy storage due to the unique features of lithium metal like light weight, high specific capacity, and the lowest anode potential. Nevertheless, the uncontrollable growth of dendritic and mossy Li, resulting in a low coulombic efficiency and serious safety concerns, has hindered the practical application of rechargeable Li-metal batteries. Here we report an environmentally friendly nanocomposite separator, comprising polyvinyl alcohol and hydroxyapatite, which exhibits an outstanding Young's modulus and high mechanical flexibility. We show that this separator can efficiently suppress the growth of dendritic Li and enable a homogeneous stable solid electrolyte interphase. Compared to lithium metal batteries using a commercial polyolefin-based separator, cells using the reported nanocomposite separator demonstrate a superior electrochemical performance with a much higher coulombic efficiency during the charge/discharge cycling at a practical current density of 2 mA cm−2. This work indicates that nanocomposite engineering could be a promising strategy to develop stable, safe and sustainable Li-metal batteries. To date, plenty of efforts have been devoted to revealing the detailed mechanism of the Li dendrite formation. Chazalviel proposed that the large electric field caused by the anion depletion near the cathode could lead to the growth of Li dendrites.22 This theory indicates that electrolytes with high ionic conductivity and stable anion mobility are beneficial for preventing anion depletion, and thus to some extent relieving the generation of Li dendrites. On the other hand, it is recognized that as the Young's modulus of the separator is twice that of Li metal, the interfacial roughening could be mechanically suppressed.23 According to the abovementioned two strategies, many approaches have been proposed to build Li metal batteries with suppressed Li dendrite formation, for instance, using suitable electrolyte additives,24,25 solid phase electrolytes,26-28 network polymer electrolytes,29 organic or/and inorganic-coated separators,30,31 and three-dimensional current collectors.32-34 In recent years, constructing mechanical protective layers is of particular interest to impede the growth of Li dendrites and to achieve satisfactory coulombic efficiency. Cui fabricated a monolayer of interconnected amorphous hollow carbon nanospheres on a Li metal anode to isolate the Li metal deposition and facilitate the formation of a stable SEI layer.35 By the way, Cui also prepared a trilayer separator with a structure of polyethylene/SiO2 particles/polyethylene to delay the penetration of Li dendrites through the separator, thus prolonging the life of batteries.36 Hu designed a thermally conductive separator, mainly comprising of boron-nitride nanosheets, to improve the electrochemical stability of Li metal anodes.37 Additionally, Guo et al. designed an artificial Li3PO4 SEI layer to restrain the unfavorable reaction between the Li metal and the electrolyte and the dendritic Li growth in LiFePO4|Li systems.17 Nevertheless, in most cases, complicated processes (such as synthesis of templates or an artificial SEI layer and a complex manufacturing process), expensive instrumentation requirements, being time consuming and high cost of raw materials restrain the further practical application. Moreover, even with numerous efforts, the long-time suppression of dendritic Li growth at high current density (>0.5 mA cm−2) is still a challenging task impeding Li metal batteries from being commercialized in the market.", 'In addition to hydrolytically degradable systems, several studies have explored for truly biodegradable battery systems─including those using inorganic electrodes─where the degradation occurs through microbial or enzymatic processes. (30) For instance, Kang et al. reported a fully biodegradable battery with sodium- and iron-based polyanion compound cathode, pyroprotein-based carbon anode, propylene carbonate electrolyte, cellulose-based separator, and cellulose/polyester/silicon-based packaging, all of which biodegraded under composting conditions. (31) These works underscore the need for degradable polymer backbones under mild conditions while maintaining electrochemical stability, mechanical integrity, and scalability for practical applications. Designing degradable and redox-active polymers requires rational selection of a biodegradable backbone that maintains mechanical strength during use and degrades under mild conditions after end-of-life. Additionally, redox-active sites should be easily incorporated into the polymer structure. Polymer degradation has been extensively studied for environmental and recycling applications, providing a rich library of options, primarily for substrates and packaging films. (32−35) This library includes natural biodegradable polymers, such as cellulose derivatives (33) and polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA), (36) alongside synthetic ones such as polycaprolactone (PCL), (37,38) polyglycolide (PGA), (39) and polylactic acid (PLA). (40) Their degradation byproducts were reported to be nontoxic in vivo. Thus, these polymers are promising platforms for designing sustainable organic redox batteries with improved degradability and reduced environmental hazards. In this study, we develop a biodegradable radical polymer-based cathode material, PCL-TEMPO (Figure 1), achieving fast-rate charging/discharging (1 C-30 C), and ∼93% capacity recovery after high-rate cycling, with an approximate capacity of 30 mAh g-1. To ensure both biodegradability and redox activity, α-bromo-ε-caprolactone is polymerized via ring-opening polymerization, and TEMPO is incorporated into the PCL backbone via a bromo-thiol click reaction. All synthesis steps are mild with reasonable yields, enabling easy scale-up. The ester groups in the backbone and pendant linkage enable hydrolytic degradation under acidic (1 M HCl, 80 °C, 24 h) and basic (KOH, 90 °C, 12 h) conditions, yielding water-soluble byproducts for eco-friendly disposal. PCL-TEMPO maintains fast redox reactions, while allowing on-demand disposal at end-of-life. This work highlights the balance between degradable polymer structures and electrochemical performance, advancing sustainable organic electrode materials for next-generation batteries.', 'Although the use of filter paper as a simple separator in inorganic supercapacitors is relatively frequent, some studies deserve special mention because the applications of those devices were intimately related to conventional applications of cellulose-containing materials. For example, Cui and co-workers125 reported a structure where MnO2 nanoflowers were electrodeposited onto CNT-wrapped polyester fibres. Supercapacitors prepared using this conductive textile, which could be considered as an extension of a previously reported conductive paper,29 were assembled using paper sheets as separators. Thus, polyester fibres and paper low-cost materials were essential to propose these elements as promising large-scale wearable devices for energy storage.69,126 In summary, in the last few years there have been promising reports on paper-/cellulose-based materials being applied to fabricate both electrodes and separators for supercapacitors, in which their rough and porous surface has proved a strong advantage where both high surface area and electrolyte absorption are demanded. Recyclability and biodegradability are significant benefits considering that the cost of waste management and the impact on the environment could be considerably low. Gui et al.128 focused on the electrolyte absorption properties of CFs as a potential substrate in energy storage devices. More specifically, these authors considered that natural CFs behave like a cell wall that takes up the electrolyte from bulk electrolyte baths. Electrolytes are then transported via the pores through the CF matrix to the energy-active material. On the basis of these assumptions, different hybrid electrodes were prepared even though the best ion diffusion and electrochemical properties were obtained for CF/CNT/MnO2/CNT electrodes prepared by dip-coating (Fig. 12). This system exhibited dual ion diffusion and electron transfer pathways demonstrating superior supercapacitive performance (i.e. specific capacitance of 327 F g−1 and excellent cyclic stability, retaining 85% of the capacitance up to 50000 cycles). Hence, these results highlight the merits of the mesoporous CFs as substrate for supercapacitor electrodes: the water-swelling effect of cellulose fibres induce absorption of the electrolyte, whereas their mesoporous internal structure provides channels for ions to diffuse towards the electrochemical energy storage material.', 'Currently, the most commonly used commercial separator for ZIBs is the glass fiber (GF) separator, possessing high porosity and electrolyte wettability. However, its large pore size (micron scale) and irregular pore structure accommodate a large number of SO42− and H+ ions, triggering side reactions and non-uniform Zn2+ flux, thereby accelerating dendrite formation.9 Its poor mechanical strength renders it susceptible to penetration by Zn dendrites during repeated cycling, leading to internal short circuits and safety risks.10 Moreover, the production process of GF separators is relatively complex, raising environmental concerns. Recent studies reveal that surface modification of GF separators has proved to be a promising strategy for improving electrochemical properties, which can be categorized into three key aspects: first, modified surfaces with optimized pore structures and zincophilic functional groups effectively regulate Zn2+ flux distribution, thereby suppressing Zn dendrite growth; second, advanced coatings such as inorganic ceramic layers or polymer-based films demonstrate superior electrolyte wettability and serve as robust physical barriers to eliminate side reactions; third, the introduction of negatively charged functional groups through surface modification can repel SO42−, thereby reducing byproduct formation. However, their high cost and excessive thickness (typically >300 μm) hinder energy density and scalability of ZIBs.11 In recent years, biomass materials (e.g., cellulose, chitosan, chitin, and lignin) have emerged as promising alternative candidates for ZIB separators (Fig. 1b). Not surprisingly, cellulose is the more widely used biopolymer as a separator for ZIBs (Fig. 1c). Beyond their inherent biodegradability and sustainability derived from renewable sources, these biomass-based separators offer distinct advantages, including tunable microstructures and abundant functional groups, which collectively contribute to superior wettability, enhanced mechanical strength, and dendrite suppression. Specifically, their intrinsic polar functional groups (-OH, -COOH, and -NH2) provide abundant binding sites, thus reshaping the Zn2+ solvation structure and promoting uniform Zn nucleation/deposition.12 In addition, the hierarchical porous structures of biomass-based separators can effectively regulate Zn2+ flux, and targeted chemical modification of biomass materials can significantly improve their mechanical strength and electrochemical stability.13 Nevertheless, several challenges remain to be addressed for the practical application of biomass-based separators, such as ensuring sufficient mechanical strength, optimizing the pore structure for rapid ion transport, and maintaining compatibility with aqueous electrolytes. To our knowledge, recent reviews on separators of ZIBs provide a comprehensive overview of advanced design strategies focused on functionalized architectural design and chemical modification for dendrite suppression and interfacial stability enhancement. However, there is still a lack of comprehensive discussion regarding the advantages and challenges of biomass-based separators compared with GF separators, especially in terms of underlying mechanisms and large-scale applications. This review provides an in-depth examination of the recent achievements in biomass-based separators for ZIBs, highlighting fundamental requirements, structural configurations, preparation methods, and modification strategies. We also present the classification, summary, and discussion of biomass-based separator studies from the perspective of similar modification methods and operational mechanisms. Finally, the remaining challenges and future development directions of biomass-based separators for ZIBs are summarized and analyzed to promote further research and development for large-scale applications.', 'For example, Aeby et al. developed low-power supercapacitors using biodegradable cellulose substrates and aqueous inks, although their energy density and lifespan restrict broader applicability.64 Similarly, Huang et al. introduced a magnesium-iodine battery with complete dissolution under physiological conditions, achieving coin-cell-level energy density.65 Yet, neither study included formal environmental assessments, leaving their broader environmental trade-offs unquantified. Biodegradable stretchable batteries are also advancing. Rahmanudin et al. designed a soft battery system with plant-based components and mild degradation pathways.66 While the use of bio-sourced materials and their biodegradability may be justified, the low battery performance and quantification of embodied energy, sourcing impacts, or scalability was not conducted, leaving open questions about broader environmental trade-offs at larger scales. Similarly, Karami-Mosammam et al. used kirigami-structured magnesium and molybdenum electrodes on biodegradable substrates to achieve high mechanical durability and energy density, but again only material degradation under physiological conditions was tested.67 Ilic et al. took a novel approach by developing an entirely edible, rechargeable battery using food-grade components.68 All battery components were proven to be non-toxic and digestible according to food safety standards, offering a safe pathway for disposal through biological metabolism. Environmental performance was considered using biodegradable, renewable, and food-safe materials, although no LCA was conducted. As with other transient technologies, scalability, mass production energy demands, and sourcing impacts remain to be fully considered for broader environmental evaluation.', 'In recent years, the issue of population aging has promoted significant interest in the development of implantable biomedical devices.1,2 However, conventional batteries in these devices have introduced challenges, such as limited battery life and the need for secondary surgical extraction, imposing risks and financial burdens to patients.3,4 Consequently, the quest for an alternative solution has led to a burgeoning interest in implantable solid-state biodegradable energy storage devices.5 Although implantable biomedical devices powered by conventional batteries are highly reliable and convenient, they are not without drawbacks:6-8 (1) their rigid and bulky nature occupies considerable space within implantable devices, (2) non-biodegradability necessitates a second surgical procedure, and (3) the presence of toxic substances in electrodes and electrolytes poses severe safety hazards. Considerable efforts have been made to develop an effective and safe power supply for implantable devices, yet the desired results remain exlusive.9-13 Recent reports highlight solid-state biodegradable supercapacitors (SBSCs) as the most promising implantable bioenergy storage devices due to their exceptional energy/power density and biocompatibility.14-16 SBSCs boast biocompatible components that can be broken down into nontoxic compounds or elements that already present in the human body through hydrolysis.17 However, these implantable devices face challenge of poor electrochemical performance due to their inappropriate shape size, significant mechanical stiffness, and inadequate contact between the active material and the current collector.15,18 Ideally, implantable energy devices should possess certain characteristics, including small size, large capacity, mechanical flexibility to conform to biological tissue, and complete biodegradability.19 Recently, Mo-based metal oxides emerged as a promising electrode material for SBSCs due to the water solubility of Mo metals.20,21 For example, Hassan et al. reported that molybdate-chelated biodegradable supercapacitors achieve a maximum energy density of 95.1 Wh/kg at a power density of 15 kW/kg.22 However, their selection of KOH as an electrolyte introduces safety risks and hinders self-degradation within living organisms. Moreover, strong alkaline electrolytes are less suitable for implantable energy storage devices.23', 'We demonstrated in this work the fabrication of flexible solid state SCs made with 95% of biodegradable components. Particularly, we employed coconut fibers coated with graphene as conductive electrodes instead of carbonized coconut fibers or shells, which saves time and energy because high temperature furnaces were not necessary in our case to carbonize the coconut fibers. Based solely on the provided context, the direct contribution of biodegradable separators to **energy density** is not explicitly quantified. However, the context highlights several ways these separators **indirectly support or enable higher energy density** in batteries:

1.  **Enhanced Ionic Conductivity:** Biodegradable cellulose-based separators/gel polymer electrolytes (GPEs) exhibit high ionic conductivity (e.g., guar gum-cellulose aerogel: ~4.73 × 10⁻² S cm⁻¹ in [14]). Higher conductivity reduces internal resistance, enabling more efficient energy delivery and potentially supporting higher power/energy density operation.
2.  **Suppression of Dendrites and Side Reactions:** Biomass-based separators (e.g., cellulose, chitosan) prevent zinc dendrite formation and inhibit parasitic side reactions through functional groups, optimized pore structures, and water confinement ([1], [2], [10], [14]). This improves electrode stability and cycling performance, allowing the battery to maintain its capacity (a key factor in energy density) over many more cycles compared to using less stable separators like glass fiber.
3.  **Superior Cycling Stability:** By mitigating degradation mechanisms (dendrites, side reactions), these separators enable excellent cycling stability (e.g., 100% capacity retention after 200 cycles for a Zn-ion battery using a guar gum-cellulose aerogel separator in [14]). Sustained high capacity over many cycles is crucial for maintaining usable energy density throughout the battery's lifespan.
4.  **Potential for Thinner Designs:** The context criticizes thick glass fiber separators (>300 μm) for hindering energy density ([10]). Biomass-based separators, developed using optimized processing techniques (e.g., directional freezing, sol-gel), offer the potential for thinner, equally robust separators. Thinner separators increase the volume available for active electrode materials within the same battery casing, directly boosting volumetric energy density.
5.  **Enabling Stable High-Capacity Electrodes:** The ability to suppress dendrites and side reactions is particularly crucial for enabling the use of high-capacity metal electrodes (like Zn or Li), which are essential for achieving high energy density batteries ([1], [7], [14]). The separator's role in stabilizing these electrodes is vital for realizing their high-energy-density potential.

**Conclusion from the Context:** While biodegradable separators themselves are not the primary source of energy storage, their key properties—**high ionic conductivity, effective dendrite suppression, inhibition of side reactions, and enabling long-term cycling stability**—are critical for maximizing and maintaining the energy density delivered by the electrodes and electrolyte. They address failure modes that rapidly degrade energy density in batteries using conventional separators like glass fiber. Furthermore, their potential for **thinner designs** offers a direct route to improved volumetric energy density.

Based solely on the provided context, the differences between alkaline and acid hydrolysis for polyesters are:

1.  **Mechanism:**
    *   **Alkaline Hydrolysis:** Involves nucleophilic attack by hydroxyl anions (OH⁻) on the carbonyl carbon of the ester bond. This leads to the formation of a carboxylate ion and an alcohol (saponification). The carboxylate ion formation is thermodynamically favorable and prevents re-esterification (Contexts [2], [6]).
    *   **Acid Hydrolysis:** Involves protonation (by H⁺) of the carbonyl oxygen of the ester bond, making the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic and susceptible to nucleophilic attack by water. This leads to the formation of a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. Protons (H⁺) act as catalysts but can also catalyze the reverse esterification reaction between the resulting carboxylic acid and alcohol (Contexts [1], [2], [6]).

2.  **Kinetics & Efficiency:**
    *   **Alkaline Hydrolysis:** Generally results in **faster degradation rates** for polyesters compared to acid hydrolysis under comparable conditions. Hydroxyl anions effectively lower the energy barrier for ester bond breakage (Contexts [1], [2], [4], [6], [8], [14]).
    *   **Acid Hydrolysis:** Generally results in **slower degradation rates** compared to alkaline hydrolysis for polyesters (Contexts [1], [2], [4], [14]). PET is particularly resistant to hydrolysis using solid acids due to its hydrophobicity and rigidity (Context [2]). Acid hydrolysis of PLA involves intramolecular hydrogen bonding leading to lactic acid formation (Context [1]).

3.  **By-Products & Environmental Effects:**
    *   **Alkaline Hydrolysis:** Produces carboxylate salts (e.g., disodium terephthalate from PET) and alcohols (e.g., ethylene glycol from PET) (Context [2]). The formation of the charged carboxylate ion contributes to the irreversibility and faster kinetics.
    *   **Acid Hydrolysis:** Produces carboxylic acids (e.g., terephthalic acid (TPA) from PET, lactic acid (LA) from PLA) and alcohols (e.g., ethylene glycol from PET) (Contexts [1], [2]). Acidic by-products like LA can lower the surrounding pH significantly, potentially causing issues like cell necrosis (Context [1]). The resulting carboxylic acids can undergo re-esterification catalyzed by protons (Context [6]).

4.  **Susceptibility & Catalysis:**
    *   **Alkaline Hydrolysis:** Significantly accelerated by higher alkali concentrations as OH⁻ acts as a reagent, not just a catalyst (Contexts [2], [6]). Can be further promoted by phase-transfer catalysts (e.g., quaternary ammonium salts) and co-solvents (e.g., ethanol) (Context [2]). Ester bonds are highly susceptible to OH⁻ attack (Context [4]).
    *   **Acid Hydrolysis:** Requires concentrated acid solutions to achieve significant rates for hydrolysis over competing esterification (Context [2]). Protons act as catalysts for both hydrolysis *and* esterification (Context [6]). PET hydrolysis is rarely conducted with solid acids (Context [2]). Cotton is highly sensitive to acid hydrolysis, while polyester is resistant, allowing separation (Context [3]).

Furthermore, the combination of polymer and cellulosic materials also contributes to the development of unique dielectric properties [10]. Therefore, we are interested in cellulose materials to enhance the biodegradable plastics dielectric properties for electrical applications.', 'With the rapid advancement of electronic equipment and the increasing emphasis on sustainable development, there is a growing need for high dielectric environmental-friendly materials.1 Polymer materials are widely recognized as suitable candidates for developing dielectric materials due to their desirable properties, such as low dielectric loss, processability, and flexibility.2 Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is suitable as a substrate for polymeric dielectric materials due to its biodegradability and biocompatibility.3 However, low dielectric constant (ε’) and poor toughness limit its application in the electronics industry. The dielectric constant (ε') of pure polylactic acid (PLA) is relatively low, typically in the range of **3–5** at low frequencies (e.g., 1 kHz), which limits its direct application in electronics requiring high dielectric performance. However, through modifications such as **filler incorporation**, **blending with other polymers**, or **biaxial stretching**, the dielectric constant of PLA-based composites can be significantly enhanced. Key findings include:  
- **Unmodified PLA**: Low ε' (~3–5) due to limited polarization from C=O dipoles and molecular rigidity.  
- **PLA composites**:  
  - PLA-MCC/Cu composites achieved ε' = **11.47** (unstretched) and up to **51.05** (4×4 biaxially stretched) [1].  
  - PLA/PCL blends with core-shell Ni-coated fillers (e.g., Ni-GRA) reached ε' = **124.6** at 1 kHz [4].  
  - Blending PLA with PVDF and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) improved ε' from 5.81 to 11.08 [6].  

### Implications for Electronics:  
1. **Energy Storage**: Enhanced ε' enables PLA-based composites (e.g., stretched PDLA films) to achieve high energy densities (~18.5 J/cm³) suitable for capacitors, outperforming PVDF at high temperatures [11].  
2. **Biodegradability**: PLA composites address e-waste challenges by offering eco-friendly alternatives to petroleum-based dielectrics [1, 6].  
3. **Flexibility & Processability**: PLA’s compatibility with fillers (e.g., CNTs, graphene) and polymers (e.g., PCL, PBAT) improves toughness and dielectric properties, enabling use in flexible electronics [2, 4, 12].  
4. **Thermal Stability**: Oriented PLA films retain dielectric performance at elevated temperatures (~100°C), critical for automotive and industrial applications [11].  

### Challenges:  
- **Dispersion & Compatibility**: Agglomeration of fillers (e.g., CNTs) can limit dielectric improvements without compatibilizers [6].  
- **Dielectric Loss**: While composites reduce loss (tan δ < 1 in some cases), balancing high ε' with low loss remains critical [4].  

In summary, PLA’s dielectric constant can be tailored via material engineering, making it a sustainable candidate for capacitors, sensors, and energy storage devices in the electronics industry.

retrieved_contexts: ['The LbL self-assembly method can be used to construct nanoscale ultra-thin films on solid substrates. This strategy is based on electrostatic interactions between polyelectrolytes or other ionic species with opposite charges, which promotes the deposition of materials via alternating adsorption. Specifically, the substrate is alternately exposed to solutions containing positively and negatively charged substances, leading to the spontaneous and orderly adsorption of these substances on the substrate surface to form a highly organized multilayer membrane structure [7] The LbL self-assembly technology applied in this study is characterized by precise microstructural control, high reproducibility, wide material adaptability, broad application prospects, and environmental friendliness [8]. Controllability is a particularly valuable advantage because it enables command over the structural and physicochemical properties of the obtained multilayer films according to the properties of the raw materials and the assembly conditions (e.g., pH, ionic strength, temperature) [9]. To date, the LbL self-assembly strategy has been applied in various fields, including the preparation of anti-corrosion films on the surface of magnesium alloys. For example, Xiao et al. [10] prepared polyelectrolyte-coated magnesium alloys using the LbL self-assembly method with polyallylamine hydrochloride (PAH) and sodium alginate (ALG), which increased the corrosion resistance of magnesium alloys. Chen et al. [11] used phytic acid (PA), branched polyethylenimine (BPEI), and graphene oxide (GO) to prepare films on Mg-1Zn alloys via LbL self-assembly, thereby forming a physical barrier against corrosion. These studies demonstrated that an LbL self-assembled multilayer film can increase the corrosion resistance of magnesium alloys. Despite these promising applications, existing LbL multilayer coatings for magnesium alloy protection still face several critical challenges that limit their practical implementation: (1) the hydrophilic nature of polyelectrolytes makes the coatings susceptible to delamination during prolonged immersion, (2) inadequate interfacial adhesion between the coating and magnesium substrate compromises long-term durability, and (3) the continued use of non-environmental solvent systems in some fabrication processes contradicts the sustainable advantages inherent to LbL technology. Urushiol, a naturally occurring phenolic compound extracted from lacquer trees (Toxicodendron spp.), has gained increasing attention as a sustainable and eco-friendly material for advanced coatings and functional applications [12, 13]. Its unique molecular structure, comprising catechol groups and long alkyl chains (C15-C17 with 0-3 olefins), endows it with intrinsic hydrophobicity and the ability to form dense crosslinked networks upon polymerization, significantly enhancing corrosion resistance and waterproofing properties [14]. Notably, the catechol moieties mimic mussel-adhesive proteins, enabling urushiol to form robust chemical bonds with diverse substrates, including metals, polymers, and inorganic surfaces, thereby improving interfacial adhesion and long-term durability [15]. Beyond its protective capabilities, urushiol exhibits remarkable biological activity, such as antioxidant, antibacterial, and antitumor effects, making it a promising candidate for biomedical and environmental applications [16]. For instance, Fang et al. [17] demonstrated that urushiol-modified melamine sponges (UMS) exhibit excellent hydrophobicity and selective oil-adsorption capacity, while Jie et al. [15] developed chitosan-urushiol nanofiber membranes with enhanced acid resistance and broad-spectrum antimicrobial properties. Given its renewable sourcing, biodegradability, and multifunctionality, urushiol presents a viable green alternative to synthetic coatings, combining environmental sustainability with high-performance material characteristics. To address these persistent challenges in LbL coatings for magnesium alloys, this study proposes an innovative approach by introducing urushiol, a molecule containing catechol groups, as a self-assembly building block. The catechol moieties in urushiol can not only form strong bonds with the magnesium alloy substrate through chelation but also undergo crosslinking reactions during film formation, significantly enhancing coating stability. Based on this design, we report for the first time the LbL assembly of branched polyethyleneimine (BPEI) and urushiol on magnesium alloy surfaces to construct a novel eco-friendly protective coating. This strategy is expected to simultaneously overcome the challenges of weak interfacial adhesion and solvent sustainability, providing new insights for developing high-performance surface coatings for magnesium alloys.', 'The LbL technique as a classical bottom-up technique has emerged recently as widely used method to design material coatings with different molecules, mostly polyelectrolytes (PEL).29 With this technique, chemical cues can be introduced to biomaterial surfaces that address cell receptors.30,31 Moreover, parameters like wetting properties, surface potential, topography, thickness, and viscoelasticity can be regulated by selection of PEL and by control of process parameters during multilayer formation.31-33 In case proteins and glycosaminoglycans (GAG) were used for multilayer assembly, the structure and composition of ECM could be mimicked.33,34 Moreover, the rather high water content of such multilayer systems offers specific viscoelastic properties that can be tailored either by the complexation conditions or by chemical cross-linking.35,36 In previous studies we could show that LIL can be used to design defect-free structures of gold of different size and periodicity on silicon as model surface.24 We could demonstrate further that spreading of human adipose-derived stem cells (hADSC) decreased with increasing feature dimensions, which had an effect on cell differentiation.24 In another study we studied how polyelectrolyte multilayers (PEM) made of hyaluronic acid (HA) and poly-L-lysine (PLL), either as native or cross-linked system varying in elastic modulus, guide hADSC adhesion, growth, and differentiation.37 We found that hADSC spread and grew more on stiffer, highly cross-linked than on soft native PLL/HA multilayers. It was also observed that hADSC moved towards the osteogenic lineage on stiffer and to adipogenic on soft, non-cross-linked multilayers.
