Especially the use of spray-assisted coating of the structured surfaces is reported here for the first time. Hence, a unique system of topographical and viscoelastic cues is generated to study the effect on hADSC adhesion, signal transduction, and cell differentiation. Results are reported herein. Quantitative analysis of AFM and SEM images revealed changes in gold area fraction and surface height profiles after multilayer deposition (Fig. 2). Before multilayer formation, the area fraction of gold structures increased from 17% (L) over 24% (M) to 28% (S) with increasing angle of incidence. After deposition of PLL and HA, the area fraction of the nanofeatures significantly increased on all surfaces, ranging from 20% (L) over 26% (M) to 31% (S), respectively. In addition, an obvious change in the progression of the height profiles was found (Fig. 2B). The height of the largest features significantly increased, while it significantly dropped to a lower value on medium and small features. Thereby, the decrease was largest on the smallest nanostructures.', 'The abuse of traditional plastic food packaging has caused severe food safety and environmental pollution, urgently necessitating the development of green and sustainable biodegradable packaging materials. Chitosan (CS) belongs to an inexpensive and readily available biopolymer; however, the poor mechanical properties and weak resistance to UV light and water make it unsuitable for the food packaging industry. In this study, a layer-by-layer (LBL) assembly of CS decorated with anthocyanins as a polycationic electrolyte and carboxylated graphene oxide (GO-COOH) as a polyanionic electrolyte is used to fabricate bio-based films with the aim of improving comprehensive properties of CS-based films. The results indicate that the LBL assembly extremely enhanced the UV-blocking ability (the average transmittance in the UV-B region drops to 1.68%), tensile strength (TS) (53.52 MPa), toughness (71.81%), thermal stability, water resistance, hydrophobicity (the water contact angle is up to 109.5°), and antioxidant activities of the films, attributed to hydrogen bonds among CS, anthocyanins, and GO-COOH and electrostatic interactions between GO-COOH and CS along with anthocyanins. In addition, the LBL films show exceptional advantages in the storage application for fresh-cut apples. In general, the study demonstrates that a novel and sustainable CS-based film can be fabricated by the LBL technique for food packaging. The carboxylated graphene oxide and chitosan decorated with anthocyanin are deposed by a layer-by-layer assembly to fabricate the bio-based films for food packaging. The films exhibit enhanced mechanical properties, UV-blocking ability, water resistance, and antioxidant as well as unique potential in preserving fresh fruits, thereby providing new strategies for the future development of food packaging.', 'First published on 5th October 2017 The adhesion of bacteria is one of the most important stages in biofilm formation and bacterial infection. Once bacteria have adhered to a biomaterial surface, it is hard to eliminate them, and bacterial growth and infection are inevitable. In the current study, we have designed and constructed enzymatically degradable (hyaluronic acid/chitosan)n-(hyaluronic acid/polylysine)n ((HA/CHI)n-(HA/PLL)n) composite multilayer films via a layer-by-layer self-assembly method. Spectroscopic ellipsometry and scanning electron microscopy cross section measurements showed the exponential growth behavior of (HA/CHI)10-(HA/PLL)10 multilayer films (∼2 μm). The increased secretion of hyaluronidase and chymotrypsin in the bacterial infection microenvironment led to the fast degradation of the outer (PLL/HA)n multilayer films in the first 24 h. Enzymatic degradation of the multilayer films efficiently reduced the adhesion of both Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli (>99%). Bacterial live/dead staining demonstrated the bactericidal action of the remaining bottom (CHI/HA)n multilayer films against the two kinds of bacteria. In vivo subcutaneous tests on New Zealand white rabbits, wound appearance and histopathology analysis showed that the implantation of composite multilayer film-modified PDMS promoted wound healing and the materials demonstrated a self-defense antibacterial effect. The material demonstrated both anti-adhesive and bactericidal properties and could be used to modify biomedical implants. The development of bacterial infections can be divided into three stages: bacterial adhesion, bacterial growth and biofilm formation, among which bacterial adhesion is the first and most crucial stage.5-7 Once bacterial adhesion becomes irreversible, biofilm formation and bacterial infections are inevitable.8-10 To date, many kinds of antibacterial surfaces, including those incorporating conventional anti-adhesive/anti-fouling properties,11,12 bactericidal properties13,14 and the release of antibacterial agents,15,16 have been developed to reduce the incidence of infection. However, it is difficult for antibacterial surfaces with just one type of antibacterial property to produce ideal and long-term efficacy.17-19 For example, hydrophilic coatings (such as polyethylene glycol, polyvinyl alcohol, and polyvinylpyrrolidone) can be contaminated by adhesive proteins, blood platelets and inflammatory cells in body fluids after being implanted in the body and their anti-adhesive properties can be compromised.20-22 In addition, pure bactericidal surfaces without an antifouling function will be covered by the remains of dead bacteria, which can facilitate bacterial adhesion, making the situation worse.23-25 Consequently, bio-inspired antibacterial surfaces, multi-functional composite antimicrobial surfaces and smart antibacterial surfaces that are responsive to the bacterial infection microenvironment have attracted increasing attention.', 'First published on 8th June 2020 The build-up and degradation of cytocompatible nanofilms in a controlled fashion have great potential in biomedical and nanomedicinal fields, including single-cell nanoencapsulation (SCNE). Herein, we report the fabrication of biodegradable films of cationic starch (c-ST) and anionic alginate (ALG) by electrostatically driven layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly technology and its application to the SCNE. The [c-ST/ALG] multilayer nanofilms, assembled either on individual Saccharomyces cerevisiae or on the 2D flat gold surface, degrade on demand, in a cytocompatible fashion, via treatment with α-amylase. Their degradation profiles are investigated, while systematically changing the α-amylase concentration, by several surface characterization techniques, including quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation monitoring (QCM-D) and ellipsometry. DNA incorporation in the LbL nanofilms and its controlled release, upon exposure of the nanofilms to an aqueous α-amylase solution, are demonstrated. The highly cytocompatible nature of the film-forming and -degrading conditions is assessed in the c-ST/ALG-shell formation and degradation of S. cerevisiae. We envisage that the cytocompatible, enzymatic degradation of c-ST-based nanofilms paves the way for developing advanced biomedical devices with programmed dissolution in vivo. Nature-derived biopolymers are strong candidates for the cytocompatible LbL assembly.16,17 Among them, marine polysaccharides, such as alginic acid, chitosan, chondroitin sulfate, heparin, and hyaluronic acid, have widely been employed in the formation of LbL films because of their diversity in chemical composition, properties, and functions.18 In particular, the varied charge identities in marine polysaccharides make them highly suitable for electrostatically driven LbL process.19,20 For instance, alginic acid is negatively charged at the neutral pH,21,22 and chitosan is positively charged under mild acidic conditions.23,24 In comparison, starch (ST), the most abundant polysaccharide in the plant, has scarcely been used for the formation of LbL films due to its low charge density.25-27', 'Biomimetic systems play an important role in biomedical sciences. Native tissues follow a hierarchical conformation and organization, from the nano to macroscales, which are difficult to mimic using conventional methodologies, such as solvent casting, freeze-drying or melt-based technologies. The use of non-physiological processing conditions and also the inability to control spatial distribution over the material triggered urgent investigation for multiscale-based devices for biomedical applications [1], based on both bottom-up and top-down methodologies. The layer-by-layer (LbL) method has been exploited to produce such controllably sized-architectures and has been growing fast [2, 3]. This technique was first suggested by Decher et al [4], and follows a very simple foundation of consecutive and alternative deposition of oppositely charged polyelectrolyte solutions, being usually described as a user-friendly way to prepare thin coatings. LbL technology promises control over the architecture at both nano and microscales, mainly due to the possibility of using different adsorption conditions such as pH, ionic strength, charge density, polymer nature, functionality and concentration [5-9]. Other advantages include the abilities to incorporate different biomolecules, from synthetic [6] to natural polymers [10, 11] and different bioactive agents like growth factors [12], polypeptides [13] and nuclei acids [14], to repeat the process of assembly hundreds of times and to extend from planar substrates [15] to three dimensional (3D) ones [16, 17]. LbL approaches have mostly been applied for surface modification of different substrates; for example, Cai et al [18] improved the biocompatibility of titanium films by modifying their surface with the alternate deposition of chitosan (CHT) and gelatin. The possibility of producing structural 3D systems using such technology has permitted the extension of its applicability in the biomedical field [2]. In particular, efforts have been made to develop freestanding films from polyelectrolyte multilayers (PEMs) [18, 19]. These are obtained by removing the multilayer assembly from a solid substrate, where they were absorbed, using different strategies like neutralization of charged layers, sacrificial layers, dissolution of initial layers or even by applying mechanical forces [15]. Jiang et al [20] took advantage of a sacrificial layer of cellulose acetate to fabricate freely suspended nanocomposite polyelectrolyte membranes. Even so, the use of solvents or even mechanical forces can compromise the morphology and respective integrity of the membrane [15, 21]. To overcome this drawback, the production of easily detachable freestanding membranes was obtained via spontaneous detachment from an underlying low surface energy substrate [22]. The studied membranes were based on the combination of CHT and alginate. Upon crosslinking, the biological properties of the membranes were improved, but their maximum tensile strain decreased significantly [23]. Many biomedical applications require the use of more stretchable membranes, with elastic stretchablility being an important characteristic of the living tissues; thus other polyelectrolyte combinations should be explored. CHT has been broadly studied with LbL approaches, with many prospective works revealing its high potential for biomedical and tissue engineering applications [24, 25]. Furthermore, CHT is a positively charged biopolymer, widely available from natural resources, biodegradable and is also a nontoxic compound [26]. Besides alginate, other natural polymers have been combined with CHT; Schneider and her group [27] combined CHT with hyaluronic acid to observe the improvements on cell viability, elasticity and biodegradability and Neto et al [28] functionalized hyaluronic acid with dopamine to obtain a bioactive LbL coating, with more adhesive properties. Chondroitin sulfate (CS) is a naturally-derived polyanion and constituent of an extracellular matrix, with an important role in the elasticity and function of cartilage and connective tissues [29, 30]: we combined CHT and CS to produce reservoirs for calcium phosphate biomineralization [31] and to fabricate 3D, highly porous scaffolds [32].', 'The second strategy for triggering the release by biochemical process is through the enzymatic action on biofunctional materials. This occurs in those cases in which some of the molecules can act as substrates for enzymes [179], several examples of LbL materials built by polypeptides or polysaccharides has been tested successfully against enzymatic release, e.g. materials formed by poly(lactic acid) and PEI are easily degraded due to the action of the α-chymotrypsin [180] or capsules formed by dextran sulfate and CHI can be degraded by Chitonase [110]. In real systems, it has been found that capsules formed by poly(l-arginine) and dextran sulfate are easily degraded in vivo by the action of proteases after being included by different types of cell [181]. Degradation of microcapsules made of biopolymers after internalization by cells was also demonstrated for hyaluronic acid (HA)/PLL capsules [180], suggesting their potential as carrier for intracellular drug delivery. Design and enzymatic degradation by α-chymotrypsin of multilayer assemblies made of biodegradable PLA NP was reported recently by Orozco et al. [181]. The biodegradation process was colorimetrically monitored with UV-vis spectroscopy thus opening the way for facile and real-time monitoring applicable for biotechnology. Cookie Settings', "Layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly is a versatile technique based initially on the adsorption of oppositely charged polyelectrolytes (PELs) on a substrate.1 LbL assembly was designed in the first place for macroscopic surfaces.2 Recently, coating of nanoparticles (NPs) with PELs using the LbL technique has received great interest due to the advantage of obtaining NPs with controlled surface properties. Indeed, the shell can be tuned in thickness, composition, and functionality by choosing various constituents and adjusting the layer number, offering several applications in the biomedical and pharmaceutical field such as drug3 and siRNA delivery.4 Generally, core-shell NPs obtained via the LbL self-assembly technique are formed by the consecutive deposition of polymers interacting through intermolecular forces such as electrostatic interactions5 or hydrogen bonding.6 So far, a wide range of synthetic PELs such as poly(diallyl-dimethyl-ammonium chloride),7 poly(ethyleneimine),3 poly(allylamine) hydrochloride,8 poly(styrenesulfonate),8 and poly(acrylic acid)3 or natural PELs like alginate or chitosan5 have been studied to build several layers onto NPs. The buildup of multilayers could be monitored using several characterization techniques such as fluorescence,8 dynamic light scattering (DLS),9 ζ-potential,10 UV and IR spectroscopy11 or gravimetric analysis using a quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) dissipation.9 Inorganic cores such as gold12 or magnetic NPs13 are usually reported as they display several advantages like superior mechanical and thermal stabilities14 compared with the cores based on a polymeric system as micelles,6 liposomes,5 microcapsules,15 nanocapsules,16 microparticles,17 or NPs.11, 18 However, the major interest of using polymer cores lies in their ability to load lipophilic drugs. For biomedical applications, polymers should display biocompatibility and biodegradability properties. Hence, ideal candidates could be biodegradable polyesters polymer such as poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA),3, 9 poly(lactic acid) (PLA),18 or poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV).15, 19 In drug delivery, particularly, LbL self-assembly is an appealing technique to extend drug action. Indeed, by controlling the layer number, it becomes possible to reduce the initial burst release.3 In our previous work,20 core-shell NPs have been designed and fully characterized. They are based on a hydrophobic and biodegradable PLA core and an adsorbed neutral β-cyclodextrin polymer (poly-β-CD) shell. β-Cyclodextrins (β-CDs) are torus-shaped cyclic oligosaccharides composed of seven d-glucopyranose residues, which have a hydrophilic exterior and a relatively hydrophobic internal cavity.21 We have demonstrated that benzophenone (BP), a lipophilic molecule, can be incorporated into these NPs and we have investigated the release mechanisms.22 It has been shown that the release was mainly controlled by the diffusion of BP through the NPs and by its host-guest interaction with the β-CD cavities present at the surface of the NPs. Quantitative analysis in terms of diffusion coefficient and equilibrium constant determinations have indicated that the poly-β-CD layer played a major role in the control of the release. Core-shell NPs bearing β-cyclodextrin polymers have also been reported in Ma's group.23, 24 These NPs, though assembled via host-guest associations, have shown sustained release as well. Further studies have also reported the incorporation of β-cyclodextrin polymers into LbL films using either electrostatic interactions, for instance, between a cationic polymer and a neutral β-cyclodextrin polymer complexing low-molecular-weight polyanions25 or host-guest interactions between a β-cyclodextrin polymer and an amphiphilic polymer-bearing guest groups.26 In the latter case, the growing of the multilayer films was limited to 3-4 layers because of the competition between host-guest associations in solution and at interfaces. In the present work, an electrostatic association process was chosen to grow LbL onto the NPs. The performance of this kind of core-shell NPs is essentially related to the concentration of β-CD on the shell surface. Thus, the main objective of this work was to design NPs with larger amount of β-CD on the surface of the PLA NPs by using the LbL technique allowing a better control of the release of the encapsulated molecule. This paper starts with the description of the synthesis of the anionic and cationic β-CD polymers and the buildup of the LbL shell. 1. **Multilayer Formation**: Alternately exposing the biodegradable substrate to solutions containing cationic and anionic components (e.g., chitosan, alginate, carboxylated graphene oxide, or urushiol), which adsorb spontaneously to form a structured, nanoscale multilayer film. For example, chitosan (polycation) and graphene oxide (polyanion) form hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions to enhance UV-blocking, mechanical strength, and water resistance in biodegradable films [3, 6].

2. **Tailored Functionality**: Adjusting assembly conditions (pH, ionic strength, temperature) and material selection to control film properties. For instance:
   - **Barrier Properties**: Polycaprolactone (PCL) and chitosan layers improve oxygen and water vapor barrier performance in biodegradable films [11].
   - **Corrosion/Fire Resistance**: Ammonium polyphosphate (polyanion) and chitosan coatings on magnesium alloys or cotton reduce corrosion/flame spread via condensed-phase char formation and gas-phase inhibition [1, 10].
   - **Biomedical Applications**: Enzymatically degradable hyaluronic acid/chitosan multilayers exhibit anti-adhesive and bactericidal effects for implants, while cytocompatible cationic starch/alginate films enable controlled drug release [4, 5].

3. **Enhanced Biodegradability**: Using natural or biodegradable polymers (e.g., chitosan, alginate, PLA) ensures environmental sustainability. For example, chitosan-based LbL films maintain biodegradability while improving mechanical and barrier properties [3, 6, 11].

4. **Scalability and Adaptability**: Techniques like spray-assisted LbL or slot-die coating enable large-scale production of functional coatings without compromising biodegradability, as seen in waterborne layered films for packaging [13].

The **drug release mechanism** from a surface-eroding polyanhydride wafer involves **surface hydrolysis of anhydride linkages**, leading to **layer-by-layer polymer erosion** that releases the drug. This process is governed by:  

1. **Surface Erosion Dominance**:  
   - Polyanhydrides degrade **primarily at the surface** due to the slower water penetration into the polymer matrix compared to the rapid hydrolysis of anhydride bonds ([2], [8]).  
   - Degradation progresses inward, maintaining a constant surface area over time, resulting in a **release rate proportional to the wafer’s surface area** ([1], [2]).  

2. **Combined Diffusion and Erosion**:  
   - Drug release occurs via **diffusion** of the drug molecule through the polymer matrix **and simultaneous polymer erosion** ([1], [5]).  
   - Unlike bulk-eroding polymers (e.g., polyesters), surface erosion minimizes bulk water uptake, reducing rapid, uncontrolled drug release ([5], [6]).  

3. **Controlled Release Factors**:  
   - **Polymer structure/composition**: Hydrophobic components (e.g., CPP, SA) slow degradation, while hydrophilic modifications (e.g., PEG) alter erosion rates and hydrophilicity ([3], [4], [7]).  
   - **Crystallinity** and **device geometry** (e.g., wafer thickness, surface area) directly impact erosion kinetics ([2], [8]).  
   - **Environmental conditions** (pH, enzymes) can catalyze hydrolysis or enzymatic degradation ([1], [14]).  

4. **Sustained Release Profile**:  
   - The surface-eroding mechanism avoids an initial burst release, enabling **linear or near-zero-order kinetics** over days to weeks ([2], [7]).  
   - Example: Poly(CPP:SA) systems release chemotherapeutics like BCNU for brain cancer treatment via this mechanism ([3], [8]).  

In summary, drug release from polyanhydride wafers is **dominated by surface hydrolysis-driven erosion**, with release kinetics tunable via polymer design and environmental factors.
